The `remember` is doing real work here — the call happens once per `userId` instead of on every execution — and the code is still wrong. A blocking read now sits on the thread running composition; the call cannot be cancelled when the screen goes away; there is no loading or error state, because a composable body has nowhere to express one; and if the composable leaves the Composition and is re-entered, the work starts again from nothing. Memoization made the symptom rarer and left every one of those properties exactly as it found them.

Using `remember` as a substitute for placement — "I wrapped the call in `remember`, so it only runs once." Running once was not the property that was missing. What was missing is an owner that outlives the screen, can report loading and failure, and can be cancelled; and no cache placed **inside** the thing that is supposed to be cancelled can supply any of it.

There is a second separation to make, and getting it wrong is the most common way a fix fails to fix anything. **Moving work to a `ViewModel` or a use case moves the responsibility. It does not move the thread.** A function called from a `ViewModel` runs on whatever thread called it, and that is very often the main thread. Kotlin's guidance puts the duty with the code doing the work rather than with its caller: a class performing long-running blocking operations is in charge of moving execution off the main thread, and that applies to every class in the app regardless of which part of the architecture it sits in. Memoization is not background execution either — `remember` runs its lambda synchronously, during composition, on composition's thread.

Which coroutine builder, which dispatcher, and which effect API carries suspending work into a composable are real questions with careful answers, and they belong to the effects and coroutine material later in this path. What this lesson needs from them is only the boundary: "somewhere else" and "some other thread" are two decisions, and making one does not make the other.

The layering argument is short, and it stops early on purpose. The UI layer's job is to consume application data, convert it into something the UI can present, and display it; the state holder — usually a `ViewModel` at screen level — is the class responsible for producing that state and for the logic that produces it; business logic is placed in the domain or data layers and never in the UI layer. That is enough to answer "not in the composable". It is deliberately not enough to answer "therefore write a use case".

The domain layer is documented as optional. The guidance says plainly that not every app needs one, that use cases should be added only when required — for complex business logic, or simple logic reused by several state holders — and that the cost of ignoring this is being forced to add use cases that are simple pass-through calls to the data layer, complexity for little benefit. So "move it out of the composable" does not resolve to a fixed destination. Four questions decide it, and they are worth asking in this order.

items: **Cost.** How expensive is one execution, and is it on a path that runs often? A cheap calculation on a screen that rarely recomposes has no problem to solve.
**Lifetime.** How long must the result outlive whatever produced it? Anything that has to survive longer than a composable's presence in the Composition cannot be owned by a composable.
**Reuse.** Does anything else need the same answer? A second consumer is the clearest signal that a calculation is not presentation.
**Responsibility.** Does this describe the data or decide what it means? Decisions about meaning are business logic, and that is the one band with no discretion.

blocks.text: None of that is a measurement, and saying so matters. The costs described throughout this unit are engineering reasoning about where work sits and how often it repeats — illustrative, not benchmarked — and nothing here claims how many milliseconds any of it takes. Unit 3's standard for turning an observation into a finding is unchanged and applies to placement too: a symptom someone could notice, expensive work identified on the path that produces it, and a causal link between the two. Restructuring code because a diagram says it belongs elsewhere, with no symptom and no measurement, is the same mistake as chasing a recomposition count.

The mirror-image error deserves an equally clear warning, because this lesson is the one most likely to cause it. "All calculations must leave composition" is not the conclusion. A screen that formats two fields and picks a colour from a status has nothing to move, and moving it produces a state holder that exists to perform string concatenation. The genuinely interesting cases feel obvious in hindsight because they fail several of the four questions at once: expensive, needed beyond this screen, wanted by more than one consumer, and a decision about data rather than a description of it.

The question arrives as "how do you handle an expensive operation in a composable?", and the checklist answer — `remember`, `derivedStateOf`, stability — is the weak one, because it never asks what the operation is. Split it instead: cheap presentation stays and is calculated directly; a repeated pure transformation is memoized against its inputs; anything that reads, writes or decides belongs above the UI and arrives at the screen as state. Then add the sentence most candidates miss — moving it to a `ViewModel` changes who owns it, not which thread it runs on, and main-safety is the responsibility of the code doing the work.

units.title: Snapshot Fundamentals
units.summary: Four units have each answered a different question, and every answer rested on the same unstated machinery: something has to notice that a value changed and work out who cared. This unit names that machinery and stops there. One model — state objects that report reads and changes, contexts that record reads while they run, and invalidation that marks whoever recorded one — explains why the counter did not count, why the list did not appear, why moving a read moved the blast radius, and why a derived value can decline to wake its reader. The second lesson takes the same model somewhere the UI is not, turning observable state into a `Flow` a coroutine can process.

lessons.title: How Compose Observes State
lessons.summary: The last four units each ended with a rule. All of them come from one mechanism: state objects that report reads and changes, a context that is recording reads while it runs, and invalidation that marks whoever recorded one as out of date. What that model promises, what it does not, and how to use it to find the cause of an update that never arrived.

blocks.text: Each of the last four units left you holding a rule. A plain `var` changes and the screen does not. Adding to a list held in state updates nothing. Moving a read into a child narrows how much re-executes. A derived value can decline to wake the composable reading it. Those read like four separate facts about four separate APIs. They are one mechanism seen from four angles, and this lesson names it.

The mechanism is the **snapshot system**, and the first thing to understand about it is that Compose's state objects are not ordinary containers. The values produced by `mutableStateOf`, `mutableStateListOf`, `mutableStateMapOf` and `derivedStateOf` report what happens to them. When one of them is read, whatever is currently recording reads is told which object was read. When one of them is changed, everything that recorded a read of it is marked out of date.
Four things therefore have to line up before anything appears on screen.

items: **An observable state object.** Only Compose's own state types take part. An `Int` field, an `ArrayList`, a `var` on a class you wrote — none of them can report anything, so none of them is inside this mechanism at all.

**A read that happens inside an observing context.** An observing context is code that is recording reads while it runs: a composable executing during composition, a `derivedStateOf` calculation, and — as the next lesson shows — a `snapshotFlow` block. Reading the same object from a click handler, or from an ordinary function running outside any observing context, returns the current value and records no dependency. An ordinary helper called during composition does participate in the caller's observing context, as Unit 3 explained.

**A change the state object agrees is a change.** `mutableStateOf` compares the new value against the current one with structural equality by default, so assigning a value equal to the one already held is not a change and is never reported.
**Invalidation.** What a reported change actually does is mark the contexts that recorded a read as out of date. It does not run them, and it certainly does not draw anything.

blocks.text: That last point is the one worth slowing down on, because the word people reach for is "refresh" and nothing about a write refreshes anything. A write is a recording, not a command. It leaves behind the information that some set of contexts is now describing an old value, and the runtime decides when to act on that — possibly coalescing several changes that arrive together into one pass. Composition is also only the first of three phases, with layout and drawing after it, so "the screen has caught up" is a strictly later event than "a write happened".

Observation is a relationship between a state object and a read, established at the moment of the read, by whichever context was recording at the time. Declaring state, passing it as a parameter, and writing to it all create nothing. This is why "why didn't my UI update?" almost always resolves into one of two findings: no observable change was reported, or the read that would have recorded the dependency happened somewhere other than where you assumed.

Two assumptions are worth stating plainly, because the model is easy to over-generalise in both directions. Not every read subscribes anything: a read outside an observing context is just a read. And not every write produces an update: a write of an equal value is not a change, and a genuine change that no context ever read invalidates nobody.

The quickest way to make the model usable is to take three screens that fail in exactly the same visible way — a value demonstrably changes and the UI does not move — and find a different cause in each.

`Cart` is an ordinary class. Its field can be read inside a composable perfectly well, and that read is recorded against nothing, because there is nothing in an ordinary field to do the reporting. Measured on this project's JVM target: after the field was changed from 0 to 1, the composable did not execute again, and reading the field afterwards confirmed it really did hold 1. No part of the mechanism was ever involved.

This one is more interesting, because a state object *is* present and the composable *is* reading it — `items.value` is a genuine recorded read. Measured on the same target: after `add`, the list held two elements and the composable still did not execute again. The dependency was recorded on the holder, and the holder was never written. `add` changed the object the holder points at, which the holder has no way to notice. This is the failure Unit 2's lesson on collections and observable mutation exists for, and its three fixes live there.

State object, recorded read, and a write that reaches the holder — and still nothing. Measured: assigning 0 to a state already holding 0 produced no execution at all, while the assignment of 1 that followed produced one. The default policy compares with structural equality, an equal value is not a change, and there was consequently nothing to report.

No
No — there is nothing to record against
No
Nothing updates, and the value really did change
Mutates a collection held inside a state object
Yes
Yes, of the holder
No — the holder itself was never written
Nothing updates, and the collection really did grow

blocks.text: Those four rows diagnose those four examples, and that is exactly the limit of what this lesson claims. "Nothing observable was written" is the first thing to check and it is not a universal explanation for stale UI. A composable can lose its state because its identity changed rather than because a write was missed. A `remember` can hand back a stale result because a captured value was never made a key. A change can be reported correctly and the consumer still be skipped because its parameters compared equal. Those are the identity, stability and derived-state units' subjects, and they are separate failures with separate fixes. What this model gives you is the question that tells them apart: was a change reported at all? If it was, the problem is downstream of observation and this is not the lesson you need.

Reading "invalidated" as "executed". An invalidated scope is scheduled, not run, and how many times it eventually runs is not something to reason about: changes that land together can be coalesced into a single pass, and a call whose inputs did not change can be skipped inside that pass. Reason about which contexts a change *can* invalidate, which is well defined, and stop there.

Derived state is not an exception to any of this, and noticing that is what makes the model feel like one idea rather than a list. `derivedStateOf` produces a state object, so reading its value inside a composable records a dependency exactly as reading a `mutableStateOf` does. Its calculation is itself an observing context, which is why the state the calculation reads is what the derived value depends on — and why a value the calculation merely closed over is not. And the reason a derived value can withhold an update is the third item in the list above: before invalidating a context that read the result, the runtime compares the new result against the one that context last saw, and an equal result is not a change. One mechanism, applied at two levels.

The name is worth unpacking, because "snapshot" is not decoration. A snapshot is a view of the values of state objects, and the guarantee the runtime documents for it is narrow and precise: every state object has the same value inside the snapshot that it had when the snapshot was taken, unless it is explicitly changed inside that snapshot. Code reading state inside one is therefore pinned to a single version of the world — a write landing elsewhere while it reads does not change what it sees partway through.

Be careful how far you carry that, because it is the sentence most likely to be over-claimed in an interview. The guarantee is about state objects — the values held by `mutableStateOf`, the snapshot-aware collections, and derived state. It does not make your own classes transactional, it does not make an `ArrayList` safe to share between threads, and it does not turn an ordinary object graph into anything it was not before. An object reached *through* a state object is still just an object; only the holder takes part. That is the same boundary as the collection failure above, seen from the other side.

What consistency buys, and the reason it belongs in a lesson about observation at all, is that reading Compose state from somewhere that is not composition is a reasonable thing to do: a reader is never handed a value that shifts underneath it mid-read. The next lesson is built directly on that property.

There is a second limit, and it is the one that actually bites in production code. The guarantee is about one version of the values; it is not a guarantee about one *update* of yours. Two ordinary assignments to two state holders are two separate changes, and an observer that gets a chance to run between them sees the first holder's new value beside the second holder's old one. Measured on this project's JVM target: a reader of both holders observed the pair `(1, 0)` between `(0, 0)` and `(1, 1)` when each write was applied before the next was made, and observed only `(0, 0)` and `(1, 1)` when both writes landed before either was applied. The second outcome is a scheduling accident rather than a promise, so it is not something to design around. When two values form one invariant, the answer is not to hope they are written closely enough together — it is to put them in one state object, so that changing them is a single assignment of a single new value. That is the conclusion Unit 2 reached about collections and nested data, arriving here from the other direction.

The design question worth being able to answer is why the system records reads at all, when the write is the thing that actually happens. The answer is that a write knows nothing useful. A state object has no idea which parts of a UI display it; only the act of reading, performed by code that was recording at the time, establishes that relationship. Recording reads is therefore the only way to get invalidation proportional to what is genuinely affected instead of proportional to the size of the tree. It is also why the same machinery extends past composition: anything that can record reads can be a dependent, whether that is a composable, a derived calculation, the layout and drawing phases that track their own reads, or a coroutine building a stream.

Expect "how does Compose know when to recompose?" and answer it as a mechanism rather than an API list. State objects report reads and writes; a read performed while an observing context is running records that context as a dependent; a change — a write the state object's own policy agrees is a change — invalidates the contexts that recorded a read, which schedules them rather than running them. Then volunteer the boundaries, because that is what separates the model from the slogan: a read outside an observing context records nothing, an equal write is not a change, and mutation reached through a state object is invisible to it. If pushed on snapshot consistency, say plainly what it is and what it is not: it is about state objects rather than your own data structures, and it pins a reader to one version rather than making an update spread across several writes atomic.

lessons.title: `snapshotFlow` and Crossing Into Flow
lessons.summary: Sometimes the code that has to react to a UI value is not UI: an analytics call, a draft that saves itself, a request that follows the scroll position. `snapshotFlow` turns observable Compose state into a cold `Flow` a coroutine can process — what it evaluates and when, why its emissions are not a record of everything that happened, and where the collector's lifetime comes from.

blocks.text: Every consumer so far has had the same shape: a composable that reads state and describes UI from it. Some consumers are not that. An analytics event should be sent the first time the user scrolls past the top of a list. A draft should be saved a second after typing stops. A search request should be issued when the query settles. None of those describe UI, all of them need to know when a UI-owned value changed, and none of them can be a composable — composition is for describing, not for doing.
What that kind of consumer wants is a stream it can filter, transform, delay and suspend on. Kotlin already has one, `Flow`, and `snapshotFlow` is the adapter between the two worlds.

Four facts about `Flow` are enough for this lesson to stand on its own. The full subject is taught by the Flow Fundamentals unit of this curriculum: the first two facts are its treatment of cold flows, and the last two its treatment of collection lifetime and cancellation, both linked below. Operators, hot streams and sharing, and back pressure follow in the units after it.

items: **A cold flow produces nothing until it is collected.** The code inside the builder does not run when the flow is created. It runs when a collector arrives, and each new collector starts an independent execution.

**Collection is what starts it.** `collect` is a suspending call, so it needs a coroutine, and it does not return until the flow completes or the coroutine is cancelled. A `snapshotFlow` never completes on its own.
**The collector's lifetime is the coroutine's lifetime.** Whatever launched the collecting coroutine is what decides how long collection lasts.
**Stopping collection means cancelling that coroutine.** Collection stops and the `snapshotFlow` unsubscribes from the state it had been watching. There is nothing to dispose by hand.

blocks.text: With that in place, `snapshotFlow { }` is short to describe. It takes a block, and:

items: when collection begins it runs the block once and emits the result, unconditionally — the first value does not wait for anything to change;
while the block runs, it records which snapshot state the block read, which makes the block an observing context in exactly the sense of the previous lesson;
when a change is applied to any state the block read, it runs the block again and records the reads again;
it emits the new result only if that result is not equal to the last one it emitted. The documentation compares this to `distinctUntilChanged`, and the comparison really is `equals`.

blocks.text: `firstVisibleItemIndex` is snapshot state owned by the list state, and it is read **inside** the block. That is the whole reason it becomes a dependency: the block is the observing context, and the read happened while the block was running. Everything after `snapshotFlow` in that chain is ordinary `Flow`, doing ordinary `Flow` things.

`snapshotFlow` is the previous lesson's model with a different kind of dependent attached. The block plays the part the composable played: it reads state while something is recording, so a reported change re-runs it. What is new is only the destination — instead of invalidating a scope that will describe UI, the result travels to a coroutine as a `Flow` value.

A cold flow needs a collector, and the collector needs a coroutine whose lifetime is tied to the UI that produced the value. Inside composition that is `LaunchedEffect`: it launches a coroutine when it enters the Composition, cancels that coroutine when it leaves, and — if it is recomposed with different keys — cancels the running one and launches a new one. That is as much as this lesson needs; the effect APIs as a family, and how to choose between them, are a later unit's subject.

The keys in `LaunchedEffect(listState, analytics)` are doing real work, and getting them wrong is a correctness bug rather than a style point. The coroutine captures both values, and a captured value stays frozen for as long as that coroutine lives — the same capture problem `remember` and `derivedStateOf` have. In the snippet above `listState` comes from `rememberLazyListState()`, so it is stable for the life of that call site, while `analytics` is a parameter a caller can change at any recomposition: keyed only on `listState`, the effect would go on reporting to the `Analytics` it captured first. Hoist that list state to a caller and the mirror-image failure becomes possible too — an effect still watching the previous list's scroll position. The rule transfers without having to work out which holders happen to be stable today: key on every holder the effect must not outlive.
The mistake that produces the most confusing behaviour, though, is not about keys. It is about which side of the block the state is read on.

This compiles, it runs, and it emits exactly one value and then nothing ever again. By the time the block sees `index` it is an ordinary `Int`; the read that could have recorded a dependency happened in the composable, so the block reads no snapshot state at all. Measured on this project's JVM target: a block returning a captured plain value evaluated once, emitted once, and was never evaluated again after the underlying state changed. Note what this does *not* say — capturing a value is not a defect in itself and an ordinary captured value is not somehow half-observable. It is simply not observable. There is also a second, quieter cost here: the composable now reads `firstVisibleItemIndex` itself, so it is invalidated by every scrolled row, which is precisely what routing the value through a flow was supposed to avoid.
A subtler version of the same question arrives as soon as the state is a snapshot-aware collection, and it is worth being explicit about because the intuitive code is the wrong code.

The first block returns the `SnapshotStateList` reference without reading its contents, so two things go wrong at once and either alone would be fatal. No element read is recorded, so a change to the list never re-runs the block; and if it did re-run, the value it produced would be the same object it produced last time, equal to itself, so the emission would be suppressed anyway. Measured on this project's JVM target: adding an element after collection began produced no further evaluation and no further emission. The second block calls `toList()`, which reads the contents — creating the dependency — and returns an immutable list that genuinely differs from the previous one; the same measurement gave two evaluations and two emissions. This is not a trick to memorise: the runtime's own documentation for `SnapshotStateList.toList()` recommends it specifically for returning the value of the list from a `snapshotFlow`, and records that it is an O(1) operation returning the immutable list used internally rather than copying anything.
With that settled, the comparison people actually reach for — `snapshotFlow` or `derivedStateOf`? — turns out not to be a close call, because the two are not competing for the same job.

rows: Who consumes the result
Composition — a composable reads it
A coroutine — a collector receives it
What it produces
A `State<T>`
A cold `Flow<T>`
What it is for
Keeping a reading scope from being invalidated while the answer is unchanged
Applying stream processing — `map`, `filter`, `debounce`, suspend calls — to a changing value
What starts it
Reading the value
Collecting the flow
Where it lives
In the Composition, held by a `remember`
In a coroutine, held by whatever launched it

blocks.text: The single question that decides between them is who is on the other end. If a composable is going to read the answer, you want observable state and `derivedStateOf` is the tool that can filter its invalidations. If a coroutine is going to process the answer, you want a stream. Two things are true of both and worth saying out loud: neither is a persistence mechanism — nothing either produces outlives the Composition or the coroutine holding it — and neither moves work to another thread for you. A `snapshotFlow` collector runs in whatever context its coroutine was given, so if the work it does is not safe on the main thread, arranging a dispatcher is your job.

Using `snapshotFlow` as a record of what happened. It is a stream of *states*, not of *events*, and the runtime's documentation is unusually direct about the difference: state changes are conflated, only the most recent state matters, and an observer may legitimately skip intermediate values or see the same value twice. If a value moves through 0, 1, 2, 3 faster than the collector is scheduled, seeing only 0 and 3 is correct behaviour rather than a dropped event. Anything that must record every transition — an undo stack, an audit trail, a keystroke log — has to be fed where the change is made, not observed afterwards.
Evaluations of the block, writes to the state, and emissions to the collector are three different counts, and expecting them to line up is where most of the surprising behaviour comes from.

Measured on this project's JVM target, with the collector already running before any change was made and each change allowed to be applied and the scheduler allowed to settle before the next one, unless a row says otherwise:

items: A block returning an `Int` state: one evaluation and one emission when collection began, then one evaluation and one emission for the change that followed.
The same block, then assigned the value the state already held: no evaluation and no emission at all. An equal write is not a change, so nothing was ever reported.

A block returning `index > 2`, with the index driven through 1, 2, 3 and 4: five evaluations and two emissions. Every reported change re-ran the block; only the two results that differed from the previous one were emitted.

The `Int` block of the first row again, with 1, 2 and 3 written with no opportunity to settle in between: two evaluations and two emissions, the second carrying 3. The values 1 and 2 were read by nobody.

blocks.text: The first and last rows use the identical block, and the only difference between them is whether each write was allowed to be applied before the next one was made — which is what decides whether the collector sees every value or only the latest. Those numbers therefore describe when things were observed at least as much as they describe the code, which is why the runtime's documentation declines to promise any of them: the block "may run more than once for equal sets of inputs or only once after many rapid snapshot changes".

That sentence is also the reason for the constraint on what the block may contain. Because it can run an unpredictable number of times, it must be idempotent and free of side effects — and Compose enforces the strong half of that rather than trusting you with it. The block runs inside a read-only snapshot, and writing snapshot state from within it fails collection with an `IllegalStateException`; running that case on this project's JVM target produces exactly that, with the message `Cannot modify a state object in a read-only snapshot`. Which rules out the tempting debugging move of counting evaluations by incrementing a counter held in state. Keep the calculation a calculation and do the work in the collector, where side effects belong.

The deeper framing behind all of it is in the runtime's own words, and it is a good thing to be able to say: observable state is a lossy compression of the events that produced it. An event happens at a point in time and every one of them may carry meaning, so an observer of events must see all of them. State is only ever the latest value, so an observer of state has to be able to arrive late and still be correct. `snapshotFlow` models snapshot changes as events, but what it is observing is state, so the events it can offer are conflated by construction. That is a property of the thing being observed, not a limitation waiting to be worked around.

Expect the identification question — which API turns Compose `State` into a cold `Flow` — and answer it, but do not stop there, because it tests recall rather than understanding. Say what the block is: an observing context whose reads become the flow's dependencies, which is why the state has to be read *inside* it rather than captured from outside. Say what governs emission: the block re-runs on a reported change and emits only when its result is not equal to the previous one. Say where collection lives and what ends it: a coroutine, usually launched by `LaunchedEffect` and keyed on the holders it captures, cancelled when that effect leaves the Composition. Then give the boundary unprompted — conflated states rather than an event log — because that is the reasoning that decides whether `snapshotFlow` is the right tool for the problem in front of you.

units.title: Production Screen State and Unidirectional Data Flow
units.summary: A production screen contains several kinds of state at once, and correctness depends on giving each one the owner whose readers, writers and lifetime require it. This unit applies the earlier state-hoisting and state-down/events-up foundations to one complete question-library screen: local element state, state coordinated inside a Compose subtree, one immutable screen value from an outside owner, a stateless rendering boundary, intent callbacks, and the precise lifetime that an outside owner does and does not provide.

lessons.title: Three Classes of State on One Screen
lessons.summary: A realistic question-library screen needs local menu state, a filter shared by sibling composables, and question data supplied by a screen-level owner at the same time. Place each value by applying the reader, writer and lifetime tests, then make the costs of putting it one level too low or several levels too high concrete.

blocks.text: The earlier state-hoisting lesson asks where one value should live. A production screen asks a larger question: what happens when several values with different responsibilities share the same screen? Treating the whole screen as one ownership problem is how teams end up with either a child that cannot coordinate with its siblings or a screen-level owner that contains every open menu and visual toggle. The right result usually has more than one owner.

Use the three tests you already know: who reads this value, who writes it, and how long must it live? They are applied here, not derived again; `lesson_state_hoisting` contains the full ownership argument. Consider a question-library screen with a difficulty menu, a result count, a list of interview questions, saved-question markers, and retry when loading fails. Three pieces of state on that one screen have three different answers.

rows: Whether the difficulty menu is expanded
Only `DifficultyMenu` reads it and its button and dismissal callback write it
Only while that menu is composed; closing or recreating it may reset the detail
Local to `DifficultyMenu`
The selected difficulty filter
The filter control writes it; the result count and question list both read it
While this screen's Compose subtree remains the owner; no application rule depends on it
Hoisted to the lowest composable above those siblings
Loaded questions, saved markers and load failure
The whole screen reads them; retry and save intents start changes whose source is outside the UI
For the lifetime promised by the screen-level owner, including times when this destination is retained but not composed
A screen-level owner outside the Composition

blocks.text: The first row is meaningful state even though it stays local. It changes what the user sees and accepts input, but no sibling coordinates through it and no longer-lived owner needs it. Production Compose does not mean moving every value into a ViewModel or another state holder. It means making each lifetime and write path deliberate.

A production screen can correctly have all three at once: local UI-element state, state hoisted only far enough to coordinate a subtree, and screen state supplied by an owner outside the Composition. `ViewModel` is not a synonym for production, and upward is not the goal. The goal is the lowest sensible owner that satisfies reads, writes, coordination and required lifetime.

A value placed too low fails visibly. If `DifficultyMenu` owns the selected filter as well as its expanded flag, the result count and list cannot read the same selection. Copying the selection into each child creates several truths; threading it sideways creates hidden coordination. The selected filter must move to their common Compose parent because several siblings read it and one of them writes it.

The opposite failure is quieter. Suppose every UI detail is pushed into the outside owner because the screen is considered important enough to deserve one. Its state and event surface might become this:

blocks.code:
data class QuestionLibraryState(
    val questions: List<QuestionItem>,
    val savedIds: Set<QuestionId>,
    val selectedLevel: QuestionLevel,
    val isDifficultyMenuExpanded: Boolean,
    val isHelpTextExpanded: Boolean,
    val pressedQuestionId: QuestionId?,
)

@Composable
fun DifficultyMenu(
    selectedLevel: QuestionLevel,
    expanded: Boolean,
    onExpandedChange: (Boolean) -> Unit,
    onLevelSelected: (QuestionLevel) -> Unit,
) { /* ... */ }

items: The screen state is inflated with menu, help-text and press details that have nothing to do with producing question data.
Purely local interactions require owner methods and callbacks, so the parameter list grows with implementation details rather than screen intent.
Changing the menu implementation now changes the outside owner's contract and every caller that wires it.
Updates to unrelated local details travel through the screen-level state and its consumers instead of staying inside the smallest affected subtree.
Those details inherit the owner's longer lifetime even though their readers and writers disappear with one element.

blocks.text: Return `isDifficultyMenuExpanded`, `isHelpTextExpanded` and press interaction state to the elements that use them. Keep `selectedLevel` at the common Compose parent unless a real product rule or required lifetime makes the outside owner a reader or writer. Keep loaded questions and saved markers at screen level because the UI does not produce those values by itself. This is a concrete reduction in coupling, ownership surface and lifetime, not merely less boilerplate.

"Hoist state as high as possible" turns a direction into a policy and loses the stopping condition. Moving a value upward is justified only until all necessary readers and writers share one owner and the required lifetime is met. Past that point, every extra level is additional coupling.

The difficult cases are not decided by whether a value looks visual. The selected difficulty is visual in this example, so the Compose subtree can own it. If selecting a difficulty starts a server query, changes a persisted preference, or must be restored after this subtree is removed, the readers, writers or lifetime have changed and screen-level ownership may become correct. The same field can have a different owner under a different requirement.

That is also why ownership should be justified from the requirement rather than from a type name. A `Boolean` can represent a local menu expansion or a business decision; a data class can be local UI logic or screen-level state. The owner follows coordination and lifetime, not apparent complexity.

Given several values on one screen, classify each independently. State what breaks if it stays below a required reader, what becomes coupled if it rises above every required reader and writer, and which lifetime the chosen owner actually provides. A strong answer should leave at least one meaningful production value local when its requirements say local.

lessons.title: The Stateless Content Boundary
lessons.summary: Separate a production screen's owner and state wiring from the composable that renders ordinary values and reports intent. The split is useful because content can then be rendered with arbitrary states, reused with another owner, and reasoned about without constructing the real application boundary.

blocks.text: Once a screen has several owners, it needs one place where their values and events meet. That place is the screen composable. Its job is wiring: obtain the current screen-level value, keep any Compose-owned coordination state at the level chosen in the previous lesson, and connect UI events to the owner that handles each one. The content composable has a different job: render the supplied value and report what the user asks to do.

`QuestionLibraryScreen` is stateful even though not every value it uses is stored in the Composition. It knows the outside owner and it owns the selected filter for its subtree. `QuestionLibraryContent` is stateless in the useful API sense: its signature contains only an immutable current value and callbacks. It does not know whether those inputs came from a ViewModel, a remembered plain state holder, a preview, or a test.

This is a screen boundary, not the stateful/stateless overload pair from the earlier hoisting lesson. There is no promise that both functions are interchangeable convenience overloads. The screen function is the application-facing wiring point; the content function is the rendering surface. Their different responsibilities are the reason for two names.

Screen composable means wiring boundary. Content composable means rendering plus reporting intent. Keeping that distinction visible gives the screen one obvious place where owners, current values and event handlers are connected.

The benefits are easiest to see as consequences of the signature rather than as adjectives. A preview can call `QuestionLibraryContent` with an empty state, a long list, an error state or an unusual saved selection. It does not need to construct the production owner, start dependency injection, or wait for data. Preview tooling is not the subject here; the important fact is that ordinary parameters make arbitrary states directly renderable.

The same property enables isolated UI tests: the caller supplies a state and records which callback an interaction invokes. That explains testability without teaching a testing framework. It also enables reuse. A demo host, another platform shell, or a future owner can render the same content because none must pretend to be the original owner type.

The split also limits wiring drift. Without it, a descendant may obtain the owner for retry, another may mutate the selected filter, and a third may read a separate saved-state source. The screen no longer has a single place where the rendered value is assembled. With the boundary, replacing the outside owner or changing how the selected filter is retained changes `QuestionLibraryScreen`; the rendering tree keeps the same value-and-callback contract.

rows: Content accepts ordinary immutable values and callbacks
Any caller can render a chosen state and decide what each event means
Content accepts the production owner
Rendering now requires that owner and inherits its construction, lifetime and dependencies
Descendants obtain their own owners or state sources
There is no single boundary where the screen's current inputs and event routes can be inspected

blocks.text: When reviewing a screen, inspect the content signature. If independently rendering it requires a production owner, dependency graph or live data source, the rendering boundary still owns wiring. A stateless content boundary makes reuse, preview and isolated verification possible because those dependencies have already been translated into values and callbacks.

sources.title: Preview your UI with composable previews

lessons.title: One Screen State Value, Events Back Up
lessons.summary: Make the content boundary a value-based contract: one immutable current screen value travels down, while callbacks describing retry, selection and save intent travel up. Passing writable state or an owner reference downward creates extra write paths, hides ownership and couples rendering to a particular mechanism.

blocks.text: The content boundary becomes easiest to understand when it receives one answer to one question: what does the screen render now? For the question library, a small immutable data class can carry the current questions, saved markers, load result and selected filter together. The type is an example that makes the contract visible, not a prescription for modelling every application's loading and error states. Detailed state modelling belongs to later architecture curriculum.

One screen state value does not outlaw local UI-element state. The difficulty menu can still own whether its popup is expanded. The claim is bounded to the screen contract: the values crossing from screen wiring into content form one immutable current snapshot rather than a collection of writable channels. The wiring layer may assemble that snapshot from an outside owner's state and Compose-owned coordination state.

The callbacks describe user intent, not storage operations. `onLevelSelected(level)` says what the user selected; `onRetry()` says they asked to retry; `onToggleSaved(id)` says which question they acted on. The caller decides whether each event changes Compose-owned state, asks the screen owner to do work, or is ignored because the current state no longer permits it. This is state down and events up applied to the complete screen contract, not a new definition of UDF.
The content renders one immutable current screen value and reports intent upward. It neither owns a second writable copy nor chooses the mechanism that will handle an event.

A writable parameter can look convenient because it removes a callback, but it removes the ownership boundary with it. This version gives the content two direct mutation mechanisms: a `MutableState` for the filter and the production owner for everything else.

items: Another write path now exists lower in the tree: any descendant that receives `selectedLevel` can assign it, whether or not that component should make the decision.
Ownership is no longer visible in the signature. The reader cannot tell which layer validates a selection or coordinates it with the rest of the screen.
The child is coupled to `MutableState` and to the particular production owner instead of to the value it renders and the intents it emits.
Preview and reuse require constructing or faking those mechanisms rather than supplying an arbitrary screen value and callbacks.
The content can no longer be reasoned about as rendering a supplied snapshot because it reaches through the owner for some values and can mutate another in place.

blocks.text: The rewrite is the value-and-callback signature above. The wiring screen reads the current values once, assembles `QuestionLibraryScreenState`, maps `onLevelSelected` to its Compose-owned filter, and maps retry and save intents to the outside owner. All writes pass back through the layer that owns the affected value. Content remains unaware that those events have different destinations.

Replacing `MutableState<T>` with a mutable holder interface does not fix the direction if the child can still call arbitrary setters. The important boundary is capability: give content the immutable value it must render and only the intent callbacks it is allowed to report.

An immutable state value is also an understandable observation point. A log, preview or failing test can name the exact snapshot the content received. If fields are mutated behind the same object, neither a reader nor Compose's change detection has a trustworthy boundary at which one screen value became another. Replacing the value makes the transition explicit.

This connects to `lesson_stability_and_skipping` without re-teaching stability. Equality-based reasoning only helps when the value's contract and implementation agree: an immutable snapshot can be compared as a value, while a mutable object whose contents change behind the same reference defeats that reasoning. This lesson needs no `@Stable` or `@Immutable` annotation to make the point.

UDF is the architecture-side name for the direction, but this unit stops at the Compose boundary. It does not require reducers, action types, state machines or MVI. One current value and constrained callbacks are enough to make ownership inspectable; how an application produces that value is a later design problem.

When a child receives writable state, name the concrete damage rather than saying only that it violates UDF: an extra write path, unclear ownership, coupling to a state mechanism, harder isolated rendering, and loss of a single supplied snapshot. Then rewrite the contract as immutable state down and intent callbacks up.

lessons.title: The Screen-Level Owner as a Bounded Bridge
lessons.summary: Moving screen state outside the Composition changes who owns it; it does not itself make the state persistent. Determine what survives from the new owner's actual lifetime, using this app's entry-scoped ViewModels as one concrete multiplatform Navigation 3 example, and stop before application architecture begins.

blocks.text: The question-library data in this unit belongs to a screen-level owner outside the Composition. That sentence tells you who no longer owns it: a composable call site does not. It does not tell you how long the new owner lives. Moving a value across the boundary changes its owner; it grants no persistence by itself.

A ViewModel is a familiar example because a host supplies it from a `ViewModelStoreOwner`, but the same reasoning applies to any outside owner. State survives exactly the events that leave that owner and its storage alive. If the host retains the owner while a composable re-executes or temporarily leaves composition, the value survives. If the host destroys the owner, being outside the Composition offers no further protection.

headers: Does entry-scoped owner state survive in this app?
rows: The composable recomposes or its body executes repeatedly
Yes
The back-stack entry and its owner are unchanged; recomposition is not the owner's lifetime
The destination is composed again while the same entry remains
Yes
The existing entry still supplies the same owner
Android recreates the UI for a configuration change
Yes for a retained ViewModel owner; this is an Android-specific guarantee, not a universal meaning of outside Composition
Android retains the relevant `ViewModelStore`, not the fact that the value was moved from a composable
The learner navigates forward and this destination remains on its back stack
Yes
The Navigation 3 entry remains, so its entry-scoped `ViewModelStore` remains
The destination is popped and its entry is removed
No
The entry's `ViewModelStore` is cleared, which ends that owner's lifetime

blocks.text: Process recreation is a separate rung. A ViewModel does not survive process death on its own, and an outside owner is not durable storage. Small restorable keys and durable application data use other mechanisms, introduced in their owning curricula. The earlier `lesson_remember_saveable` provides the lifetime ladder; this lesson applies its central question to a screen-level owner.

"Outside the Composition" tells you who no longer owns the state. It does not by itself tell you how long the new owner lives. Ask which host owns it, when that host releases it, and whether a different persistence mechanism is required.

This repository supplies a concrete example in shared Compose code. Its `NavDisplay` installs a saveable-state entry decorator followed by the lifecycle ViewModel entry decorator. Each relevant Navigation 3 back-stack entry therefore receives its own `ViewModelStore`. Screen ViewModels are resolved at that destination boundary, remain while their entry remains on the area's back stack, and are cleared when the entry is removed.

The snippet is evidence about ownership, not a Navigation lesson. The important chain is entry exists, therefore its store exists, therefore the ViewModel and its in-memory state exist. Pop the entry and the chain ends. Navigating forward without removing it is different from popping it even if both actions make the question-library content leave the visible Composition.

Compose Multiplatform provides lifecycle and ViewModel APIs in common code, but the host still supplies the ownership lifetime. Android configuration recreation is one platform-specific case. Desktop, iOS and web hosts do not acquire an Android rotation guarantee merely because the shared owner class is called `ViewModel`; reason from the owner supplied by the actual host.

The screen/content contract does not change when the owner changes. `QuestionLibraryContent` still receives an immutable current value and sends retry, selection and save intent upward. Only `QuestionLibraryScreen` knows how the owner is reached and how its current value enters Compose. Converting an outside observable value into Compose state is the next unit's subject, so no collection mechanism belongs here.

Saying "the ViewModel survives" without naming the event and the owner is incomplete. It may survive a particular Android recreation and remain while a navigation entry is retained, yet be cleared on pop and lost with the process. The owner-lifetime chain, not the class name, is the explanation.

An outside owner is justified when coordination or lifetime crosses the Composition boundary, not when a screen merely looks production-sized. The selected filter in this unit still belongs to a Compose parent because its readers, writers and lifetime stop there. A remembered plain state holder could encapsulate more complicated filter UI logic without moving that state outside the Composition.

Conversely, screen data does not become durable when a ViewModel owns it. The ViewModel can coordinate production and hold the current in-memory value for its scope; persistence requires a mechanism designed for the event to be survived. That distinction prevents three concepts from collapsing into one: ownership says who may change the state, lifetime says when that owner disappears, and persistence says how a value can be reconstructed after it does.

This is where the Compose curriculum deliberately stops. How to construct the owner, divide responsibilities among repositories and use cases, model complete UI states, select MVVM or MVI, inject dependencies, or launch owner-scoped work are application-architecture and dependency-injection decisions. The bounded bridge here is only the contract at the Composition edge.

For each event, trace the real lifetime: recomposition leaves the outside owner untouched; Android configuration recreation can retain a ViewModel through its store; a retained back-stack entry retains its entry owner; removing that entry clears it; process death destroys in-memory state unless another mechanism reconstructs it. Then state which fact is general and which belongs to the current host.

sources.title: Apply logic or wrappers to destinations

units.title: Observable State Collection and Lifecycle
units.summary: A screen-level owner can expose a perfectly useful Flow or StateFlow and still not give Compose anything it can observe directly. This unit follows that outside value across the boundary: collection converts it into Compose State, the returned state drives ordinary recomposition, the collection has a composition-owned lifetime and real cost, and lifecycle-aware collection adds a second gate whose meaning is supplied by each Android, desktop, iOS or web host.

lessons.title: What a Composable Can and Cannot Observe
lessons.summary: Reading a StateFlow's current value gives a composable data, but it does not connect later stream updates to Compose invalidation. Trace the two separate observation systems and see why collection into Compose State is a real bridge rather than ceremonial syntax.

blocks.text: Unit 7 ended with a screen-level owner outside the Composition. Suppose that owner exposes `val state: StateFlow<QuestionScreenState>`. The value is observable, but observable to whom? `StateFlow` notifies collectors. Compose invalidates a composition when state from its own snapshot-aware state system that the composition read changes. Those are two observation systems with no automatic connection between them.

At this execution, `owner.state.value` returns the StateFlow's current value and `QuestionContent` can render it. If the StateFlow later emits another value, however, that update does not itself invalidate this composition. The body did not read a Compose `State.value`; it performed an ordinary Kotlin property read on a type whose notification mechanism is collection.

Do not overstate the defect as "the UI can never show a newer value". If some unrelated observed state change causes `QuestionScreen` to recompose, the body can execute again and read the newer `StateFlow.value`. The precise defect is that the stream update itself is not connected to Compose invalidation, so rendering depends accidentally on some other cause of recomposition.

The missing operation is a bridge: collect the external stream, write each collected value into Compose `State<T>`, then read that state while rendering. The path is external observable stream -> collection -> Compose State -> snapshot-observed read -> rendering. Once the value crosses that boundary, the snapshot observation model from `lesson_snapshot_observation` applies normally.

A value can be observable without being observable to Compose. StateFlow owns a collector protocol; Compose owns a snapshot-state protocol. Reliable rendering requires an explicit conversion that connects the first protocol to the second.

This is the same question-library boundary as Unit 7, one step later. The owner still owns loaded questions, saved markers and load failure. The content still receives one immutable current screen value and callbacks. Nothing about ownership is being reconsidered. Only the wiring composable gains the responsibility to adapt the owner's observable state into the kind of state its rendering system observes.

rows: `composeState.value`
Compose snapshot observation records the read
A recorded state change invalidates the reading composition
`stateFlow.value`
No StateFlow collector is established by this property read
A later StateFlow update does not itself invalidate the composition
An arbitrary mutable Kotlin property
No observation mechanism unless its type supplies one and the caller subscribes
Assignment alone gives Compose no notification

blocks.text: StateFlow's retained current value still matters: it gives the conversion a synchronous value to expose immediately. That contract belongs to `lesson_state_flow`; this lesson does not re-teach hot streams, replay or conflation. Likewise, `snapshotFlow` travels in the opposite direction - Compose snapshot State into a Flow - and remains the subject of `lesson_snapshot_flow`.

The conversion belongs at the stateful screen wiring boundary. `QuestionContent` should not know about Flow or the owner. It continues to accept the current `QuestionScreenState`, which preserves the previewable, reusable contract Unit 7 established. The next lesson names the purpose-built conversion API.

When asked why reading `StateFlow.value` is insufficient in a composable, identify the missing notification path. The read can return useful data now, but it neither starts collection nor records a snapshot-state dependency. A later emission therefore has no direct route to invalidate the composition.

lessons.title: `collectAsState`: Converting a Stream into Compose State
lessons.summary: Use collectAsState as the purpose-built bridge from Flow to renderable Compose State. Compare the StateFlow and plain Flow overloads, distinguish a supplied initial value from upstream retention, trace the recomposition path, and treat stream identity as part of collection lifetime.

blocks.text: When the requirement is "turn this observable stream into the current state this composition renders", Compose provides `collectAsState`. It starts collection for the conversion, returns `State<T>`, and updates that state as values arrive. Reading the returned state's `value` - directly or through `by` delegation - establishes the Compose-observed dependency the previous lesson was missing.

For `StateFlow<T>`, the resolved Compose runtime's overload is `StateFlow<T>.collectAsState(context)`. It uses `StateFlow.value` as the returned Compose State's initial value. The screen therefore has the owner's real current state on first composition; the caller does not invent a loading placeholder merely to start collection. Why StateFlow can supply that value is already taught in `lesson_state_flow`.

A plain `Flow<T>` has a different overload: `Flow<T>.collectAsState(initial, context)`. It requires an explicit initial value because an arbitrary Flow does not necessarily expose a current value synchronously before collection begins. The supplied value is simply what the returned Compose State exposes until collection supplies another value. It is not a hidden cache in the Flow, SharedFlow replay, StateFlow retention, saved state or durable persistence.

The complete path is now visible: Flow emission -> the collector writes the returned State -> Compose observes that State change -> the composition that read it is invalidated -> recomposition reads the new value. This is ordinary state-driven recomposition, not a special rendering mode for Flow. `lesson_composition_and_recomposition` owns the deeper recomposition model.

`collectAsState` is state conversion. StateFlow supplies its own current value as the initial Compose value; plain Flow requires the caller to supply what should be rendered until the first collected value arrives.

A common near-miss is to build the stream inline. In this example, `observeQuestions()` may return a stable stream, but `map` creates a new Flow object whenever `QuestionScreen` executes. The resolved runtime keys its state producer on the initial value, Flow instance and context. When the supplied Flow instance changes, the previous conversion is replaced and a new collection starts.

Do not turn that into "Flow operators in composables are always slow". The issue is identity and intended lifetime: changing the stream supplied to the conversion means replacing the collection. That is correct when an input such as a question id deliberately selects a different stream. It is wasteful or behaviourally surprising when recomposition accidentally constructs an equivalent stream and restarts cold upstream work. Give the stream a stable owner or memoize the derived stream against the inputs that should actually replace it. Operator semantics remain E24's subject.

The optional `context` parameter controls the coroutine context used for collection. With the default empty context, collection uses the state producer's existing context; with a supplied context, the resolved implementation collects inside that context. This is not a general dispatcher lesson and it does not replace `flowOn`: the Flow curriculum owns context preservation and dispatcher placement.

Do not make a remembered `MutableState`, launch an effect, collect the Flow by hand and assign every value merely to render ongoing state. Such code can be made to work, but it hides the requirement behind a general effect mechanism. `collectAsState` states the job directly. Manual collection belongs where receiving values performs an effect rather than exposes current renderable state; later units make that distinction precise.

The verified Compose runtime 1.11.2 source implements the Flow overload through `produceState(initial, this, context)`. That source relationship proves why stream identity and context participate in replacement and why equal assignments are conflated by the returned State. It is evidence for the public contract, not the mental model learners should lead with: Unit 11 teaches `produceState` as its own mechanism.

Initial-value choice is part of UI correctness. A fabricated empty state can briefly claim "there are no questions" while a cold Flow has not emitted; an explicit loading state says what is actually known. StateFlow avoids that invented gap only because its contract already includes a current value. The API removes a placeholder requirement, not the need to model honest screen states.

A strong explanation names both overloads, then follows one emission all the way to invalidation. It also treats the Flow object supplied to the composable as a lifetime input: a deliberately changed stream should replace collection; an accidentally fresh equivalent stream should not.

lessons.title: Collection Has a Lifetime and a Cost
lessons.summary: Ordinary collectAsState keeps a collector active while its state producer remains in Composition. Make that lifetime concrete through database observation and transformation work, then keep UI collector cancellation separate from ownership of a cold or shared upstream producer.

blocks.text: Conversion is active work. Ordinary `collectAsState` owns a collection for as long as that state producer's composable call site remains in Composition. Recomposition by itself does not mean "start another collector" when the relevant inputs are unchanged. When the call site actually leaves Composition, the composition-owned producer is cancelled and its collection ends.

That statement is deliberately about Composition, not about an informal idea of a visible screen. A navigation system can remove destination content from Composition, retain it, or keep related host structures alive according to its own design. The precise claim is: when this destination's collection call actually leaves Composition, ordinary `collectAsState` cancels that conversion. Whether a destination is visible is a separate fact.

rows: The composable recomposes with the same Flow, initial value and context
The existing conversion remains; recomposition alone does not create a second collector
The Flow instance supplied to the call changes
The previous producer is cancelled and collection restarts for the replacement stream
The call site actually leaves Composition
Its producer is cancelled and this UI collection ends

blocks.text: Cancellation is ordinary cooperative coroutine cancellation. Compose does not "kill the Flow", and cancellation cannot instantly interrupt arbitrary blocking or CPU-bound work. `lesson_flow_collection_lifetime` and `lesson_cooperative_cancellation` own those mechanics; here they explain what ending the composition-owned collector requests.

Ask two separate lifetime questions: is this conversion still in Composition, and does the exact Flow identity supplied to it still represent the same source? Those facts decide whether ordinary collection remains active or is replaced.

Imagine the question library observes a Room query, maps database rows into display models, combines saved markers, and records the latest result in screen state. Keeping the UI collector active can mean four concrete things: a collector coroutine remains alive; every emission is still processed; database observation or another upstream subscription may remain active; and the conversion keeps producing Compose-state updates for UI the user is not currently looking at. A different source might poll a service or keep a socket subscription, making the resource consequence larger.

items: The collector itself occupies a coroutine and remains ready for values.
Mapping, combining, filtering or other upstream work may still execute for each value.
A cold source collected only here may keep its database observer, polling loop or callback subscription alive.
A shared source may stay active because another scope and sharing policy own its production.
The conversion can write new UI state even while the host is not active enough for those updates to matter.

blocks.text: None of this means every Flow is expensive. A quiet in-memory StateFlow may cost very little, and continuous collection may be intentional when the UI must remain current. The defect is a lifetime that exceeds the requirement, especially when upstream work is scarce, battery-sensitive, networked or produces frequent transformations. Cost is a reason to choose a policy, not a reason to fear Flow.

Do not use "navigated away" as proof that collection stopped. First establish that this destination's content actually left Composition. If it did, this composition-owned collector ends. If the content remains composed, ordinary `collectAsState` has no host-visibility gate and continues.

Stopping the UI collector does not by itself prove that upstream production stopped. For a cold Flow whose producer runs only in this collecting coroutine, ending collection normally ends that production too, subject to cooperative cancellation. For a hot or shared stream, production can belong to an owner scope that outlives this screen. The upstream owner's lifetime and sharing policy decide whether it continues.

That is the whole sharing bridge this unit needs. `lesson_sharing_cold_flows` teaches `stateIn`, `shareIn`, `SharingStarted` and their timers. At the Compose boundary, keep the responsibility split visible: collection policy decides whether this UI subscribes; sharing policy decides what the shared producer does as subscribers appear and disappear. Changing one does not silently rewrite the other.

This distinction also prevents a misleading performance claim. Lifecycle-aware collection can remove one unnecessary subscriber and its downstream processing, yet an eagerly owned shared producer may correctly continue. Conversely, a cold database Flow may release its only observer as soon as the UI collection ends. Measure the real producer and owner rather than inferring resource use from the UI API's name.

Trace both sides of the boundary. First say when the Compose collector ends. Then identify whether the upstream is cold and owned by that collection or hot/shared and owned elsewhere. Only the second answer tells you whether production stopped.

lessons.title: Lifecycle-Aware Collection and the Lifecycle a Screen Actually Has
lessons.summary: A composable can remain in Composition while its host is not active enough to justify upstream collection. Add lifecycle as an independent gate with collectAsStateWithLifecycle, then predict default STARTED behavior from the actual Android, desktop, iOS and web host mappings used by this KMP project.

blocks.text: Composition lifetime and host lifecycle answer different questions. A conversion may still be in Composition while its host window, scene or page is no longer active enough to justify database observation, polling or repeated transformations. Ordinary `collectAsState` has only the composition gate. Lifecycle-aware conversion adds a policy for pausing upstream collection without requiring the composition itself to disappear.

rows: `collectAsState`
While the Compose state producer remains in Composition, subject to replacement when its inputs change
`collectAsStateWithLifecycle`
While the state producer remains in Composition and the relevant lifecycle is at least the configured active state

blocks.text: In this repository's configured lifecycle runtime Compose 2.11.0-beta01, `collectAsStateWithLifecycle` defaults to `LocalLifecycleOwner.current` and `minActiveState = Lifecycle.State.STARTED`. At or above that state, it collects upstream. Below it, collection stops; when the lifecycle reaches the threshold again, collection restarts. `INITIALIZED` is not a valid threshold and the API rejects it with `IllegalArgumentException`.

The StateFlow overload uses the stream's current `value` initially. The plain Flow overload requires `initialValue`, just as plain `collectAsState` does. Overloads can also take an explicit `LifecycleOwner` or `Lifecycle`; the default owner is usually the portable screen-level choice because the host provides it through the composition.

Lifecycle-aware collection has two independent gates: is this conversion still in Composition, and is its lifecycle at least the chosen active state? Upstream is collected only when both answers are yes.

`collectAsStateWithLifecycle` is not Android-only in this project. The dependency `org.jetbrains.androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-compose:2.11.0-beta01` is declared in `commonMain`, resolves to the AndroidX multiplatform implementation in package `androidx.lifecycle.compose`, and production destination composables already import it from shared code. The API is common; the lifecycle that drives it is supplied by the actual platform host.

rows: Android
The relevant Activity, Fragment or navigation-entry LifecycleOwner supplies state
Collection is active at STARTED or RESUMED and stops when that owner falls below STARTED
Desktop
Visible and focused maps to RESUMED; visible but unfocused to STARTED; minimized or detached to CREATED; disposal to DESTROYED
Losing focus alone keeps collection active; minimizing stops it
iOS
Appeared, foreground and active maps to RESUMED; appeared and foreground but inactive to STARTED; background or not appeared to CREATED
An inactive foreground scene keeps collection active; backgrounding stops it
Web
Focus resumes, blur pauses to STARTED, and a hidden page stops; the documented normal host model skips CREATED and does not reach DESTROYED
A visible but blurred page keeps collection active; hiding the tab stops it

blocks.text: The portable model is not to memorize four event tables. `STARTED` expresses one common threshold, but each platform decides how window, scene or page activity maps onto lifecycle states. Therefore common API availability does not imply identical user-action behavior. Given a bug report such as "collection continues when the desktop window loses focus", inspect the host mapping before assuming the API failed: an unfocused visible desktop window is still STARTED in the configured Compose Multiplatform 1.11.1 host.

For desktop, JetBrains also notes that lifecycle coroutine scopes rely on `Dispatchers.Main.immediate`, which needs a Main dispatcher implementation. This repository's desktop application already declares `kotlinx-coroutines-swing`; that configuration supports the host contract. It is a platform setup note, not a reason to teach dispatcher selection again.

Do not reduce the decision to "always use `collectAsStateWithLifecycle` because it is safer". Continuous collection can be the requirement, and some sources are cheap. Choose lifecycle-aware conversion when upstream should pause below a host-activity threshold; choose plain conversion when composition lifetime is the intended policy.

The resolved source builds lifecycle-aware conversion from `produceState` and `repeatOnLifecycle`. That implementation evidence explains the two gates: Compose owns the returned State and cancels its producer when the call leaves Composition; the lifecycle block starts and stops upstream collection around the active threshold. This lesson uses that relationship to verify behavior, while Unit 11 remains responsible for teaching `produceState` itself and lifecycle curriculum remains responsible for `repeatOnLifecycle` in View hosts.

Pausing the lifecycle-aware collector still does not settle the upstream producer's lifetime. When the lifecycle falls below STARTED, this subscriber is removed and later re-established. A cold source tied only to it normally stops and starts with that collection. A shared source follows the owner scope and sharing policy taught in `lesson_sharing_cold_flows`. Lifecycle policy and sharing policy must be reviewed together when resource use matters.

Version precision matters here because the configured lifecycle artifact is beta. These overloads, defaults and mappings were rechecked against this repository's resolved 2.11.0-beta01 lifecycle sources and its Compose Multiplatform 1.11.1 host sources, with Compose runtime resolving to 1.11.2. A future dependency update should re-read those contracts rather than preserve this table by assumption.

Given a target, current host state and collection API, answer in order: is the call still in Composition; which LifecycleOwner is relevant; what state does this host map the user action to; is that state at least the threshold; and who owns upstream production after this collector stops?
