units.title: Effect Lifecycle and LaunchedEffect
units.summary: A composable body describes UI; it does not give arbitrary imperative work a reliable owner or lifetime. This unit starts from that missing contract, then uses LaunchedEffect to tie suspend work to one place in the Composition. It traces entry, ordinary recomposition, key change, removal and re-entry, and treats keys as declarations of what should end one effect lifetime and begin another.

lessons.title: Why Compose Needs an Effect API
lessons.summary: Starting imperative work directly while a composable executes leaves its start count, owner, cancellation and cleanup disconnected from the UI lifetime the programmer intended. Repeated execution, skipping and abandoned recomposition expose different parts of that defect and motivate controlled effect mechanisms.

blocks.text: A composable body describes the UI for its current inputs. It is not an imperative lifecycle callback around everything written between its braces. In particular, a composable is not an `onCreate` callback. The equally simple replacement, "a composable runs many times", is not a useful guarantee either. The runtime owns whether and when the body executes; application code must not derive an imperative lifetime from one execution of that body.

Inspect those two imperative statements before asking which API should replace them. How often do they run? Who decides when `questionWork` stops? What happens if the composition attempt that executed them is abandoned? What cancels or cleans up what they started? What happens if this body executes again? The code answers none of those questions. Its defect is deeper than "recomposition might call it twice": arbitrary work started from the body has no controlled lifecycle matching the Composition.

The execution rules themselves belong to `lesson_composable_execution` and `lesson_composition_and_recomposition`. This unit applies them. A body may execute repeatedly, may be skipped, may execute in an order its caller must not depend on, and may participate in an optimistic composition whose result is discarded. This contract does not claim that Compose currently executes composables in parallel. It says that application code does not own their timing or count.

The missing abstraction is ownership. Work needs a start condition, an end condition and a cleanup or cancellation path that agree with the UI lifetime it serves. A raw statement in a composable body has execution timing, not that lifecycle contract.

Repeated execution makes the first failure visible. If the body executes again, `screenOpened` records another opening and `questionWork.start` starts another operation. That can duplicate analytics, registrations or requests and leave several operations claiming to represent one screen. This is conditional wording on purpose: not every recomposition executes every composable. The precise rule is that whenever this body does execute, its ordinary imperative statements execute with it.

Skipping exposes a different mistaken assumption. Suppose correctness depends on "this function body will run now because this logical screen event happened". The code is using composition as an event dispatcher, but Compose may decide that this composable does not need re-execution. Skipping is not a bug; it is evidence that body execution is the wrong contract for an action that application code expects once per conceptual event.

An abandoned composition exposes the external-state hazard. Compose may begin calculating an updated UI and discard that result before it becomes the successfully applied UI. The UI described by that pass never takes effect, while an analytics mutation, request or registration performed during body execution cannot necessarily be unhappened. Successful composition and controlled effect execution matter because external work must not escape from a UI result that was never committed.

headers: What direct body work gets wrong
rows: The body executes again
The statement runs again even when the logical work should still have one owner
The body is skipped
The statement cannot stand for a guaranteed application event
The composition attempt is abandoned
External mutation may survive even though the calculated UI is discarded

blocks.text: Do not fix this by inventing a `Boolean` that says the body has already run. That flag still needs an owner, a lifetime and a rule for re-entry. The problem is not syntax for suppressing a second call; it is defining what owns the work and what ends it.

The Compose effect family exists because different work needs different ownership answers. Suspend work may belong to a place in the Composition. An external registration may require paired cleanup. A user event may start work at a time chosen by the callback rather than by composition. Long-lived work may need a current value without ending its lifetime. These are four motivating problems, not four APIs to memorize; later units provide the remaining mechanisms.

The right review question is therefore not merely "is there a side effect in this function?" It is: which event should begin this work, which owner should bound it, and which event should cancel or clean it up? If the work must continue after this UI position leaves the Composition, a composition-owned effect is the wrong owner. Choosing the longer-lived owner is architecture material outside this unit.

Given work started directly in a composable, explain all three failure dimensions: repeated execution can duplicate it, skipping makes body execution an unreliable event signal, and abandoned composition can discard the UI without rolling back arbitrary external mutation. Then identify the missing owner and lifetime rather than stopping at "use an effect".

lessons.title: `LaunchedEffect`: Work a Composition Owns
lessons.summary: LaunchedEffect launches suspend work when its remembered position enters the Composition and bounds that coroutine by the position's lifetime. Equal keys preserve the running effect across ordinary recomposition; a changed key cancels and replaces it; removal cancels it; re-entry begins a new lifetime.

blocks.text: `LaunchedEffect` supplies the ownership contract missing from direct body work. When the effect enters the Composition, Compose launches its block in a coroutine. The effect belongs to its remembered position and call-site identity in the Composition, not merely to the fact that a composable function happened to be called. Compose establishes the owner and lifetime; coroutine cancellation supplies the mechanism.

headers: What happens to the call site
What happens to the effect coroutine
rows: It enters Composition
The block is launched and one effect lifetime begins
The body executes again and `questionId` still compares equal
The existing coroutine keeps running; ordinary recomposition does not restart it
`questionId` changes according to key comparison
The old coroutine is cancelled and a replacement is launched for the new id
The call site leaves Composition
Its coroutine is cancelled
The call site later re-enters Composition
A new effect instance and coroutine lifetime begin

blocks.text: Two events that are often collapsed are now separate: the composable body executes again, and the effect coroutine restarts. The first can happen without the second. If the effect remains at the same composition identity and every key continues to compare equal, recomposition preserves the current effect. A restart is a lifecycle transition caused by a changed key or by leaving and later re-entering, not a synonym for recomposition.

Say "the effect enters Composition", not "the composable was called". LaunchedEffect owns one coroutine lifetime at one remembered position. Ordinary re-execution with equal keys keeps that lifetime; changed identity or keys end it.

Key change matters most while work is in flight. If `questionId` changes from `q1` to `q2`, Compose cancels the `q1` coroutine and launches the block for `q2`. Cancellation is not an update to the old coroutine's captured variable, and both operations are not intentionally kept alive. Old work is asked to stop; new work starts with the new key.

That stop uses the ordinary coroutine model from `lesson_coroutine_scope_ownership` and `lesson_cooperative_cancellation`. Cancellation is cooperative. A suspending operation that cooperates observes it and unwinds; arbitrary blocking or CPU-bound code that neither suspends nor checks cannot be forcibly preempted by Compose. Therefore "leaving Composition cancels the effect" describes the ownership request and coroutine protocol, not an immediate kill switch.

When `question` becomes null, that branch and its `LaunchedEffect` call site leave the Composition, so the pulse coroutine is cancelled even if the surrounding screen remains. If a question later becomes non-null, the call site enters again and launches a new effect. `lesson_composable_identity` contains the full identity model; here it explains exactly which UI lifetime owns the work.

Do not say "recomposition reruns LaunchedEffect". Recomposition can execute the call again while the remembered effect and its coroutine continue unchanged. Ask whether the position remained in Composition and whether its keys still compare equal.

The resolved Compose runtime 1.11.2 contract says the coroutine context comes from the Composition's applying context, and the runtime launches and cancels the remembered effect through that context. That is enough context detail for this unit. It is not a universal promise that every Compose Multiplatform effect runs on the Android main thread, and dispatcher selection remains coroutine curriculum.

Cancellation also does not provide transaction rollback. If an effect has already sent analytics, written a remote record or otherwise completed an external side effect, cancelling the coroutine cannot unhappen it. Cancellation bounds continued work. Code still needs idempotency or an application-level consistency design when completed external mutations matter.

Trace five moments precisely: entry launches; recomposition with equal keys preserves; key change cancels and replaces; removal cancels cooperatively; re-entry launches a new lifetime. Then state which call-site identity owns the effect and why body execution is not itself a restart event.

lessons.title: What an Effect's Keys Declare
lessons.summary: An effect key declares a lifetime dependency: a change means the current work is no longer the right work and should end. Keys use the same equality comparison as remember keys, not the instance comparison used for unstable parameters in strong-skipping decisions, and a constant key claims the call site's whole composition lifetime.

blocks.text: A key list is a declaration about lifetime. For every candidate value, ask: if this value changes, is the current effect instance no longer the right work? If yes, that value probably participates in the lifetime and belongs in the key declaration. If no, cancelling valid work solely because the value changed may be incorrect. This is stronger than the mechanical rule "put every value read by the block in the key list".

Here a changed `questionId` means the current hint sequence describes the wrong question, so it should end and a new sequence should begin. `questionId` is a lifetime dependency. By contrast, a changing value that the same long-lived work merely needs to read currently does not automatically deserve to end that work. A later unit solves that latest-value problem; this unit stops at recognizing it.

Current Android guidance gives a useful heuristic: variables used by an effect generally belong among its keys. That catches captured inputs whose changes really should invalidate the work. The heuristic is a review prompt, not the final mental model, because some captured values should become current without redefining the effect's lifetime. Always return to the question: what should end this lifetime?
Keys do not declare everything the block can read. They declare which changes mean "the current work is no longer the right work; cancel it and begin again."

In the resolved AndroidX Compose runtime 1.11.2, this comparison is exact: `LaunchedEffect(key)` is built with `remember(key)`, and `remember` retains its value when the new key compares equal with `==`/`equals`. Effect keys are therefore compared like remember keys. This is the runtime/API contract, not merely an analogy. `lesson_remember_key_memoization` owns the memoization half of the model.

Each body execution can allocate a fresh `QuestionKey("same")`. Fresh allocation alone does not restart the effect: two data-class values with the same `id` compare equal, so the remembered key is unchanged. A newly allocated value restarts an effect only when the supplied key stops comparing equal to the previous key.

rows: Should this effect restart?
Effect/remember-key equality: `==` / `equals`
Can this composable invocation be skipped under strong skipping?
Stable parameters use object equality; unstable parameters use instance equality `===`

blocks.text: Those are different runtime/compiler decisions. A fresh structurally equal object can preserve an effect key while, if its type is unstable, the same fresh instance may prevent a composable invocation from being skipped. `lesson_stability_and_skipping` owns stability and strong skipping; the point here is to keep its parameter comparison out of the effect-key decision.

Lambda keys obey the same equality contract, but source syntax does not tell you whether the instance supplied on a later pass is equal. A probe against this repository's Kotlin/Compose compiler 2.4.10 and runtime 1.11.2 observed one effect start for a non-capturing lambda, one for a lambda capturing unchanged data, and one for an explicitly remembered lambda. A lambda capturing changing data produced a changed instance and four starts across four passes.

The equality comparison is the durable API/runtime contract. The exact lambda instances above are current-toolchain measured behavior: strong skipping memoizes lambdas from their captures, and compiler transformations can evolve. Therefore "a fresh lambda always restarts an effect" is not a sound rule. Establish whether the supplied key actually stopped comparing equal, then decide whether it should have been a lifetime dependency at all.

A constant key does not mean "run once". It declares that no changing value should restart this effect: the lifetime depends only on this call site remaining in the Composition. That can be exactly right for work intended to last for the call site's whole composition lifetime. It can also hide a missing dependency behind an imperative one-time assumption, so ask explicitly whether that whole lifetime is the requirement.

For each key candidate, answer two independent questions: does it compare equal to the previous supplied key, and should a real change end the current work? Comparison predicts what Compose does; the lifetime requirement decides whether the declaration is correct.

lessons.title: Two Ways to Get Effect Keys Wrong
lessons.summary: Too few lifetime dependencies let stale work continue after it should have ended. Keys that needlessly stop comparing equal cancel and replace still-valid work, discarding progress and possibly repeating completed external actions. Diagnose both directions from behavior rather than from key-list style.

blocks.text: Wrong keys fail in opposite directions. Too few lifetime dependencies preserve work that has become stale. Keys that stop comparing equal more often than the logical lifetime changes cancel useful work and replace it. Both bugs come from a false declaration about ownership and lifetime, so counting keys or copying every captured value cannot diagnose them.

If this call site remains in the Composition while `questionId` changes, `Unit` still compares equal. The effect does not restart, so the old hint sequence may continue using the previous ID while the screen now shows another question. The diagnosis is not merely "forgot a key". The false declaration is that `questionId` does not define this work's lifetime, when in fact a changed question makes the current sequence the wrong work.

The repair follows from the requirement: use `questionId` as the lifetime dependency so a changed question cancels the stale sequence and launches the right one. A constant key was not inherently wrong; it was wrong for this lifetime.
Too few keys produce a lifetime that is too long: stale work continues after the value that made it correct has changed. Name the omitted lifetime dependency, not just the missing argument.

The two fresh keys do not behave alike. `ValueKey` is a data class, so a new value with the same `id` is structurally equal and does not restart its effect. `IdentityKey` inherits default identity equality, so recreating it supplies a value unequal to the previous instance. If the body executes again while `questionId` is unchanged, the second effect is cancelled and replaced even though its logical work is still valid.

A needless restart is not another ordinary function call. `LaunchedEffect` cancels the current coroutine before launching the replacement. A delay or timer resets; animation progress can be discarded; partial UI work can be abandoned; a request can be issued again. If the key keeps becoming unequal on successive passes, the work may never get far enough to finish.

rows: The screen changes item but work continues for the previous id
Too few dependencies: a change that should end the effect was omitted
Valid progress repeatedly resets while the logical item is unchanged
A supplied key keeps becoming unequal even though it should not define a new lifetime
The composable executes again and the effect keeps running
Not a bug by itself: equal keys correctly preserve the current effect

blocks.text: Do not report "a new object caused the restart" until you inspect equality. Fresh, structurally equal data-class keys preserve the effect. The restart requires a supplied key that actually stops comparing equal, such as a newly created identity-equality wrapper.

Lambda keys need the same evidence. With this repository's current compiler, a non-capturing lambda and a lambda whose captures stayed unchanged were memoized in the measured cases; neither restarted the effect. A lambda capturing changing data supplied a different instance and restarted on every measured pass. These observations explain a possible restart storm, but the lasting review rule remains equality plus lifetime intent, not lambda syntax.

Cancellation limits future cooperative work; it does not roll back an external action that already completed. If an effect sent an analytics event before a needless restart, cancelling it cannot retract the event, and the replacement may send another. Key correctness therefore affects both wasted in-flight work and non-transactional external consequences.

Sometimes a long-lived effect should keep running while a value it reads changes. Adding that value as a key may create exactly the restart cost described here, while omitting it naïvely may leave a stale capture. Unit 10 starts from that tension and supplies the appropriate mechanism. This lesson establishes the problem and stops before teaching the solution.

A composable can recompose without restarting its effect, and an effect restarts because a key changed, not because "recomposition reruns side effects". Diagnose stale work as a lifetime that is too long and restart storms as lifetimes that are too short.

units.title: Latest-Value Effects and Event-Driven Coroutine Work
units.summary: Some changing values should be visible to work that is already running without ending that work, while some suspend work should begin only when a user event asks for it. This unit separates those two ownership problems: rememberUpdatedState preserves an effect lifetime while exposing a current value, and rememberCoroutineScope gives callbacks a composition-bounded scope without launching anything by itself. The final lesson chooses between composition-driven and event-driven work from who owns the trigger.

lessons.title: Reading the Current Value Without Restarting
lessons.summary: A value can matter to long-lived work without defining that work's lifetime. rememberUpdatedState keeps a remembered State holder current across recompositions so an existing effect can read the latest value when it needs it, while keying the effect remains correct when a changed value should cancel and replace the work.

blocks.text: Unit 9 gave effect keys a lifetime meaning: put a value in the key list when its change should end the current effect and begin replacement work. That leaves an important case. What if a changing value matters, but the current effect is still exactly the right work? Restarting would throw away valid progress, while capturing the launch-time value naively can leave the running coroutine with stale data.

Suppose this call site's contract is one 30-second timer for as long as this question remains in the Composition. The constant key is justified because the timer is intentionally tied to that whole composition lifetime; it is not shorthand for "run once". If recomposition supplies a different `onTimeout`, the existing coroutine does not restart, and the lambda captured when the effect launched may no longer be the callback the screen currently intends.

`rememberUpdatedState` answers the value problem without changing the timer's lifetime. Compose remembers a `State` holder and updates its current value when this call recomposes with a new value. The coroutine itself is not updated or relaunched. When the already-running coroutine reaches `currentOnTimeout()`, it reads the holder then and obtains the callback current at that read.
Keep two decisions separate: keys decide when the current work ends; rememberUpdatedState decides which current value that still-valid work reads.

Reading time matters. If the coroutine first copies `val captured = currentOnTimeout`, then delays and invokes `captured()`, that local still refers to the callback read before the delay. If it delays first and then invokes `currentOnTimeout()`, the State read happens after the delay and can observe a callback supplied by a later recomposition. State makes a current value available when read; it does not retroactively rewrite ordinary local variables.

rows: A changed callback makes the old timer obsolete
LaunchedEffect(onTimeout) { delay(...); onTimeout() }
The old timer is cancelled and a full new timer starts
The original timer remains valid, but completion must use the current callback
rememberUpdatedState(onTimeout) plus LaunchedEffect(Unit)
The timer continues; its later State read obtains the current callback

blocks.text: The keyed alternative is not inferior. Use `LaunchedEffect(onTimeout)` when a changed callback really means that all work based on the previous callback is obsolete. It cancels the in-flight delay and begins the whole block again whenever the key stops comparing equal. Use the current-value pattern only when that restart would violate the intended lifetime or discard work that remains valid.

rememberUpdatedState does not prevent, reduce or optimize recomposition. It is Compose State. If composable code reads the returned State during composition, ordinary state-read invalidation rules apply. The timer survives here because the changing callback is read inside the running coroutine and is not a changing effect key.

The public runtime contract describes a remembered State whose value is updated on recomposition so a long-lived lambda, object or operation can persist without cancellation and restart. In the resolved Compose runtime 1.11.2 source, the implementation is equivalent to `remember { mutableStateOf(newValue) }.apply { value = newValue }`. That implementation confirms the model, but the public purpose is the durable lesson: preserve the long-lived operation and change what it reads currently.

Callback syntax does not settle the choice. Unit 9 explains how equality and current compiler memoization affect whether a callback used as a key actually changes. This decision begins one level earlier: even if the callback would compare differently and restart the keyed effect, should that change end this work? If the answer is no, separate value currency from lifetime.

Explain both valid models. Key on a value when its change makes old work obsolete. Use rememberUpdatedState when old work remains valid and only the value read later must be current. Neither choice is a recomposition optimization.

lessons.title: `rememberCoroutineScope`: Launching From an Event
lessons.summary: rememberCoroutineScope returns a remembered CoroutineScope and starts no work. A click or other callback chooses whether and when to call launch, while the Composition still owns the scope's lifetime and cancels it when the call leaves Composition.

blocks.text: Some suspend UI work belongs to a screen but should not begin merely because that screen is being composed. Showing a snackbar after a save tap, scrolling after a button press, or driving a transient animation begins when an event occurs. Composition can provide the lifetime, while the event owns the trigger.

`rememberCoroutineScope()` launches nothing. It returns the same remembered scope across recompositions of that call site. Only when `onClick` calls `scope.launch` does a coroutine start. The caller therefore owns whether work starts, when it starts, and whether another click launches another coroutine. The builder and returned `Job` mechanics are covered by `lesson_coroutine_builders`.

rows: Composition creates and remembers the scope
Composition owns the scope lifetime
The user taps Save and the callback calls launch
The event/caller owns the trigger
The call site leaves Composition
Composition cancels the remembered scope

blocks.text: Trigger owner and lifetime owner are separate axes: the event starts this coroutine, while the Composition bounds the scope in which it runs.

Suppose the user taps Save and `showSnackbar` is still suspended when navigation removes this screen. The call that remembered the scope has left Composition, so Compose cancels the scope and cancellation propagates to work launched in it. Cancellation remains cooperative: cancellation-aware suspending work unwinds normally, while arbitrary blocking code is not forcibly stopped at the exact line the UI disappears.

A remembered scope does not make direct body launching controlled. The composable body may execute repeatedly, be skipped, or take part in an abandoned composition, so calling `launch` there recreates the uncontrolled-body-work defect from Unit 9. Put event-driven launch inside the event callback. Use a composition-triggered effect when entering or changing composition state really should start the work.

Calling `scope.launch` returns a `Job`. The event handler may retain that handle when a real requirement calls for manual cancellation or coordination, but another click is otherwise free to start another child. This lesson does not prescribe a concurrency policy; `lesson_coroutine_scope_ownership` and the structured-concurrency material own the deeper Job rules.

rememberCoroutineScope fixes the coroutine's lifetime owner. It does not turn the composable body into an event callback, start a coroutine automatically, or give launched work a lifetime beyond the screen.

The resolved runtime 1.11.2 KDoc says the scope is bound to this composition point, uses the Recomposer's applying dispatcher when no dispatcher is supplied, and is cancelled when the call leaves Composition. The optional supplied context may not contain a parent `Job`, because this scope is already a child of the Composition. That stable restriction is usually all application code needs.

The same KDoc says a violated context precondition does not throw directly from the composable call. In the resolved implementation, the returned scope instead contains a failed `Job` and cannot launch children. This is a diagnostic detail, not a reason to customize the scope's parent: ownership should remain with the Composition.

Describe the sequence precisely: composition remembers a scope; an event calls launch; a child coroutine starts; leaving that composition point cancels the scope and requests cooperative cancellation of its children.

lessons.title: Composition-Driven or Event-Driven?
lessons.summary: Choose coroutine work from who owns its trigger. LaunchedEffect starts when a composition state enters or changes and composition owns both trigger and lifetime; rememberCoroutineScope lets an event choose launch time while composition still bounds the lifetime. Work required to outlive the screen belongs to neither.

blocks.text: Two coroutines can have the same composition-bounded lifetime and still need different triggers. Ask what occurrence should begin the work. If the answer is "this composition now represents a particular state or identity", Composition owns the trigger. If the answer is "the user clicked" or "this callback fired", the event owns the trigger.

rows: LaunchedEffect
Composition state entering or changing
Composition
rememberCoroutineScope plus launch
Event or callback
Composition

blocks.text: The timer is genuinely composition-driven: when this composition starts representing `questionId`, the question-specific delay should begin; when the id changes, the old question's timer is obsolete and should be replaced. No click is required. Implementing this requirement only in a click callback could mean it never starts when the active question appears, because the trigger would be attached to the wrong occurrence.
Use LaunchedEffect when entering or changing a particular composition state should start or restart work. Use rememberCoroutineScope when an event should decide whether and when work starts.

Now apply the distinction to one screen requirement: when the user taps Save, show a confirmation snackbar. In the incorrect version below, `showSavedMessage` is persistent rendered state. While it remains true, the UI describes that a saved message is current; it does not represent one consumable tap. If this branch leaves and later re-enters Composition while the flag is still true, the effect enters again and the transient snackbar can fire again.

The correct direct UI-mechanics version lets the click own the trigger. The screen remembers a composition-owned scope, and that particular callback invocation launches the suspend snackbar work. This comparison is deliberately bounded: it does not define an application-wide transient-event delivery architecture or guarantees for times when no UI is present.

Do not reduce the rule to "LaunchedEffect is automatic and rememberCoroutineScope is manual". Name the occurrence that owns the start. A rendered condition and a user occurrence carry different meaning even when both eventually call the same suspend function.

Both mechanisms are wrong when the requirement says the operation must continue after this screen leaves Composition. A committed upload, durable save, payment submission or background synchronization cannot take its required lifetime from a composition-owned effect or remembered scope. Move it to an owner whose lifetime actually matches the requirement. Choosing and designing that owner belongs to later architecture curriculum; this unit does not turn `viewModelScope`, a repository, a queue or background-work API into a default escape hatch.

For work that is correctly composition-owned, leaving or rekeying requests normal coroutine cancellation. Cancellation-aware suspension unwinds cooperatively; blocking or non-cooperative work is not magically preempted; and an external action that already completed is not rolled back. Trigger choice changes when work begins, not these coroutine guarantees.

Latest-value handling is another independent decision. `rememberUpdatedState` solves which value a still-valid long-lived object or effect reads. `rememberCoroutineScope` solves who decides when a new coroutine begins. A design may eventually need both responsibilities, but one API is not a substitute for the other and current values are not event delivery.

Give a three-part answer: name the trigger owner, name the lifetime owner, and test whether that lifetime is long enough. Composition state can trigger LaunchedEffect; an event can launch into a remembered scope; work that must survive the screen needs a different owner.

units.title: Cleanup, External Synchronization and State Producers
units.summary: A screen touches a world Compose does not manage, and each direction across that boundary is a different ownership problem. This unit separates them: a registration the Composition acquires and must release, a value that must be published outward only after a composition has succeeded, and an asynchronous or callback-based source that must become Compose State the UI can read. The last lesson decides where an adapter for such a source belongs, from ownership and reuse rather than API preference.

lessons.title: Registration and Release as One Decision
lessons.summary: Some work a screen needs is not a coroutine but a registration with an object outside Compose that must be given back. DisposableEffect owns that registration for one key, releases it when the key changes and when the call site leaves the Composition, and pairs acquire with release in a single place so neither can be written without the other.

blocks.text: Unit 9 and Unit 10 asked who owns a coroutine. A screen also touches objects that Compose does not manage at all: a session that accepts listeners, a lifecycle that accepts observers, a platform service that accepts callbacks. Handing one of those a reference is not work that finishes; it is a registration. Something outside the Composition now holds something the Composition created, and it will keep holding it until it is told not to.

That is a resource ownership problem, and it has a different shape from "run this suspend work while this screen is here". The question is not when the work completes. The question is which composition lifetime is responsible for giving the registration back, and at which exact moment.

`DisposableEffect` is the mechanism whose shape matches that problem. Its block runs when the effect enters the Composition for a given key, and it must end with an `onDispose` clause. The block acquires; `onDispose` releases. The resolved Compose runtime 1.11.2 states the guarantee plainly: there is one call to `onDispose` for every call to the effect block, and both run on the composition's apply dispatcher.

The ownership model is worth stating as a sequence, because every later question in this lesson is answered from it: the effect enters with key K, the block acquires or registers something for K, that registration is owned for as long as this effect lifetime lasts, and when K changes or the call site leaves the Composition, that exact registration is released.

Registration and release are one decision, not two. The API forces them into one call precisely because a registration written without its release is not half-finished code — it is a defect that only shows up later, somewhere else.

Delete the `onDispose` body from the example above and say concretely what happens. A learner opens a session and moves through three questions, and each question composes `QuestionSessionStatus` at a new call site that leaves when the next one arrives. The session now holds three listeners. When the next answer is graded, the session delivers it three times. Two of those deliveries belong to screens that are no longer composed, and each of them writes into a `MutableState` that nothing renders. Meanwhile every one of those listeners closes over the screen's state, so none of it can be collected while the session is alive: the session outlives the screens, and it is holding them.

That is what a missing release actually costs — duplicated observer work, callbacks delivered to a screen that no longer owns them, and retained references. It is not "this could cause problems"; it is a specific number of stale listeners that grows every time the call site re-enters.

headers: What happens at the call site
rows: The effect enters the Composition with key K
The block runs once and registers for K
The body executes again and K still compares equal
Nothing. The existing registration stays; the block does not run again
K changes to L
`onDispose` for K runs first, then the block runs and registers for L
The call site leaves the Composition
`onDispose` for the current key runs and the registration is released
The composition attempt is abandoned before it is applied
The effect was never remembered, so nothing was registered and nothing is disposed

blocks.text: Keep the third and fourth rows distinct. A key change disposes and re-establishes; leaving the Composition disposes and does not re-establish. Ordinary recomposition with equal keys is neither — it does not dispose, and it does not re-register. The Compose documentation describes the key-change path as disposing the current effect and resetting by calling the effect again, performing cleanup for the old operation before initializing the new, so the obsolete registration is released before the replacement exists. On the configured runtime this was observed directly: a key change produced setup for A, then dispose for A, then setup for B, in that order. The two registrations never coexist.

Setup and cleanup necessarily share one key declaration because they are literally one call. The `onDispose` clause is created by the same execution of the block that performed the registration, so it closes over exactly the listener and exactly the session that execution used. Release therefore cannot drift onto a different object than the one acquired — which is why the real key failure is not an asymmetric cleanup but a key list that does not name what the registration depends on.

With a constant key the effect claims the whole composition lifetime of this call site. When `session` changes, nothing disposes and nothing re-registers: the screen keeps listening to the session it no longer displays, and the session it does display has no listener at all. The eventual `onDispose` is still correct for what was registered — it removes the first session's listener — but the screen was wrong for the entire interval in between. `lesson_effect_keys_as_dependencies` owns the key-comparison rules; this is what getting them wrong does to a registration.

An `onDispose { }` with an empty body is not a way to satisfy the compiler. It is a claim that this effect acquired nothing that needs releasing — and if that claim is true, `DisposableEffect` is the wrong mechanism. Ask what the block acquired. If the answer is nothing, the work is either a publication, which is the next lesson's subject, or a coroutine, which is Unit 9's.

The difference between `DisposableEffect` and `LaunchedEffect` is not that one has cleanup. A `LaunchedEffect` can perfectly well release something in a `finally` block, and `lesson_cancellation_cleanup_and_timeouts` already covers how a cancelled coroutine unwinds. The difference is what kind of lifetime the Composition is holding.

rows: A suspend operation that should run while this position is composed
`LaunchedEffect`
Cooperative cancellation of the coroutine; any release happens as the coroutine unwinds
A registration or resource held by an object outside Compose
`DisposableEffect`
A synchronous `onDispose` call at a defined moment on the apply dispatcher

blocks.text: Read the two rows as two questions. Is the thing being owned an in-flight computation whose end condition is "stop running"? Then cancellation is the end mechanism and a coroutine is the right owner. Is the thing being owned a reference some other object is holding on the Composition's behalf, whose end condition is "hand it back"? Then there is a specific call that must happen, and it must happen even though no coroutine is involved.

One combination is worth naming because it comes up whenever a registration invokes a caller-supplied callback. The registration's identity may be perfectly stable while the callback it should invoke changes with recomposition. Keying the effect on the callback would tear down and re-register the external observer for a reason the external world does not care about, discarding a valid subscription. Unit 10's `rememberUpdatedState` solves the value half without touching the lifetime half.

The rule this expresses is narrow and must not be over-applied: do not re-register an external observer merely because a callback changed, as long as the registration itself remains valid. If changing a value genuinely means the registration belongs somewhere else — a different session, a different lifecycle owner — then that value decides the registration and belongs in the key list. `session` is in the key list here for exactly that reason.

Say what `DisposableEffect` is for before describing what it does: the Composition is taking ownership of a registration that some object outside Compose will otherwise hold forever. Then give both release paths — key change and leaving the Composition — and one concrete consequence of omitting the release, such as three listeners on one session delivering every result three times.

lessons.title: `SideEffect`: Publishing to Non-Compose Code
lessons.summary: An object Compose does not manage sometimes has to hold the value the UI is currently built from. SideEffect schedules that publication to run when a composition completes successfully and applies its changes, which is what separates it from the same assignment written directly in a composable body.

blocks.text: Some objects a screen talks to are not part of the Compose world at all. An analytics client holds properties that are attached to every event it later records. A logging context holds the identifier of whatever the user is looking at. None of them is snapshot-backed, none of them participates in composition, and none of them can observe Compose state. They simply hold a value until something assigns a new one.

The requirement is therefore narrow and specific: a non-Compose object must be given the value that corresponds to the state Compose has actually settled on. Not a value from an intermediate calculation, and not a value from a composition that was discarded — the value the composed UI was built from.

`SideEffect` schedules its block rather than running it. The resolved Compose runtime 1.11.2 describes it as scheduling the effect to run when the current composition completes successfully and applies changes, so that objects managed outside the Composition are not left in an inconsistent state if the composition operation fails. The block runs on the composition's apply dispatcher and always after `RememberObserver` callbacks, and the documentation states the resulting guarantee as executing after every successful recomposition.

Compare it with the same assignment written in the body. That version publishes while the composable is executing — which is before anything has decided whether this composition attempt will become the applied UI.

`SideEffect` exists to tie a publication to a successful composition. A plain property assignment on an object Compose does not manage cannot be rolled back, so the moment it happens is the whole point.

Unit 9 established that Compose may calculate an updated UI and discard the result before it becomes the applied UI. That is the case the direct assignment gets wrong. If the attempt is abandoned rather than applied, the UI it described never takes effect — but `analytics.userType` was already overwritten, and the analytics client now reports a state the user was never shown. A `SideEffect` scheduled by that same abandoned attempt is not run, so it publishes nothing: the recorded effect never reaches the apply step it was recorded for.

Skipping is a different situation and needs different words. If the composable containing a `SideEffect` is skipped in a pass, its body is not executed for that pass, so that pass schedules no `SideEffect` from that call. Whatever was published last simply remains published, which is correct, because a skipped composable is one whose inputs have not changed.

headers: What happened to this composition pass
rows: The call executed and the composition was applied successfully
The scheduled block runs on the apply dispatcher, after remember callbacks
The composable was skipped in this pass
This call scheduled nothing in that pass; the previously published value still stands
The composition attempt was abandoned instead of applied
Nothing that attempt scheduled publishes the state it attempted

blocks.text: On the configured runtime this was observed directly. A parent that recomposed twice published twice, while a child composable whose parameter had not changed was skipped on the second pass and published once. Note carefully what that does and does not say.

Do not compress the skipping row into "SideEffect only runs when state changes". The contract is about successful composition passes in which this call participates, not about which state changed. A pass that executes this call and is applied publishes, whatever caused the pass.
The most expensive misreading of `SideEffect` is treating it as a general place to make something happen. It is not an event handler.

A publication point runs after every successful composition it participates in, and nothing in the API tells you how many of those there will be. A payment submitted from here is submitted again on the next successful recomposition. The defect is not that the code is ugly; it is that the API's contract is a frequency the caller does not control, which is the wrong contract for anything that must happen a specific number of times.

The bridge back is a question about the trigger, which Unit 10 already made the deciding one. If a click should start suspend work, the click owns the trigger and a remembered scope launches it. If entering or changing a composition state should start work, `LaunchedEffect` owns it. If an object outside Compose must be handed something back later, `DisposableEffect` owns it. `SideEffect` answers only the remaining case: composed state must be pushed synchronously into a non-Compose object once that composition has succeeded.

Two further limits follow from where the block runs. It is not a coroutine scope and cannot suspend, so it is not somewhere to launch work from. And because it runs on the composition's apply dispatcher, and appliers are never run concurrently with applying changes to the composition tree, expensive work placed here delays the application of the frame it belongs to. Keep it to assignment-shaped publication.

State the contract as timing, not as purpose: the block is scheduled and runs when the composition completes successfully and applies its changes. Then explain why that matters — an external assignment performed during an abandoned attempt cannot be unhappened — and finish by saying what `SideEffect` is not: not a callback, not a coroutine launcher, and not a general post-recomposition hook.

lessons.title: `produceState`: a Composition-Scoped Producer
lessons.summary: produceState turns an asynchronous or external source into a Compose State the UI can read, with a producer the Composition launches on entry, cancels on exit and restarts on a key change. Its returned State is remembered independently of those keys, which decides what the screen displays in the interval after a key change and before the new producer writes.

blocks.text: Unit 8 answered one half of the observation problem: when a screen already has a `Flow`, `collectAsState` converts it into renderable Compose `State`. The other half is a source that is not a stream yet. A one-shot suspend load, or a platform object that pushes values through a callback, produces data the UI needs but exposes nothing a composable can read.
`produceState` is the composition-scoped answer: a producer whose output is a Compose `State<T>`. The composable gets something it can read; the producer gets a lifetime the Composition owns.

The contract has four parts, and all four come from Unit 9's effect model rather than from anything new. The producer is launched when `produceState` enters the Composition. It is cancelled when `produceState` leaves the Composition. If a key changes, a running producer is cancelled and re-launched for the new source, using the same key comparison every effect uses. The producer writes results by assigning `value`, and the returned `State` is what Compose reads.

`initialValue` deserves a precise reading, because it is the part most often assumed to do more than it does. It establishes the value the returned `State` holds when that state producer is first created, and it holds it until the producer writes something else. It is not a loading marker Compose reapplies later, it is not persisted, it is not a replay of anything, and it is not a cache.

`produceState` is a producer with a composition lifetime and a `State` output. Everything about when it starts, stops and restarts is the effect-lifetime model you already have; what is new is that the result is a value the UI can read.

Now answer the question this Lesson exists for. `questionId` changes from `q1` to `q2`. The `q1` producer is cancelled and a `q2` producer is launched, but loading takes time. What does the returned `State` hold in that interval?

It holds the last value produced under `q1`. It does not revert to `initialValue`. This is measurable and it matters, because the screen is now showing the previous question's preview under the new question's id.

The reason is visible in the resolved Compose runtime 1.11.2 implementation, and it is not stated on the documentation page. `produceState` is a `remember { mutableStateOf(initialValue) }` plus a `LaunchedEffect(key)` over that state. The `remember` has no keys. The key belongs to the producer, not to the holder, so a key change replaces the producer and leaves the holder — and its current value — exactly as it was. On the configured toolchain a probe confirmed it: key `A` produced `A-result`, changing the key to `B` restarted the producer while the returned `State` still read `A-result`, and only the `B` producer's own write changed it.

If the requirement is "show Loading whenever the question changes", the producer has to say so. Writing the loading value as the first statement of each producer lifetime is the fix, because that statement does run again when the producer restarts.

The returned `State` also conflates. The runtime states it directly: no change is observable if a value equal to the current one is assigned, and observers may only see the latest value if several values are set in rapid succession. A probe on the configured runtime matched that — a producer that assigned the same loaded value three times produced exactly one observable change, and the reading composable executed twice in total, once for the initial value and once for the loaded one.

"The key changed, so the state resets to `initialValue`" is false on this runtime, and it is the assumption behind a real production defect: the previous item's data displayed under the new item's key while the new load is in flight. Predict the value from the implementation, not from the parameter name.
Because the runtime describes `produceState` in terms of a remembered state and a launched producer, it is worth writing both forms side by side. The second is the packaged version of the first.

These two behave the same way on a key change, including the part that surprises people — the hand-written `remember` has no keys either, so it keeps the old value too. That equivalence is the useful part of knowing the implementation: it lets you reason about `produceState` with a model you already have instead of memorising a special case.

The equivalence is not universal, though, and the difference is instructive. Writing `remember(questionId) { mutableStateOf(PreviewState.Loading) }` in the hand-rolled version would reset the holder on every key change, because a keyed `remember` recreates its value. `produceState` offers no such option: its holder is unkeyed by construction. So the two forms are the same only for the unkeyed holder, and the choice of which behaviour a screen needs remains the author's.

One boundary keeps this from being over-applied. `produceState` is not a replacement for ordinary stream collection. If the source is already a `Flow` and the requirement is simply to render its current collected value, the purpose-built conversion is Unit 8's — `collectAsState`, or the lifecycle-aware variant where the target's lifecycle should stop collection. Wrapping a collect call inside `produceState` is mechanically possible and is not the clearest abstraction for a source that is already a stream. Choose from what the source contract actually is, which is the next Lesson's subject.

Three claims separate recognition from understanding. The producer is composition-scoped, so it restarts on a key change and is cancelled on exit. The returned `State` is remembered independently of those keys, so a key change does not reapply `initialValue`. And the `State` conflates: it is a current value with equality-based change semantics, not a queue of everything assigned.

lessons.title: A Flow Below the UI, or a Producer at the Boundary?
lessons.summary: A callback-based source can be adapted into a reusable Flow below the UI or into a Compose-local state producer at the boundary. awaitDispose is what keeps a non-suspending subscription alive inside produceState and unregisters it on disposal, and the placement decision itself is answered from ownership and reuse rather than from API preference.

blocks.text: The previous Lesson's producer suspended: it called a suspend function and assigned the result. A callback-based source does not suspend. Registering a listener returns immediately, and a producer block that returns has finished — nothing is keeping the subscription's lifetime open, and nothing has been told to unregister when the producer is disposed.

`awaitDispose` is the suspension point that fills that gap. It never resumes normally — its return type is `Nothing` — and it always runs the supplied cleanup before the producer's coroutine completes, whether the producer left the Composition, a key changed, or an error occurred.

Read the block as four steps in order: register the callback; remain alive for as long as the Composition owns this producer; assign `value` as callbacks arrive so the UI re-reads; and unregister when the producer is disposed. It is the state-producer form of owning a callback subscription, and it is available in the common source set of the Compose runtime, so it is not an Android-only mechanism.
`awaitDispose` is needed exactly when the source registers instead of suspending. It gives a non-suspending subscription both a lifetime and one place for its unregistration.

This looks like the first Lesson's `DisposableEffect`, and it is not the same decision. Both register a callback and both release it, so "one is for callbacks" explains nothing. Separate them by what the composable needs as output.

rows: An external object must be told something and later told to stop; no Compose value is required
`DisposableEffect`
The registration itself
A callback source must become a `State<T>` the UI reads
`produceState` with `awaitDispose`
The subscription that was feeding `value`

blocks.text: A useful check: if a `DisposableEffect` exists only to write into a `remember { mutableStateOf(...) }` next to it, the producer shape is what that code actually wanted, and `produceState` states the intent in one call. If the registration produces no value the UI reads — a lifecycle observer that reports to analytics, a service that must be told a screen is visible — then no producer is required and `DisposableEffect` is the honest mechanism.

Unit 10's trigger distinction still applies and must not blur into this one. A listener registration is owned by a composition lifetime: it begins because the screen is composed and ends because the screen is gone. A button click that shows a snackbar is owned by an event: it begins because the user acted. Both are imperative, and that shared quality is not a reason to reach for the same API. Decide from the owner, the lifetime, the trigger, and whether a release is required.

Registering a listener inside a `produceState` block and letting the block end is a silent leak: the producer completes, but the source still holds the listener. The producer has to stay suspended for the subscription to have a lifetime at all.

There is one more question, and it is the one that separates a senior answer. The same callback source could be adapted one layer lower, as a `Flow` built with `callbackFlow`, whose `awaitClose` plays the same role for the same reason. So which side of the UI boundary should the adapter live on?

headers: Prefer a Flow below the UI when
rows: More than one consumer needs the source
The adaptation exists specifically for this Compose boundary
The adaptation is meaningful outside Compose
Composition should own the subscription's lifetime
Stream operators and composition are part of the source contract
The required output is specifically Compose `State`
The producer's lifetime belongs below the UI
Extracting a reusable stream would add an abstraction nothing reuses
A platform or domain layer should expose the observation API
The value is read by one screen and has no meaning elsewhere

blocks.text: Notice that neither column is about which API is better written. Both columns are about ownership and reuse. A connection monitor that three features observe, that the data layer wants to combine with a retry policy, and whose lifetime is the application's belongs below the UI, and `lesson_flow_builders_and_callback_adapters` already covers how to build that adapter — this Lesson does not repeat it. A monitor observed by exactly one screen, whose values exist only to be rendered by that screen, is adapted at the boundary, and extracting a general stream for it produces a layer with one caller.

The reverse mistake is just as common: keeping everything below the UI on principle, so a value that is only ever rendered by one composable travels through a repository, a mapper and a state holder that add no behaviour. Fictional reusability is still an abstraction cost.

Note also that the two answers are not symmetric in what they output. A Flow below the UI still has to reach the UI, and Unit 8's collection is what does that. Choosing the Flow does not remove the Compose-side step; it moves the adaptation and gives it other possible consumers. The full comparison of every Compose mechanism against a stated requirement is the subject of a later unit in this path.

Answer the placement question with ownership and reuse, and give a concrete threshold: more than one consumer, or meaning outside Compose, or a lifetime that is not a composition's, argues for a Flow below the UI. One screen, a Compose-only lifetime and a `State` output argue for the producer at the boundary. Then name `awaitDispose` and `awaitClose` as the same registration-and-cleanup idea on the two sides of that line.

units.title: Production UI Effects and Mechanism Selection
units.summary: Every mechanism in this path has now been met on its own, and production asks a different question: given a requirement, which of them does it actually need? This unit answers that from ownership, trigger, lifetime and cleanup, and takes the smallest mechanism that satisfies all four. It then separates what a screen currently is from what the UI should do once, and ends on the question a Compose effect cannot answer by itself — what must happen to a one-off occurrence when no UI is present to run it.

lessons.title: Choosing the Smallest Sufficient Mechanism
lessons.summary: A requirement chooses a mechanism, not familiarity or power. Work the decision in a fixed order — is there state to render, who owns it, what starts the work, what lifetime it needs, what has to be released — and take the smallest mechanism that satisfies the answer, including the answer that no composition-owned mechanism does.

blocks.text: Five units have introduced these mechanisms one problem at a time, and every one of them was the right answer to the problem it arrived with. Production does not arrive in that order. It arrives as a requirement — this screen has to show something, remember something, start something, register something, or hand something outward — and the engineer has to say which mechanism that requirement needs and why. That decision is this lesson, and it introduces no new API.

The failure it replaces is rarely ignorance of the APIs. It is reaching for the most powerful mechanism that could work rather than the smallest one that does. An unnecessary effect is not free: it is another lifetime to reason about, another key list to get right, and another thing every future reader of the screen has to check before changing anything. Often the correct answer is that no mechanism is needed at all.
Four facts decide every scenario below, and a scenario is not decided until each one has an answer:

items: Who owns the state — nobody, because nothing needs remembering; this composable; the closest common ancestor of the composables that use it; or an owner that lives outside the Composition.
Who owns the trigger — whether there is any work to start, and if there is, whether entering or changing a composition state starts it or an event does.
What lifetime the requirement needs — one composition, one value of one key, the screen, or longer than the screen.
What has to be released — nothing; a coroutine that ends by cancellation; or a registration that has to be handed back to an object Compose does not manage.

blocks.text: With those four in hand the decision is a short sequence of questions, asked in order and stopped at the first one the requirement actually answers.

items: Is there state to render? If there is none, do not invent some so that an effect has something to watch. If there is, ask who should own it — an ordinary parameter, local Compose state, hoisted state, or the screen's one current value.

Is an external observable value driving what is rendered? Then it has to become Compose `State` before a composable can render it, by collection — plainly, or lifecycle-aware where the host's activity should also gate the upstream.

What starts imperative or suspend work? If entering or changing a composition state starts it, the Composition owns the trigger and `LaunchedEffect` is the mechanism. If a click or another callback starts it, the event owns the trigger and a remembered scope is.
Does long-lived work need the current value of something that should not end it? That is `rememberUpdatedState`, and it is not a key question.
Does the Composition acquire something that has to be given back? A registration paired with its release is `DisposableEffect`.
Does code outside Compose need the value the composed UI was actually built from? That is `SideEffect`.

Does an external producer have to become Compose `State`? Decide from ownership and reuse — a stream that already exists below the UI is simply collected, a source worth reusing is adapted into a Flow there, and a source that exists only for this boundary can be a Compose-local `produceState`, with `awaitDispose` when its subscription does not suspend.
Must the work continue after this screen's Composition ends? Then none of the mechanisms above is the answer, and that is a result rather than a dead end.

blocks.text: Name the four facts before naming a mechanism. Owner, trigger, lifetime and cleanup decide the answer; the API is only what that answer is called. The smallest mechanism that satisfies all four is the right one, and sometimes that is no mechanism.
Three screens from this app's own practice flow, each worked through the four facts. The first is the one most often over-engineered, because it contains nothing to run.

State owner: this composable, because nothing else reads `expanded` and nothing else writes it. Trigger owner: there is no trigger, because there is no work — a tap changes a value, and describing the UI from the new value is not work that needs starting. Lifetime: this composition, and a panel that reopens collapsed after the screen is rebuilt is acceptable here; if it were not, that is a saved-state question and not an effect question. Cleanup: nothing. The smallest sufficient mechanism is a local `remember`, and the `explanation` parameter beside it needs even less — it is rendered directly, and turning it into state would add an owner for a value nobody changes.
The second screen does start work, and the interesting part is that it needs two mechanisms for two different reasons.

State owner: none of this is screen state — which question is active belongs to the screen's current value, and the countdown holds nothing of its own. Trigger owner: the Composition, because the countdown should begin when this composition starts representing a question and no user action is involved. Lifetime: one value of `questionId`, because a different question makes the running countdown obsolete. Cleanup: the coroutine ends by cancellation on a key change or on leaving; nothing is handed back. That gives `LaunchedEffect(questionId)`. The callback is a separate fact: it must be current when the countdown fires, and it must not decide when the countdown ends. Adding `onTimeout` as a second key would answer the value question by restarting the timer, which is the wrong answer to a question nobody asked.
The third screen starts work too, and the trigger belongs to somebody else.

State owner: none. Trigger owner: the tap. Lifetime: the screen — if the learner navigates away mid-scroll, the work should stop with the screen. Cleanup: cancellation of the launched coroutine, which the remembered scope already provides. The smallest sufficient mechanism is `rememberCoroutineScope` and a `launch` from the callback, and the shape worth noticing is what is absent: no remembered flag, and nothing for an effect to observe.

Converting a click into a `Boolean` so that a `LaunchedEffect` has something to key on. The click is already the trigger. The flag adds state nobody renders, a second thing that has to be reset, and a lifetime that no longer matches the occurrence it was meant to represent.

The same four columns answer the rest of the screens this path has built towards. Every outcome in the table is a mechanism an earlier unit owns, and the last row is an outcome with no mechanism in it at all.
