blocks.text: Read the table as output rather than as a lookup. Two rows can be the same screen: the sixth and seventh are one countdown, separated because they answer different facts. The twelfth row is the eleventh with one fact changed, and what moved the adapter was ownership rather than anything about callbacks. A row can only be reached by having answered the four columns to its left, which is the part a table cannot do for you.

"Smallest" has a precise meaning here: the mechanism that satisfies the four facts and claims nothing beyond them. Each substitution below is one engineers really make, and each claims more than the requirement asked for.

items: Writing a value the screen already has into state from inside a `LaunchedEffect`. If rendering the value is sufficient, there is nothing to run and nothing to keep consistent.
Introducing a screen-level owner for a value one composable reads and writes. Hoisting has a lowest sensible position, and the top of the screen is not automatically it.

Collecting a stream by hand in a `LaunchedEffect` and assigning into a `mutableStateOf`. That is an ongoing conversion written as an effect, and the conversion already has mechanisms with the right contract.
Turning an event into persistent state so an effect can observe it. The event owns the trigger; giving the trigger to the Composition changes when the work starts and how often.

Reaching for `produceState` because a callback is involved. Its purpose is producing a `State`; a listener whose job is to notify something else produces none, and the registration mechanism is the smaller answer.

Adding a key to keep a value current. A key says "end the current work when this changes", so using one to refresh a value buys correctness in the value at the cost of a lifetime the requirement never asked to shorten.

blocks.text: Treating the mechanisms as a power ranking with `LaunchedEffect` at the top. They answer different questions, so "more powerful" is not a property any of them has. The side-effects documentation makes the same point from the other direction: because effects open up so many possibilities, they are easily overused, and the work done in one should be UI-related and should not break unidirectional data flow.

The last question in the sequence is the one worth practising, because its answer is a negative result and negative results feel like failures. A committed submission, a durable save, an upload already in flight, a payment: each names a lifetime the screen does not have, and no composition-owned mechanism can lend it one. A remembered scope is cancelled when the call leaves the Composition, and an effect is cancelled when its position leaves — that is what they are for, and it is exactly wrong for work that must not stop. Answering "none of these" is therefore a correct outcome of the decision, and it is reached by asking about lifetime rather than by trying mechanisms until one seems to fit.

What happens next is deliberately not this unit's decision. The work needs an owner whose lifetime matches the requirement; which owner that is, how it is built and where it lives belong to the architecture curriculum. This unit's contribution is the diagnosis and the vocabulary to state it precisely: the required lifetime exceeds the Composition's, so the Composition cannot be the owner.

When asked which effect API you would use, name the facts before the API: who owns the state, who owns the trigger, how long the work must live, and what has to be released. Then name the smallest mechanism those facts allow — and be willing to answer that the requirement needs no mechanism, or that it needs an owner the Composition cannot provide.

lessons.title: Rendering State and Running a Transient Effect
lessons.summary: A screen renders what it currently is, and sometimes it also has to do something once. Those are different contracts: rendering a condition again changes nothing, while executing an occurrence again is visible to the user — which is why a screen that models an occurrence as a durable flag can perform it twice.

blocks.text: Two requirements on one screen can read almost identically and behave nothing alike. "The save button is disabled while a save is in flight" describes what the screen currently is. "Confirm the save with a snackbar" describes something the UI should do once. The first is rendered, as often as Compose needs to, and rendering it again changes nothing anybody can see. The second is executed, and executing it again is immediately visible.

Current state is the ordinary case and needs no effect at all. The question that is selected, whether the screen is loading, a validation message that should stay on screen while the input is still invalid, the active filter: each of these is true until something makes it false, and a composition that describes it again is doing exactly its job. This is why the previous lesson's decision starts with rendering — most of a production screen is this, and none of it needs a mechanism.

A transient occurrence is not a value the UI shows. It is work the UI performs: show a snackbar, move focus into a field, animate or scroll to something, raise a request to go somewhere else. Performing it needs a coroutine or effect lifetime that actually runs it, which is why it belongs to the effect mechanisms rather than to rendering. The distinction is not decoration versus content; it is description versus execution.

The tempting shortcut is to sort requirements by widget, and dialogs are the clearest evidence that this does not work. "The unsaved-changes dialog is visible while an unsaved edit exists" is a condition, and modelling it as state is right — it should still be there after the screen is rebuilt. "Open the image chooser once, because the learner just asked for it" is an occurrence. Same component, different requirement, different answer. Decide from what the requirement says must be true, never from the type of UI involved.

"This condition is currently true" and "this occurrence happened once" are different contracts. Rendering a condition repeats harmlessly by design; executing an occurrence does not, and no value carries the difference unless the requirement put it there.
The failure worth seeing in full is an occurrence given the contract of a condition. Here is a screen state carrying a flag for a completed save.

blocks.code:
data class EditorScreenState(
    val draft: String,
    val saved: Boolean,
)

blocks.text: Read the field before reading the effect. `saved` says that a save succeeded, and nothing in the type says it stops being true afterwards; it is a condition, and the screen's owner keeps it as part of the current value. Now read the effect. It starts when that branch enters the Composition with `saved == true`, and it starts again every later time the branch enters with the same value — after the screen is rebuilt and collects the current state again, after the learner returns while the flag still stands, or simply after the branch left and came back. Each of those is a new effect lifetime, and each runs the snackbar, although the learner saved once.

The defect is not the API and not the key. `LaunchedEffect(state.saved)` behaves precisely as the effect unit described: equal keys keep an effect running across recomposition, and a new lifetime starts a new effect. The defect is that a durable condition was handed to a mechanism whose job is execution. The value answers "is a successful save currently recorded?" while the requirement asked "did a save just happen?", and no key list can express a difference the value does not carry.

headers: What the screen should do with it
rows: A save is currently in flight
The same disabled button is described again — nothing changes for the user
Render it
A validation message is currently set
The same message is described again — nothing changes for the user
Render it
A save succeeded at some point
The snackbar runs again — the user sees a second confirmation of one save
Establish what the occurrence actually requires before rendering or executing it

blocks.text: This is a different question from the one the trigger lesson asked about a similar shape. There the choice was between a composition-owned trigger and an event-owned one, and letting the tap launch the snackbar was the fix. Here the prior question is what contract the value has at all — because a screen whose state genuinely carries a durable fact is not repaired by moving the trigger, and a fact the requirement says must survive the screen's absence is not repaired by deleting it either.

Once a requirement really is an occurrence, the trigger still decides which mechanism runs it. A tap that should scroll, move focus or confirm is event-owned, and a remembered scope launches it from the callback. A composition state that genuinely means "this screen now represents something that should be announced" is composition-owned, and an effect keyed on whatever identifies that occurrence runs it. Neither is a default.

Compressing this into "transient effects use `LaunchedEffect`" or "transient effects use `rememberCoroutineScope`". Both rules build the wrong screen about half the time. The occurrence that owns the start is still what decides, and this lesson only changes what you ask before you get there.

A navigation request deserves naming because it is the transient action most often got wrong, and because it changes none of the reasoning. From here, "ask to show the result screen" is one more piece of UI work that should happen once: it has a trigger, it executes, and performing it twice is visible as a duplicated destination. How destinations, routes and the back stack work is the navigation curriculum's subject, and nothing in this decision depends on it.

The correction here is easy to over-apply into "one-off things must never be state", which is wrong in the opposite direction. Some occurrences have to be recorded precisely because they must survive being missed. A completed payment is not made transient by having happened once: if the screen must show it correctly after the app is reopened, the durable fact is the requirement, and rendering it is the right treatment. The mistake in the editor screen above was not that a fact was stored — it was that a stored fact was wired to a mechanism that executes.

So the useful habit is a question rather than a rule. Before turning an occurrence into transient UI execution, ask what has to be true if nobody is there to execute it. A Compose effect can only run what the UI receives while the UI is present, and whether that is acceptable is a property of the requirement rather than of the API. That question is the next lesson, and it is where the Compose boundary turns out to have an edge.

Where this stops is deliberate. Whether such an occurrence is carried in the screen's state, recorded somewhere as handled, or delivered in some other way is an application-architecture decision with real trade-offs, and the architecture curriculum owns it. What belongs here is the Compose-side diagnosis and the ability to state it exactly: an execution mechanism was given a value whose contract does not say "once", and no effect key repairs that.

State the two contracts in one sentence each — a condition is rendered and repeats harmlessly, an occurrence is executed and repeating it is a user-visible defect. Then show the failure concretely: a durable flag re-entering composition starts a new effect lifetime and runs the one-off work again. Finish by saying what you would ask next, which is what the occurrence requires when no UI is present.

lessons.title: What Delivery Guarantee Does This Occurrence Need?
lessons.summary: Before choosing how a one-off occurrence reaches the UI, state what must happen when no UI is there to receive it. May it be dropped, may a later screen see it, may it be seen twice, must anything record that it was handled — those answers decide whether a transient mechanism is sufficient, and frequently they show that the problem has left the Compose boundary.

blocks.text: The previous lesson ended with an occurrence that has to be executed and a screen that may or may not be present to execute it. That gap is the subject here, and the order of reasoning is the whole point: state the requirement first, choose the mechanism second. Picking a shared flow, a channel, a state holder, a remembered flag or a particular Compose effect before the requirement is stated is how a screen ends up with a delivery guarantee nobody asked for, or without one nobody noticed was missing.

Make the absence concrete. A learner starts a practice session, backgrounds the app and goes to do something else, so the screen that would react is not composed at all. Somewhere below the UI, work finishes — a sync completes, a purchase is confirmed, a session is scored — and produces the occurrence "show the result". Some time later the screen appears.
Six questions about that moment decide everything that follows:

items: Must the occurrence still happen when a screen finally appears, or was it only meaningful while somebody was watching?
May it simply be discarded because nobody was there?
May a screen that arrives later observe it?
May more than one observer act on it?
Is repeating it harmful, or merely untidy?
Does anything have to record that it was handled?

blocks.text: None of those is a question about a type. Each is a property of the product requirement, and together they state what any mechanism would have to provide. Asking them in this order also exposes the usual shortcut: "events are being lost, so add replay" answers only the third question, and quietly changes the answer to the fifth.

Answer the UI-absent case before choosing anything. Whether an occurrence may be dropped, may be seen later, may be seen twice, and must be acknowledged are four independent answers, and a mechanism has to satisfy all of them, not the one that made it look suitable.

The coroutines and Flow path already settled the emitter's half of this, and the job here is to apply it rather than rebuild it. One conclusion carries most of the weight: a producer accepting a value and the intended UI handling the occurrence are different facts.

blocks.code:
// Accepted by the flow under its current configuration — and nothing more than that.
val accepted = events.tryEmit(ShowSessionResult(sessionId))

blocks.text: On an unbuffered shared flow with no subscriber, that call returns `true` and the value is gone at once: `true` records that the flow took the call, and with nobody to hand the value to and no replay cache to hold it, nothing remains. The stream lesson measured exactly that on this project's toolchain, so this lesson cites it rather than re-deriving it. At the Compose boundary the consequence is blunt — a UI effect cannot execute something the UI never received, and a log line written from a `true` result is evidence about the producer, not about the screen.

The reflex repair is a replay window, and it is a real mechanism with a real cost. Replay changes what a subscriber arriving later can still recover. It does not make an occurrence delivered, and it certainly does not make it delivered once. A recreated screen is a new collector, and a new collector reads what was retained — so an occurrence kept for the screen that was absent is equally available to the screen that already acted on it. "Must not be lost" and "must happen exactly once" are two different requirements, and retention answers at most the first of them.

Reading "the event was lost" as "set a replay of one". That is a decision about retention being used to answer a question about handling, and it trades one failure for another: a missed confirmation becomes a repeated one. Which trade is acceptable depends entirely on what repeating the occurrence does, and a repeated charge or a repeated destination is far worse than a missed toast.
Answering the six questions sorts requirements into three broad classes, and the class — not the type — is what says whether the Compose side can finish the job.

headers: What the requirement says about the UI being absent
rows: If no relevant UI exists, nothing needs to happen
An ephemeral, UI-only occurrence
The Compose side is sufficient: whichever screen is present executes it
A screen arriving later must be able to see that this is currently true
A fact about current state, not an occurrence at all
A current value that somebody owns — the shape the stream curriculum calls current-value semantics
It must not disappear merely because nobody was watching, and somebody must have handled it
A delivery requirement no transient in-memory mechanism satisfies
Outside the Compose boundary, with an owner whose lifetime and record match the requirement

blocks.text: The first class is real, and choosing it is not a compromise. A brief animation when a score changes, a non-essential confirmation, a focus request on the field the learner is currently in: each of them is meaningless with no UI, and answering "nothing needs to happen" is a decision rather than an oversight. These are exactly the occurrences the previous lesson's mechanisms execute, and nothing further is warranted.

The second class is the one most often mis-filed. "There is an unfinished practice session" or "the last submission failed" sound like events because they became true at a particular moment, but the requirement is that a screen opening afterwards knows the current position. That is a state requirement, and recognising it is the correction — the stream curriculum already establishes what current-value semantics provide, and which holder should own that value is an architecture decision this unit does not make.

The third class is where the Compose boundary ends. If the requirement names persistence, acknowledgement, queueing, retries, a durable record or guaranteed later handling, then no configuration of a transient in-memory stream and no Compose effect satisfies it, because each of them lives and dies with the objects holding it. The Android architecture guidance states the same limit from the producer's side: when the producer outlives the consumer, these solutions do not guarantee the delivery and processing of those events. Say that plainly, then choose an owner whose lifetime and guarantees actually match — and stop, because designing that owner is the architecture curriculum's work and not this unit's.

Two slogans get in the way of all of this, and both should be retired. "One stream type is for state and another is for events" is half right in a way that makes the wrong half dangerous: current-value semantics really are what state needs, but the event half promises a delivery guarantee no broadcast stream provides. Replacing it with "a channel is for events" repeats the mistake with a different type, because single-receiver delivery decides which receiver gets an element, not that the work on it ever completes. Neither slogan is improved by treating a broadcast stream as the standard answer for one-off UI events; that is the same claim with the reasoning removed.

The general form is worth being able to state. A stream type describes delivery; a requirement describes handling; and no description of delivery answers a question about handling. The dimensions that actually decide were established by the stream curriculum — whether a current value is obligatory, whether observers are present at production time, what is retained for a late one, whether delivery is broadcast or single-receiver, whether duplication or loss is acceptable, and whether anything records that the occurrence was dealt with. This lesson contributes only the consumer's half of the question, and it is the half a stream cannot see.

That contrast is the reason this lesson exists beside the stream material rather than repeating it. The stream lessons ask what a given abstraction delivers. This one asks whether that delivery contract satisfies the requirement, given that this particular UI exists for only part of the time — a fact about the screen's lifetime that no configuration of the producer knows about.

The endpoint of the decision is therefore not an architecture; it is a sentence. Choose an owner whose lifetime and delivery guarantees actually match the requirement. Which owner that is, how the occurrence is recorded, how handling is marked and how the UI consumes it are genuine design questions with genuine trade-offs, and the architecture curriculum answers them. Recognising that you have arrived at them, and being able to say precisely which guarantee is missing, is what this unit is for.

Answer a one-off-event question by stating the requirement before the type: what must happen if no UI is collecting, whether a later screen may see it, whether it may be seen twice, and whether anything must record that it was handled. Then give the three consequences — a successful emission is not a delivery, retention is not exactly-once, and a requirement naming persistence or acknowledgement has left the UI layer.

units.title: Coroutine Fundamentals and Structured Concurrency
units.summary: Nearly every hard defect in asynchronous Android code comes from the same place: nobody can say what a piece of work's lifetime is. This unit builds the model that makes that answerable, in the order the ideas depend on one another. Suspension explains what a coroutine can do that a thread cannot; builders explain how work starts and what handle the caller gets back; `Job` gives that work an observable lifetime and a position in a hierarchy; `CoroutineScope` says who owns it; and structured concurrency turns ownership and hierarchy into guarantees a caller can rely on. Where code actually runs, how cancellation works, and what a failure does are deliberately later units — all three assume this material.

lessons.title: Suspension Is Not Blocking
lessons.summary: The most damaging misconception in this subject is that `suspend` means the work happens somewhere else. It does not. `suspend` is a statement about how a function may pause and says nothing about which thread runs it, which is why deciding whether a suspending call is safe on the main thread means opening it and reading what is inside.

blocks.text: Almost every interesting program spends most of its life waiting — for a response, for a file, for a timer, for the user to do something. What the machine does with that waiting time is the question this whole subject exists to answer, and there are only two broad answers to it.

One sentence of background makes the contrast work. A **thread** is a unit of execution the operating system schedules: it owns a call stack, costs memory measured in megabytes, and the JVM can typically keep a few thousand of them alive at once. Threads are how a program does more than one thing, and they are a finite resource that something eventually has to hand back.

**Blocking** is the first answer to waiting: the thread sits on the call until it returns. The thread is not doing work during that time, but it is also unavailable to anybody else. **Suspending** is the second: the coroutine pauses and the thread it was running on is released. Kotlin's documentation states it directly — coroutines "can suspend their execution instead of blocking a thread", which "allows one coroutine to suspend while waiting for some data to arrive and another coroutine to run on the same thread".

`suspend` is the keyword that marks a function as allowed to pause that way. It is a compile-time contract with two consequences and no others: the function may contain suspension points, and it can only be called from another suspending function or from a coroutine builder. That is the entire promise.

Everything people commonly read into the keyword is absent from it. `suspend` does not pick a thread or a thread pool. It does not move work into the background. It does not make a slow call fast, and it cannot change what the code inside the function actually does. A suspending function is perfectly free to sit on a thread for a second and never pause at all.

Both functions are marked `suspend` and the compiler is equally happy with both. Only one of them suspends. `delay` is documented as delaying a coroutine for at least the given time "without blocking a thread"; `Thread.sleep` holds the thread for the whole second. The keyword did not make the second behave like the first, and nothing in either signature tells them apart. (`Thread.sleep` is a JVM API, so that pair is a JVM and Android example — but the point it makes, that a blocking call inside a suspending function is still a blocking call, is not platform-specific.)

One sentence of mechanism is worth having and no more than one. A suspended coroutine is a stored **continuation** — the point to resume from, plus the local state needed to resume there — rather than a parked thread with a stack. That is why a suspended coroutine costs almost nothing, and why the thread can be handed to somebody else while it waits. How the compiler produces that continuation is not something any decision in your code depends on.

`suspend` describes how a function is allowed to pause. It does not describe where the function runs, and it cannot change what the code inside it does. A suspending function full of blocking calls blocks exactly as much as the same code would without the keyword.
Reading asynchronous code well means keeping three questions apart, because they have three different answers and only the first one is visible in a signature.

items: **Is this function allowed to suspend?** The `suspend` modifier answers this, and only this.

**Does this call actually block?** Only the code inside it can tell you. A suspending function that wraps a blocking API blocks; a suspending function that awaits a genuinely asynchronous one does not.
**Where does this run?** A separate question again, answered by the coroutine's dispatcher rather than by anything on the function.

blocks.text: The third question has a unit of its own and is deliberately left there. For now it is enough to know that the **dispatcher** is the part of a coroutine's configuration that decides which thread or thread pool runs it, that a coroutine inherits one rather than choosing one per call, and that nothing about the `suspend` keyword participates in that decision. Choosing dispatchers, and the damage a wrong choice does, is the next unit's subject.
That leaves the question you actually have to answer in front of real code: is this call safe from the main thread? Two functions with the same shape can have opposite answers.

The difference is invisible from the call site, which is why main-safety is treated as the obligation of the function being called rather than of the caller. Android's guidance states it in as many words: suspending functions "should be **main-safe**, meaning they're safe to call from the main thread", and a class that performs long-running blocking operations "must move execution off the main thread" itself. Read that for what it is — a **convention** about whose job main-safety is. Nothing enforces it: `readSettings` above breaks the convention and compiles perfectly, and no warning anywhere will mention it. So a `suspend` signature tells you what its author was supposed to have done, never what they did, and on a function you have not read the only way to find out is to open it.

The cost of getting this wrong is easy to make visible. Measured on this project's JVM target, on a dispatcher backed by a single thread: two coroutines each running `Thread.sleep(300)` took **607 ms** in total, while two coroutines each running `delay(300)` took **310 ms**. The blocking pair could not overlap, because there was one thread and the first coroutine never gave it up. On Android that thread is often the one drawing frames.

"I made it `suspend`, so it is off the main thread." Adding the keyword changes what the compiler permits and nothing about where the code runs; if the body was blocking the main thread before, it still is. The habit that replaces the belief is small: when you want to know whether a call is safe on the main thread, open it and look at what it does, and keep going until you reach either a genuinely suspending API or something that moves the work itself.

The reason suspension is worth a language feature is arithmetic. A waiting coroutine costs a continuation; a waiting thread costs a stack. Kotlin's own comparison runs 50,000 tasks that each wait five seconds: as coroutines that is roughly 500 MB, and as JVM threads it can reach 100 GB — far enough past the limit that the thread version may simply fail to start. "Many concurrent operations" is a design option in one model and an impossibility in the other.

Keeping the word "blocking" precise matters here, because two different things get called by that name and collapsing them removes the ground the next unit stands on. A **blocking call** holds a thread that is doing nothing — waiting on a socket, a lock, a sleep. A **CPU-bound loop** holds a thread that is doing work as fast as it can. They share one consequence, that the thread is unavailable and the coroutine reaches no suspension point, and they need different answers, which is exactly why the dispatchers unit separates the pools they belong on.

The shared consequence is worth seeing rather than believing. Measured the same way: on a single-thread dispatcher, a coroutine running a 250 ms busy loop finished entirely before a second coroutine launched onto the same dispatcher started at all. Nothing had gone wrong and nothing was misconfigured; there was simply no moment at which the first coroutine offered the thread back.

That points at a second consequence, which the cancellation unit later builds on. Cancellation in Kotlin is **cooperative**: a coroutine finds out it has been cancelled where it suspends at a cancellable point, or where its own code deliberately looks. A coroutine that does neither runs to the end regardless of what anybody else has asked for — the request is recorded and simply never observed. Where those checks belong, what they cost, and what a cancelled coroutine may still do are the third unit's subject rather than this one's.

"What does `suspend` do?" has a wrong answer that sounds right — "it runs the function in the background" — and interviewers ask it because the wrong answer is so common. Give the contract: the function may pause at a suspension point without holding its thread, and it can only be called from another suspending function or a builder. Then volunteer the boundary before you are pushed to it: the keyword chooses no thread and no dispatcher, and a suspending function that wraps a blocking call is not main-safe. If you can add why the model exists — a suspended coroutine costs a continuation rather than a stack — you have answered the follow-up too.

lessons.title: Starting Coroutines: `launch`, `async` and `runBlocking`
lessons.summary: A suspending function cannot start itself, so somewhere the chain has to begin. Three builders begin it, and they differ in what the caller receives and what the caller is able to do next — a handle, a future value, or a blocked thread. Choosing between them is a statement of intent that every later reader of the code will believe.

blocks.text: Suspension explains what a coroutine is able to do. It does not explain how one starts, and by itself it cannot: a suspending function can only be called from another suspending function, so the chain has to begin somewhere outside it. **Coroutine builders** are where it begins.

Three of them cover almost everything you will write. The useful way to tell them apart is not what they do to the work — all three run the block as a coroutine — but what they hand back and what the caller can do the instant afterwards.

rows: `launch`
the work has to happen and there is no result to return
`Job`
immediately, while the coroutine runs
`async`
the work produces a value somebody is going to consume
`Deferred<T>`
immediately; `await()` suspends until the value is ready
`runBlocking`
non-coroutine code has to call suspending code and there is no scope to launch into
whatever the block returns
only once the coroutine and everything launched in it has finished

blocks.text: `CoroutineScope.launch()` "starts a new coroutine without blocking the rest of the scope", and the documentation's own advice on when to use it is a description of intent rather than of mechanism: "to run a task alongside other work when the result isn't needed or you don't want to wait for it". It returns a `Job` handle, which the next lesson is about.

`CoroutineScope.async()` "starts a concurrent computation inside an existing coroutine scope and returns a `Deferred` handle that represents an eventual result", and `await()` is how you get that result: it suspends "until the result is ready". For this lesson that is the whole of `async` — it is the builder that gives you a value back.

`runBlocking` is the odd one out, and it is odd on purpose. It "creates a coroutine scope and blocks the current thread until the coroutines launched in that scope finish", and Kotlin's guidance for it is unusually blunt: use it "only when there is no other option to call suspending code from non-suspending code". Its API documentation is specific about where that is — it is "designed to bridge regular blocking code to libraries that are written in suspending style, to be used in `main` functions, in tests, and in non-`suspend` callbacks when `suspend` functions need to be called".

`launch` and `async` are extension functions on `CoroutineScope`, which is why neither can be called from nowhere: every coroutine they start belongs to something. `runBlocking` creates a scope of its own, and that is exactly what makes it a bridge rather than a fourth way of starting work inside code that already has one. As for the `{ }` after each call, that is an ordinary Kotlin trailing lambda — these are functions whose last parameter is itself a function, so the argument moves outside the parentheses, and `launch(dispatcher) { }` is the same shape with one ordinary argument in front.

Pick the builder from the intent, not from the shape of the surrounding code. `launch` says "this has to happen and there is nothing to hand back". `async` says "this produces a value I am going to use". `runBlocking` says "I am not in coroutine code, and I am willing to stop this thread until I am".
The first mistake is quiet. It compiles, it works, and it misinforms everybody who reads it afterwards.

Both run `save`, and the second is better code for a reason that has nothing to do with speed. `async` returns a `Deferred`, and a `Deferred` is a claim that somebody is going to ask for the outcome. Dropping it means the author either did not know that or did not mean it, and the next reader has to work out which — usually while looking for a bug elsewhere. `launch` states the intent exactly, and the type system stops implying anything else.

There is a second half to this that the failure unit owns. `async` stores its outcome in the `Deferred`, and a failure is an outcome, so an unconsumed `Deferred` is also an unread failure. What that failure then does to the rest of the coroutine tree is a question about propagation and supervision, and it is deliberately not answered here. The builder choice is worth making correctly on the intent argument alone.

The second mistake is loud, and the useful skill is predicting it from the definition rather than remembering a rule about it. `runBlocking` blocks the calling thread until its coroutine finishes. On Android's main thread, that thread is the one that draws frames, dispatches touches and runs lifecycle callbacks, so for the duration of the call the app renders nothing and responds to nothing; long enough and the system raises an ANR. Measured on this project's JVM target, `runBlocking { delay(300) }` returned to its caller after **306 ms**: suspending inside the block changed nothing whatsoever for the thread outside it, which is the entire point of a bridge.

Treating `runBlocking` as "the way to call a suspending function". It is not a converter from suspending to ordinary code; it is a thread being spent to wait. Inside a suspending function it is redundant by construction — the documentation's own example labels it "redundant and blocks the thread, avoid this", because you already had the ability to suspend and gave it away, "potentially leading to thread starvation issues". When `runBlocking` looks necessary in application code, the thing actually missing is a scope.

The interesting difference between `launch` and `async` is not the return type, it is the obligation the return type creates. A `Job` answers "is it still running, and has it finished?". A `Deferred` answers that and also "what did it produce?" — so choosing `async` adds a question somebody is expected to ask. Code that never asks it has an unmet obligation sitting in plain sight, which is why the unconsumed `Deferred` reads as a defect even before anything goes wrong.

Two things are deliberately absent from the builder list, and naming them is what stops them creeping in. **`withContext` is not a builder.** It starts no coroutine; it is a suspending function that runs a block with a changed context and returns the block's result. Filing it alongside `launch` and `async` is precisely how people come to believe it "starts something", and telling it apart from the scope builders is the next unit's job. And **`async` is not a parallelism feature here** — in this lesson it is the builder that returns a value, nothing more. Deciding when work should genuinely overlap, and what overlapping is worth, is a separate decision made later.

One parameter is worth recognising without reaching for it: both builders accept a `CoroutineStart`, and `CoroutineStart.LAZY` produces a coroutine that does not begin until its handle is started or awaited. It exists, it is occasionally the right tool, and it is not part of the intent decision this lesson is about.

The deeper reading of `runBlocking` is that blocking is a property of the *caller's thread* rather than of the coroutine. Nothing inside the block behaves differently; the coroutine suspends and resumes exactly as it would anywhere else. What differs is that one thread has been assigned to stand there until the whole thing is over. That is a defensible trade at a process boundary — a `main` function, a test, a callback that cannot suspend — and indefensible on a thread that has other obligations, and the same sentence explains both cases.

"What is the difference between `launch` and `async`?" invites the weak answer, "`async` returns a value". Say that and then say the thing behind it: the builder records the intent, `launch` for work with no result to hand back and `async` for a computation whose `Deferred` somebody is expected to consume, so `async { }` with a dropped handle is a statement the code does not mean. Expect a `runBlocking` follow-up, and answer it with the consequence rather than the word "bad": it blocks the calling thread until the coroutine completes, which is what you want in a `main` function or a test and what causes a frozen UI on the main thread.

lessons.title: `Job`: the Handle That Carries Lifetime
lessons.summary: `launch` returns a `Job` and most call sites throw it away, which makes it easy to read as a formality. It is the opposite: the `Job` is where a coroutine's lifetime becomes something anybody can ask questions about, and it is the edge that attaches a coroutine to its parent and its children.

blocks.text: Every coroutine has a `Job`. `launch` returns one directly; `async` returns a `Deferred`, which its documentation defines as "a `Job` with a result". The `Job` documentation's own one-line definition is worth keeping: "a job is a cancellable thing with a lifecycle that concludes in its completion". The useful reading of that is that a `Job` **is** the coroutine's lifetime, turned into an object you can hold.
Holding it lets you do three things, and they are the reasons the builders return it at all.

items: **Wait for it.** `join()` "suspends the coroutine until this job is complete", and it "resumes normally (without exception) when the job is complete for any reason".
**Ask about it.** `isActive`, `isCompleted` and `isCancelled` report which part of the lifecycle the job is currently in.
**Locate it in the tree.** A job knows its `parent` and can list its `children`, because jobs "can be arranged into parent-child hierarchies".

blocks.text: The parent-child link is not something you have to set up. A coroutine inherits its parent from the context it is started in, so a coroutine started inside another coroutine becomes that coroutine's child, and a coroutine started from a scope becomes a child of that scope's job. That inheritance is the default and it is what essentially all code relies on; it is also the mechanism underneath everything the last lesson of this unit describes. It can be overridden — passing a `Job` explicitly to a builder re-parents that coroutine out of the scope that launched it, which is a trap worth knowing about and the context unit's to take apart. Nothing in this unit does it.

Discarding the returned `Job` is normal and usually right. It is returned for the cases that need it, not as something every call has to consume: you keep it when you have to wait for exactly this piece of work, when something else has to be able to stop it, or when you want to report on whether it is still going.

One more fact belongs here in a single sentence, because the next unit builds on it. The `Job` is also an element of the coroutine's **context**, alongside things such as the dispatcher — that is how a new coroutine finds the right parent without anybody passing one around by hand. What a context is and what a child inherits from it is the next unit's first lesson.
The builder call starts the work. The `Job` is what lets anyone afterwards say anything true about that work: whether it is still running, when it actually finished, and what it is attached to.
Here is the case worth predicting before reading the answer, because the intuitive prediction is wrong and the correct one is the whole point of the parent-child link.

The parent's block has run to the end. It is nevertheless not complete, because it has a child that is not finished. Measured on this project's JVM target at the 100 ms mark: `isActive` was `true`, `isCompleted` was `false`, the job reported exactly one child, and printing the job itself gave `StandaloneCoroutine{Completing}`. After `parent.join()` returned, `isCompleted` was `true`.

**Completing** is a real state and it exists for exactly this situation. In the documentation's words: "Completion of an active coroutine's body ... transitions the job to the completing state. It waits in the completing state for all its children to complete before transitioning to the completed state." A parent finishing its own work and a parent finishing are two different events, and only the second one is what anybody waiting actually cares about.

Reading "the `launch` block returned" as "the coroutine finished". They are different moments whenever the block started anything, and the gap between them is where "the function returned but the work was still running" bugs live. The end of the block is not observable from outside; completion is, and the `Job` is the thing that tells them apart.

`Deferred<T>` is the same object with a value attached — the documentation calls it "a non-blocking cancellable future" with "the same state machine as `Job`". Everything above applies to it: it has a parent, it can have children, it can be joined. `await()` is the version of `join()` that also hands back what the computation produced, suspending without blocking the thread while it waits, and rethrowing if the computation failed instead of completing — where such a failure travels next is the failure unit's subject. A `Deferred` you have joined but not awaited has finished; you have simply not asked what it made.

One further thing a `Job` carries deserves naming here and nothing more than naming. Cancellation travels along these same parent-child edges, and the `Job` is the handle through which it is requested. How cancellation actually behaves — that it is cooperative rather than forced, what code has to do to honour it, what happens to cleanup — is the third unit's entire subject, and nothing in this unit depends on the answer. Until then, treat cancellation as a relationship the structure carries rather than a mechanism you have met.

The full state list is worth knowing because it explains the two transient states, which is where all of the interesting behaviour is. `New` is an optional initial state and `Active` is the default one.

rows: New (optional initial state)
false
false
false
Active (default initial state)
true
false
false
Completing (transient)
true
false
false
Cancelling (transient)
false
false
true
Cancelled (final)
false
true
true
Completed (final)
false
true
false

blocks.text: Two readings of that table matter. **Completing is indistinguishable from Active from outside**, and that is correct rather than an omission: to anybody waiting, a job that is waiting for its children is still running, and there is nothing useful to tell apart. And **`isCompleted` is true for both final states**, which is why "did it finish?" and "did it succeed?" are separate questions — `isCancelled` is the property that separates them.

`isActive` is used here strictly as a question about state. The same property appears in the cancellation unit for a different purpose — deciding whether a loop should keep going — and that use carries rules this unit does not cover. Keeping the two apart avoids importing an answer before the question has been posed.

There is also a reason to prefer `join()` over any of the predicates when you actually need to coordinate. Each property is a statement about a moment that has already passed by the time your next line runs, so polling a job to decide what to do is a race by construction. Waiting for a transition and sampling a state are different operations, and only one of them gives an answer that is still true when you act on it.

Taken together, this is what makes the `Job` more than a receipt. The builder call tells you work started; the job tells you where that work sits in a hierarchy, whether the hierarchy is finished, and — because a parent waits — lets a single handle stand for an entire sub-tree of work you never named.

"What does `launch` return, and why would you keep it?" The complete answer has two halves. The handle half: a `Job` lets you wait with `join()`, ask whether the work is still running, and stop it. The structural half, which is the one that distinguishes a strong answer: a `Job` is also that coroutine's position in a tree, so waiting on a parent waits for everything it started. If you can describe the completing state — the body has finished, a child has not, so the parent is not complete — you have stated the guarantee the structure actually makes.

lessons.title: `CoroutineScope` and Who Owns a Coroutine's Lifetime
lessons.summary: Every coroutine's lifetime belongs to something, and a scope is that something. The question worth practising on any piece of asynchronous code is which object owns the work and what event ends that ownership — including, concretely rather than stylistically, what goes wrong when the honest answer is "nothing in particular".

blocks.text: A `CoroutineScope` is described by its own documentation as "a scope in which coroutines run" that "allows managing the lifecycles of several coroutines simultaneously". The word carrying the weight in that sentence is *lifecycles*. A scope is not a convenience object that happens to provide `launch`; it is the thing a coroutine's lifetime is attached to.

Mechanically a scope is a very thin thing. The `CoroutineScope` interface declares exactly one property, `coroutineContext`, and no functions at all — `launch` and `async` are extensions on it. So a scope **holds** a `CoroutineContext` rather than being one, and the element of that context which matters here is the `Job` from the previous lesson. Launching from a scope makes the scope's job the parent of the new coroutine, and the identity is checkable rather than metaphorical:

Two consequences follow, and between them they are the whole lesson. Cancelling a scope cancels everything launched in it, recursively — "if a scope is cancelled, all coroutines in it are cancelled too". And a scope "cannot be completed until all its children are completed". So a coroutine's lifetime is **bounded** by the scope it was launched from: most work finishes well before its scope does, and none of it can outlast the scope. The **owner** of a scope is whatever decides where that bound falls — for a scope you construct and hold, whoever calls `cancel()` on it; for a lexical scope, the end of the block itself. A scope that is never cancelled and never ends is a bound that never arrives, which is the failure the rest of this lesson is about.
That collapses a large amount of asynchronous-code review into a single question, and it is worth asking out loud rather than by feel.

**Who owns this coroutine, and what event ends its lifetime?** If the answer names something with a lifecycle — this screen, this view model, this session, this download — the work has an owner. If the answer is "it stops when it stops", it does not, and every failure in the rest of this lesson follows from that one fact.
Here is the shape with no owner. It is common, it compiles, it passes review regularly, and nothing about it looks wrong.

One element of that constructor call is a distraction and is worth setting aside explicitly. `SupervisorJob()` changes what a child's failure does to its siblings; it changes nothing about ownership, and the failure unit teaches it properly. The defect below is present with or without it.

The scope was created and is never cancelled, so its job stays active for as long as anything holds it — and the running coroutines hold it. What goes wrong is not one thing, which is why "it leaks" is an unhelpful summary:

items: Work carries on after whatever asked for it has gone. The search still hits the network, still parses, still writes to the database, for a screen the user closed two navigations ago.
Results land on state that no longer matters, so a stale response can overwrite a newer one or call back into an object that has already been torn down.
Everything the coroutine captured stays reachable for as long as the coroutine does — the controller, the repository, whatever the lambda closed over, and transitively whatever those hold.
A failure inside the coroutine surfaces detached from any lifecycle — a crash or a log line attributable to no screen, request or object in particular.
No caller can find out whether the work has finished, because nothing was returned and there is nothing to join.

blocks.text: The last of those is measurable. Measured on this project's JVM target: a suspending function whose body launched into a separately constructed scope returned to its caller after **5 ms** for work that took **300 ms**, and that work then completed normally long after the caller had moved on. Written as a structured child of the caller instead, the same body returned after **306 ms**. Both versions "work"; only one of them told the caller anything true.

The fix is ownership, not the removal of the constructor. `CoroutineScope(...)` is a legitimate way to build a scope — the documentation's own order of preference puts lexical scopes first and this constructor second, "for entity lifecycles", with the parenthetical that does all the work: *with required `cancel()` call*. Give the class a teardown point, cancel there, and the same code becomes correct.

Android supplies scopes whose owner is already defined, and `viewModelScope` is the one worth recognising as the shape to imitate: "a `ViewModelScope` is defined for each `ViewModel` in your app. Any coroutine launched in this scope is automatically canceled if the `ViewModel` is cleared." The lifetime is a real event in a real object's lifecycle and the class launching work does not have to remember anything. Note what that is an example *of* — ownership done well — rather than an instruction about where coroutines belong; what a view model should contain is the architecture curriculum's subject, not this one's.

Some work genuinely has to outlive the screen that started it: a bookmark write, an upload that should not be abandoned because the user navigated away. That is not a reason to have no owner, it is a reason to have a longer-lived one. Android's guidance is to inject a scope whose lifetime is deliberately longer rather than reaching for a global one, so that the longer lifetime is a decision recorded in a constructor parameter and can be replaced in a test. Work that must survive the process being killed is not a coroutine problem at all — that is what a durable scheduler such as WorkManager exists for, and no scope of any lifetime will do it.

"Never create your own `CoroutineScope`" is the rule people take away, and it is the wrong lesson drawn from the right examples. The defect is never the constructor call. It is a scope with no cancellation point — a lifetime with no end, so work with no owner. A scope created in a class and cancelled in that class's teardown is correct, and a scope handed to you by a framework and then never cancelled by anybody would be broken in exactly the same way.

The reframing that survives contact with a real codebase is that a scope is a **lifetime declaration**, so the design question is which lifetime is the shortest one that is still long enough. Most work started from a screen wants the screen's. A cache several screens share wants something longer. Very little wants the process's.

`GlobalScope` is the process's, and the documentation says precisely what makes it a trap without banning it: it is "a `CoroutineScope` with the lifetime of the whole application", and "it is easy to misuse it and create memory or resource leaks when a coroutine actually should be tied to the lifecycle of some entity". Read the shape of that warning — the objection is to the *mismatch* between the work's natural lifetime and the scope's, not to the existence of a long-lived scope.

That leaves process-lifetime scopes a narrow but real use: state that genuinely is application-wide and has to survive every screen. What keeps such a scope honest is making it an injected dependency with a name and a documented reason, rather than a global reached from anywhere. That is also why Android's guidance frames its objection to `GlobalScope` in terms of testing and control: a hard-coded global scope cannot be substituted in a test, so the code cannot be told to stop — and "cannot be told to stop" is the same defect wearing different clothes.

One of the failures listed earlier — a failure surfacing with no lifecycle attached to it — is worth bounding, because it is easy to over-read. An un-owned coroutine's failure does not disappear — it surfaces somewhere, as a crash or as a log line — but it arrives detached from any lifecycle, so nothing identifies which screen, request or object it belonged to. That is a claim about diagnosability and nothing more. Where a coroutine failure actually travels, what can intercept it on the way, and how supervision changes that are the failure unit's subject; ownership does not settle them, and neither does this lesson.

One last consequence is worth stating because it is the reason the discipline pays for itself. When every coroutine has an owner, "stop everything this screen started" is one call rather than a search through the codebase for things to cancel. Ownership is not bookkeeping imposed on top of the work; it is the property that makes the work controllable at all.

Expect a short code sample and "what is wrong with this?". Answer with ownership rather than with a rule: name the scope, say what cancels it, and when nothing does, say what that means concretely — work continuing past the screen, stale results landing on dead state, captured objects retained, failures surfacing with no lifecycle attached to them, and no way for a caller to know it finished. If the follow-up is about work that must outlive the screen, do not retreat to `GlobalScope`: say the lifetime should be longer *and owned*, injected rather than reached for, and that surviving the process is a scheduler's job rather than a scope's.

lessons.title: Structured Concurrency and What It Guarantees
lessons.summary: The four ideas before this one combine into a single model: coroutines form a tree, and the tree is what makes "has this finished?" a question with an answer. Including the guarantees structured concurrency is routinely credited with and does not make, starting with everything to do with scheduling.

blocks.text: Each earlier lesson contributed a piece. A coroutine can pause without holding a thread. A builder starts one and hands back a handle. That handle is a `Job` with a place in a hierarchy. A scope owns the top of that hierarchy and decides when it ends. **Structured concurrency** is the name for what those pieces guarantee once they are put together.

Kotlin's statement of the principle is compact enough to memorise. Coroutines "form a tree hierarchy of parent and child tasks with linked lifecycles. A parent coroutine waits for its children to complete before it finishes. If the parent coroutine fails or gets canceled, all its child coroutines are recursively canceled too."

items: **A coroutine launched in a scope becomes a child of that scope's job.** The builders are extensions on `CoroutineScope`, so structured work is attached by construction rather than by somebody remembering to attach it.
**A parent does not complete until its children do**, even when the parent's own body finished long beforehand — the completing state from the previous lesson is this guarantee made observable.
**Cancellation travels down.** Cancelling a parent cancels its children recursively, so the request reaches every descendant rather than only the coroutine you named.
**Failure travels up through the same structure.** A child's failure is not a private event, and where it goes is decided by the hierarchy rather than by luck.

blocks.text: One qualification keeps that first point honest, and it is the reason the previous lesson spent so long on ownership. The attachment comes from the scope, so a scope carrying no job of its own starts **root** coroutines: coroutines with no parent. Be precise about what that costs, because a root is not outside the model — it is the top of one. The last three guarantees hold in full inside a root's own subtree: it waits for the children it launches, cancelling it cancels them, and their failures reach it. What is missing is the first guarantee and everything that depended on it — the root is attached to no owner, so nothing above it can cancel it, wait for it, or be told when it fails. `GlobalScope` is the one you will meet: its documentation describes it as a `CoroutineScope` without any `Job`, used "to launch top-level coroutines whose lifecycles are not limited by structured concurrency", which is why nothing can cancel them together or wait for them. A coroutine can also be re-parented deliberately by what is passed to the builder, and that is the context unit's subject. Structured concurrency is not something the runtime imposes on every coroutine; it is a property of coroutines started inside a structure — which is exactly why opting out is possible, and worth being able to spot.

The builder that puts a suspending function inside this model is `coroutineScope`. It "creates a root coroutine of the coroutine subtree", it is "the direct parent of coroutines launched inside the block", and it "executes the suspending block and waits until the block and any coroutines launched in it complete". Read "root" there in the local sense — root *of the subtree it creates*. Unlike the parentless roots above, this one is itself a child of the coroutine that called it, which is the entire point: its API documentation states the consequence exactly, that the new job "completes when both the block and all the coroutines launched in the scope complete. Only then can the `coroutineScope` call return a value."

Structured concurrency is a statement about lifetime, and what it buys you is that "has this finished?" becomes a question with an answer. When a structured suspending function returns, everything it started is over.
The clearest way to see what the model gives you is to look at a function that quietly opts out of it.
This compiles, it does the work, and it is a suspending function that never once suspends for the thing it started. Ask what the caller is holding after it returns.

items: Not the knowledge that the work is done. The function returns as soon as the coroutine has been launched — measured on this project's JVM target, this shape returned in 5 ms for work that ran for 300 ms.
Not the failure. If `api.load()` throws, it throws inside a coroutine attached to a different tree, and nothing reaches the caller's `try`/`catch`.
Not the ability to stop it. Cancelling the caller cancels the caller's children, and this coroutine is not one of them.
Not a lifetime it can reason about at all. The work outlives the call by an amount nothing in the signature discloses.

blocks.text: The structured form differs by one line and changes every one of those answers.

The launched coroutine is now a child of the scope this function created, so the function cannot return until it finishes; a failure inside it fails the scope and is rethrown to the caller; and cancelling the caller cancels it. Measured the same way, this version returned after **306 ms** for the same 300 ms of work. That extra 300 ms is not a cost that was introduced — it is the caller finally being told the truth.

`coroutineScope` is also what lets a suspending function do several things at once without saying so in its signature. A function that launches three children inside its own scope is concurrent on the inside and an ordinary suspending call on the outside, because the scope re-imposes a single completion point at the boundary. Whether the work *should* overlap, and what overlapping actually buys, is a separate decision the next unit makes.

Treating a suspending function that starts detached work as equivalent to one that does the work. They have the same signature and completely different contracts, and the signature is what every caller reads. If a function genuinely must start work it does not wait for, that belongs in the name and in the type — a function returning a `Job` is telling the truth, and a plain `suspend fun` that quietly leaves work running behind it is not.

Structured concurrency is credited with more than it promises, and the misattributions are worth rejecting individually, because each one implies a different wrong prediction about code that is actually running.

rows: A coroutine started in a scope is a child of that scope, with a lifetime bounded by it
That anything runs in the background. Where code executes is the dispatcher's business, and a child inherits one rather than being given a new one
A parent completes only after its children have completed
That children run one at a time. Children launched together run concurrently and may finish in any order
Cancelling a parent cancels its children, recursively
That anything runs in parallel. Concurrency is about overlapping lifetimes; parallelism additionally depends on the dispatcher and the hardware
A failure is routed through the hierarchy rather than lost
That a failure is handled, retried or recovered. The structure decides where it goes, never what to do about it

blocks.text: The scheduling confusion is the most common and the most consequential, because it is the difference between a lifetime property and a performance property. Children of one scope run concurrently, may run on different threads and may finish in any order; the structure says nothing about which of them goes first. What it says is that none of them outlives the scope. That is why wrapping three `launch` calls in a `coroutineScope` makes nothing faster and nothing slower — it changes when the enclosing function is allowed to return.

There is one deliberate exception to the failure guarantee, and naming it is enough here: a **supervising** parent changes what a child's failure does to its siblings, which is the one place the tree does not propagate upward in the ordinary way. It is the failure unit's subject and nothing in this unit depends on it. In the same way, `coroutineScope` has a close relative that switches execution context rather than creating a concurrent sub-tree, and telling those two apart is the next unit's job.

The reason all of this is worth the discipline is a property that is easy to state and very hard to obtain any other way: in a structured program the call structure and the lifetime of the work agree. If a function returned, its work is over. If a scope was cancelled, the request reached every descendant rather than the one coroutine somebody remembered, and that scope's job completing is the moment at which none of it is running any more. Systems without those properties turn "is anything still going?" into an empirical question, and answering empirical questions about concurrency is where the days go.

"What is structured concurrency?" invites a definition and rewards a consequence. Give the tree in one sentence — parents, children, linked lifetimes — then say what it buys: a parent cannot finish before its children, cancellation reaches everything below it, and a failure has a defined route rather than disappearing. Then pre-empt the usual follow-up by saying what it is not: not a scheduler, not a promise of parallelism, not a reason children run in order, and not error handling. If you can name the detached-`launch` shape and say precisely which guarantee it discards, that is the answer that lands.

units.title: Coroutine Context, Dispatchers and Concurrent Work
units.summary: Suspension did not tell us where code runs. This unit follows the execution policy from the scope's context into a child coroutine, chooses dispatchers from the shape of the work, places context changes beside the implementation that needs them, and finally decides when independent operations should overlap. Unit 1 supplies the lifetime model; context and scheduling explain how to vary execution while keeping that model intact.

lessons.title: `CoroutineContext` and What Children Inherit
lessons.summary: Read a coroutine's effective context from its launch site: which execution policy it inherits, which elements an argument replaces, and why its own Job is distinct from the Job selected as its parent. That distinction explains both ordinary child creation and the explicit-Job trap.

blocks.text: Unit 1 left two facts side by side: suspension does not choose a thread, and a Job connects work to a lifetime. A coroutine needs both an execution policy and lifetime information. CoroutineContext carries these together without making them the same thing. A scope holds a context; the scope is not itself a context, and a context is not itself a running coroutine.

Think of the context as a small collection of named slots. Each slot has a key, and at most one element occupies that key. The formal name is an indexed set. A Job occupies the Job key; a dispatcher occupies the ContinuationInterceptor key; CoroutineName supplies a diagnostic label. CoroutineExceptionHandler is another context element, but what it handles is a Unit 3 question. There is no need to memorize every possible element to read an ordinary launch.

Context composition uses `+`. For different keys, both elements remain. For the same key, the element on the right wins. The operation produces a context; it does not mutate the original context or start work. A name and a dispatcher therefore coexist, while two dispatcher choices compete for the same slot. You cannot add IO to Main and obtain a coroutine that executes on both at once.

blocks.code:
val base = Dispatchers.Default + CoroutineName("refresh")
val renamed = base + CoroutineName("profile")

check(base[CoroutineName]?.name == "refresh")
check(renamed[CoroutineName]?.name == "profile")
check(renamed[ContinuationInterceptor] === Dispatchers.Default)

blocks.text: This is common Kotlin code with kotlinx.coroutines imports and `kotlin.coroutines.ContinuationInterceptor`. The name changed, the execution policy did not, and the original value still says refresh. CoroutineName can make diagnostic output easier to connect to a task; it neither allocates a thread nor changes scheduling priority. Similarly, looking up `coroutineContext[Job]` inside a coroutine tells you about that coroutine's Job, not which worker happens to execute it.

A builder starts with its receiver scope's context and combines the supplied context with it. There is then an essential extra step: the new coroutine receives its own Job. The Job selected from the combined starting context becomes its parent, if there is one. The child does not reuse the parent's Job as its own. Otherwise two siblings would have the same completion handle and there would be no separate lifetimes to observe.

Read child creation in two steps: combine the starting context, then attach the new coroutine's own Job to the selected parent Job. Dispatcher inheritance and Job parentage answer different questions.

Suppose an Android UI owner already provides a scope whose context contains a parent Job P, Dispatchers.Main and the name screen. The following fragment requests a different dispatcher for one operation. The blocking call is a placeholder for an existing Android/JVM API; Main and IO here are explicitly platform choices.

Predict the elements before thinking about thread names. IO replaces Main under the dispatcher key. The screen name remains because the argument contains no CoroutineName. A fresh Job C represents refresh, and C's parent is P because the argument contains no Job. Inside the block, ownJob is C, not P. The returned refresh handle refers to that same coroutine. The scope still holds Main and P; neither has been edited.

A sibling started later with `scope.launch { ... }` therefore uses the scope's original dispatcher. By contrast, an unqualified `launch { ... }` inside the refresh block uses that block's receiver scope, so its default dispatcher is IO and its parent is C. An explicit `scope.launch` inside that same block still uses scope. Lexical indentation is helpful, but the receiver and context arguments are the evidence for parentage.

The lifecycle consequence follows Unit 1: C can finish long before P, while P bounds the ordinary child's lifetime. The dispatcher choice did not detach the operation. It also did not make processSmallResult cheap; if that transformation becomes substantial CPU work, choosing IO for the file read does not settle where the transformation belongs. The next two lessons make that execution decision.

Reading `scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO)` as replacing the whole scope, or reading an inherited dispatcher as an inherited Job instance. Only the matching dispatcher element is replaced; the new coroutine still has a distinct completion handle.

Now consider a diagnostic counterexample, not a construction pattern to copy. In older code you may encounter a builder passed a fresh SupervisorJob. Ignore its supervision behavior for this lesson and trace only the Job key.

The supplied object S occupies the same key as the scope's P, so it replaces P as the selected parent. The launch still creates its own Job C: the relationship is S -> C, not P -> S -> C, and C is not S. With no parent argument, this newly constructed S has no parent connecting it back to P. Other scope elements, such as the dispatcher and name, can still be inherited. An inherited scheduler is therefore not evidence of an inherited lifetime.

This is the deeper explanation of Unit 1's caveat. Explicit Job arguments can re-parent work; they are not modifiers automatically inserted beneath the old parent. The current launch API documents this as an unsupported pattern retained for compatibility, and its Job overload is deprecated. Diagnose existing code with the rule, then preserve ownership when designing new code. This example is not a recommendation for supervision. Unit 3 explains what supervision actually changes and why the parent's position matters.

The scope's original Job no longer bounds C through that original edge. That does not mean C has no Job or no parent: its parent is S. Conversely, a builder whose effective starting context contains no Job can create a root coroutine. Root coroutines can have children of their own. 'Every coroutine has the launching coroutine as its parent' would erase all of these distinctions.

For the ordinary elements taught here, a useful review method is to write three short lines beside unfamiliar code: receiver context, explicit overrides, resulting child's Job parent. If two coroutines have identical names and dispatchers, those lines can still reveal entirely different owners. If they have different dispatchers, those lines can show they belong to one structure. Context composition is what lets execution policy vary without normally abandoning that structure.

items: Find the builder's actual CoroutineScope receiver.
Resolve competing elements by key; the right-hand value wins.
Distinguish the selected parent Job from the newly created coroutine Job.
Treat an explicit Job argument as an ownership warning, not a dispatcher option.
Use Unit 3 for cancellation, failure handling and supervision rules.

blocks.text: Which element wins, and whose child is this? Explain the ordinary Main-to-IO launch first, then the fresh-Job counterexample. Neither a thread name nor the position of the braces proves parentage.
