Three questions come out of this Lesson and they are asked about code rather than about definitions. Does constructing this flow execute anything? No, and neither does adding operators to it. What does a second collector cause? A second, independent execution of the producer from the beginning, with its own database read or its own request. What starts it? A terminal operator, which runs the producer inside the collecting coroutine. Being able to answer all three about a snippet you have not seen before is the model; the operator names can be looked up, this cannot.

lessons.title: Collection Lifetime and Flow Cancellation
lessons.summary: Name the coroutine a collection runs in, and what will end it. A cold flow has no lifetime of its own: collect runs the producer under the collecting coroutine, so that coroutine's Job bounds the collection and cancelling it is the ordinary cooperative cancellation Unit 3 already taught, not a Flow-specific mechanism.

blocks.text: Two questions are worth asking of any flow collection you read: which coroutine is this running in, and what will end it. The reason this Lesson comes fourth in the curriculum rather than first is that both answers are already known — they are the coroutine model of the first three units applied to a new shape, not new rules to learn.

A cold flow has no lifetime of its own. In the simplest pipeline — a flow { } builder collected directly — there is no second coroutine anywhere: the producer body runs inside the collecting coroutine. Some operators do introduce one, and this unit meets two of them later, where flowOn runs the upstream in its own coroutine and channelFlow launches children. What does not change is the ownership. Any coroutine a flow creates is a child of the collecting coroutine, created when collection starts and finished when it ends, so nothing a flow does is scheduled behind the collector's back or outlives it. The documentation puts that in two sentences: flow collection is tied to the coroutine that calls the collect() function, and when that coroutine is cancelled, the collection stops and the upstream flow is cancelled too.

Everything follows from the second line running inside the first. The producer executes in this coroutine, in its context, under its Job, which is a child of the scope's Job. collect suspends and does not return until the flow completes or the coroutine is cancelled — and a flow that observes storage never completes on its own, so in practice cancellation is how collection ends.

That turns a scheduling question into an ownership question. Choosing where to collect is choosing who owns the collection's lifetime, because the scope you launch it in is the thing that will eventually end it. A collection launched in a screen's scope lasts as long as the screen; a collection launched in an application-lifetime scope lasts as long as the process, whether or not anything is still interested.

There is no such thing as “the flow's lifetime”. There is the collecting coroutine's lifetime, and the collection is part of it. Deciding which scope collects is therefore the whole of the lifetime decision.

Collection is often written the other way round, and the shorthand is worth reading carefully because it is frequently misdescribed. The KDoc says exactly what it is: launchIn is a terminal flow operator that launches the collection of the given flow in a scope, and it is a shorthand for scope.launch { flow.collect() }.

Two things about it are precise. It is a terminal operator, so it is the thing that starts the flow — onEach is an ordinary intermediate operator and would do nothing on its own. And it returns a Job, the same handle the Job Lesson introduced, which means the collection is an ordinary child coroutine of that scope with an ordinary lifetime. Measured on this project's JVM target, launchIn returned a StandaloneCoroutine which is a Job, and cancelling the scope ended the collection it had started.

What launchIn does not do is change the flow's contract. It does not make a cold flow hot: the source still produces per collection, and two launchIn calls on the same cold flow are two collections. Measured on this project's JVM target, the same cold adapter collected through two launchIn calls executed its producer twice, exactly as two plain collect calls would. The KDoc's own note points the same way — the provided scope takes care of cancellation, and the returned Job does not need to be used for cancellation purposes, because the scope is the owner.

Where that scope comes from is an application question rather than a Flow question. UI applications generally collect in a scope bound to the lifetime of whatever is displaying the values, so that navigating away ends the collection. The lifecycle-aware ways of arranging that, and the Compose-side ways of collecting a flow into state, are the subject of the effects and lifecycle integration material later in this curriculum; the mechanism underneath every one of them is the one this Lesson describes.

Collecting in a scope that outlives the consumer. The collection is not aware of who wanted the values: if the coroutine is still alive, the producer keeps running, the database keeps being read and the results go nowhere. Nothing about this fails loudly, which is what makes choosing the scope a correctness decision rather than a tidiness one.

“Cancelling the collector cancels the upstream flow” is true and is also the sentence most likely to be over-read. Unit 3's model is unchanged here, and Flow does not introduce a second one: cancellation is a request recorded on a Job, and the code inside stops where it can observe that request. A producer does not become forcibly interruptible by virtue of sitting inside a flow.

Measured on this project's JVM target, with a producer whose first statement was a six-hundred-millisecond blocking sleep — a JVM-specific case, used here because it is the clearest one — the collecting coroutine was cancelled after a hundred milliseconds. The blocking call ran to completion anyway, and joining the cancelled coroutine returned six hundred and ninety-four milliseconds after the start. The producer was inside a flow, it had been cancelled, and it was still not interruptible.

The ordinary case is much better behaved, and for a documented reason: the flow builder is cancellable by default, which means cancellation is checked on each emission, and on top of that almost everything a realistic producer does between emissions is itself a suspending call. Measured on this project's JVM target with a producer whose only cooperative point was emit — a tight loop with no delay, no yield and no other suspending call anywhere in it — cancelling the collector stopped it: the loop never exited normally and the coroutine completed. So the accurate formulation is the one Unit 3 already gave. Cancelling the collector requests cancellation of production, and production stops where it observes the request; in a flow built the ordinary way, that is almost immediately, and the only producers that overrun are the ones doing work that cooperates with nothing.

Notice what is absent from that formulation. There is no Flow-specific kill switch, no separate collection lifecycle, and no Job the flow owns independently of its collector — the child coroutines some operators create are exactly that, children, and they are cancelled through the ordinary hierarchy. This is worth stating explicitly because the alternative mental model, that a flow is a live thing with its own lifecycle that cancellation reaches into, leads to exactly the wrong predictions about non-cooperative producers and about who is responsible for stopping what.

Be ready for the pair. Which coroutine owns this collection, and what ends it? The one that called collect, and cancelling it — usually by cancelling the scope it belongs to. Does launchIn make the flow hot? No; it is scope.launch { collect() } and returns a Job, and the source's cold contract is untouched. Then add the precision that separates a careful answer from a slogan: cancelling a collector cancels production cooperatively, so a producer doing non-cooperative work will finish it, and the caller waits.

lessons.title: Context Preservation and `flowOn`
lessons.summary: Say which part of a chain runs in which context. A cold flow runs in the collector's context by default, an ordinary flow { } producer may not switch its own emission context, and flowOn exists precisely because of that rule — it moves the upstream and leaves the collector where it was.

blocks.text: The previous Lesson settled who owns a collection. This one settles where it runs, and the answer is again borrowed rather than new: Unit 2's context model applies unchanged, because a cold flow executes inside the collecting coroutine and therefore in the collecting coroutine's context.

The documentation states the default in one sentence: by default, a cold flow runs in the same coroutine context as the collector. Nothing about writing flow { } selects a dispatcher, and nothing about a value being asynchronous moves it off the caller's thread.

This is the same misconception Unit 1 removed about the suspend keyword, arriving in new clothing. A suspending function does not run in the background because it is suspending, and a flow does not run in the background because it is a flow. If the collection is on a UI dispatcher, so is the file read, and the screen will show it.

The property has a name — a flow is context-preserving — and the reason it is worth having is that it makes a chain locally readable. When you look at a collect call, the context that the whole chain executes in is the context you are looking at, unless an operator in front of you says otherwise. No operator halfway up the chain can quietly change the answer.

A cold flow has no context of its own. It runs in the collector's context, so “where does this flow run?” is always answered by reading the collector and then reading the operators between the collector and the producer.

Which raises the obvious question: if the file read should not happen on the UI dispatcher, why not move it inside the producer, where the work actually is? Because that is exactly what a flow may not do.

The flow builder's KDoc states the requirement — emit should happen strictly in the dispatchers of the block in order to preserve the flow context — and carries this exact case as its own illustration of an IllegalStateException. Run it against the coroutines version this repository resolves and the runtime explains itself:

blocks.code:
IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated:
	Flow was collected in [CoroutineId(1), "coroutine#1":BlockingCoroutine{Active}@..., BlockingEventLoop@...],
	but emission happened in [CoroutineId(1), "coroutine#1":DispatchedCoroutine{Active}@..., Dispatchers.IO].
	Please refer to 'flow' documentation or use 'flowOn' instead

blocks.text: The message names the two contexts it compared and then names the remedy, which is the useful part. The rule is not bureaucratic: if a producer could switch its own emission context, a reader of a collect call could no longer know which context their collection runs in without tracing every operator back to the source, and the local readability the previous section described would be gone. Preserving the context is what keeps the local reading correct — and flowOn is the sanctioned way to change it.

blocks.code:
fileLines()                    // runs in ioDispatcher
    .map { parse(it) }         // runs in ioDispatcher
    .flowOn(ioDispatcher)
    .collect { render(it) }    // runs in the collector's context, untouched

blocks.text: The direction is the entire operator, and the KDoc says it plainly: flowOn is context preserving, context does not leak into the downstream flow, and it affects only preceding operators that do not have their own context. Upstream moves; downstream, including the terminal collector, stays exactly where it was.

That makes placement a decision rather than a ritual. Moving flowOn changes which operators are above it and therefore which ones move, and a chain may carry more than one — the KDoc's own worked example uses two, each governing the operators between itself and the one before it. The question to ask is never “where does flowOn go” but “which upstream work needs a different execution context”. If the answer is none, the operator does not belong in the chain at all.

Reading flowOn(ioDispatcher) as “this flow runs on IO”. It says that the operators above it do. The collector and everything below it stay where they were, which is usually precisely what is wanted: parse off the UI dispatcher, render on it. A reader who has the direction backwards will also put the operator in the wrong place.

It is worth knowing what changing the context actually costs, because flowOn does more than relabel the upstream. When the dispatcher changes, the KDoc says, the flow's emissions are performed in a coroutine running with the specified context and the values are collected in another coroutine using the original collector's context, with a channel of default buffer size used internally between the two. Two coroutines and a channel — which is how the invariant can be honoured at all, since the producer really is emitting in its own context and something else really is receiving in the collector's.

The side effect of that arrangement is that flowOn introduces concurrency and buffering as well as a context change: the upstream can run ahead of the collector up to the buffer's capacity. What to do when a producer outpaces its collector is the buffering material in the flow composition unit later in this curriculum. Here it is enough to know that the operator is not free and is not purely declarative.

Unit 2's precision about context and threads carries forward unchanged, and this operator is a good place to see why it mattered. Measured on this project's JVM target: a chain whose upstream was moved with flowOn(Dispatchers.IO), collected from a coroutine already running on Dispatchers.Default. The upstream did run in a separate coroutine, as the KDoc describes — but the thread it landed on was named DefaultDispatcher-worker-3, and the collector's was DefaultDispatcher-worker-1. Asking for IO did not produce a thread from some separate IO pool, because there is no separate pool: the Dispatchers.IO reference states that it shares threads with Default, and that switching to it when already on Default typically does not lead to an actual switch to another thread. What flowOn guarantees is about the context. Which physical thread that turns into is a scheduling detail, and reasoning that depends on a particular one is folklore.

One last connection, named rather than taught. Context preservation is one instance of a more general transparency rule rather than a quirk of flowOn: just as a producer may not change the context its emissions happen in, an operator may not silently swallow a failure that belongs to code downstream of it. The operators that let a chain observe and transform failures are built to keep that boundary intact, and they are the subject of the failure material in the flow composition unit later in this curriculum.

Two questions, and the second is the better one. Which operators does flowOn affect? Everything upstream of it and nothing downstream, the collector included. And why is withContext around emit inside flow { } wrong? Because a flow is context-preserving, so that a collector can know its own execution context by reading its own code, and the runtime enforces it with an IllegalStateException whose message names flowOn as the remedy. The first question asks what the operator does; the second asks why it exists, which is what the invariant is actually for.

lessons.title: Flow Builders and Adapting Callback APIs
lessons.summary: Turn an existing producer into a flow without leaking it. The producer's shape picks the builder: sequential suspending work is flow, several coroutines producing at once is channelFlow, and a callback or listener API is callbackFlow — where awaitClose is what keeps the registration alive and gives unregistration one place that always runs.

blocks.text: Every flow so far has come from flow { }, which fits producers of one particular shape: sequential work, done by suspending calls, emitting from the builder's own coroutine.

Nothing about that builder limits how many values are produced or how long production takes. What it does limit is where emission may happen, which is the rule the previous Lesson established: emission has to occur in the builder's own context, from the builder's own coroutine. Two perfectly ordinary producers do not fit inside that rule, and Kotlin supplies a builder for each of them.

The first is work done concurrently by several coroutines. channelFlow allows elements to be produced by code that is running in a different context or concurrently, and it ensures thread-safety and context preservation, so its ProducerScope can be used concurrently from different contexts. Inside it, send replaces emit.

It is still a cold flow — the KDoc is explicit that the block is called every time a terminal operator is applied to the resulting flow — and what it buys is concurrency, at the price of ordering. Measured on this project's JVM target, a channelFlow with two child coroutines, one of them delayed, delivered its values in the order they were actually produced rather than the order the children were launched. That is the builder working as intended, and it is the reason to reach for it deliberately rather than by default.

The builder follows from the producer's shape rather than from preference. Sequential suspending production is flow. Production by several coroutines at once is channelFlow. A callback or listener belonging to something outside the coroutine world is callbackFlow.

The second producer that does not fit flow { } is the important one in practice, because the world outside coroutines is full of register-and-be-called-back APIs: sensors, location, connectivity, players, sockets, platform observers. Adapting one into a flow is the most common flow-authoring job there is, and it is the one with a leak built into the obvious version.

Read that block as a lifetime rather than as a snippet. Registration happens when a collection starts. trySend moves each value from whatever thread the callback arrived on into the flow's channel, which is why a plain flow { } cannot be used here at all: the callback is not running in the builder's coroutine, and emitting from it would violate the context invariant the previous Lesson described. And then the block reaches awaitClose, which is where the interesting part is.

The one thing worth adding to that line is what happens when trySend does not succeed. A callback is not a coroutine, so trySend cannot suspend and cannot apply back pressure the way emit does; it attempts the send and hands back a result. That result is a failure when the channel's buffer is full or when collection has already ended, and ignoring it means the adapter silently loses values. Which is sometimes exactly right — for a position that will be superseded a moment later, dropping is the correct policy — but it should be a decision the adapter states rather than a consequence of not looking. Inspect the result and do something honest with it: record the drop, count it, or surface it. Choosing a buffering policy instead is the subject named at the end of this Lesson.

Without awaitClose the block would return the instant the listener was registered, the channel would close, and the collection would end — with the listener still attached to the source. The library refuses to let that happen silently. Its KDoc says awaitClose should be used to keep the flow running, that otherwise the channel will be closed immediately when the block completes, and that using it is mandatory in order to prevent memory leaks. Measured on this project's JVM target, a callbackFlow whose block sent one value and returned failed with:

blocks.code:
IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end
of callbackFlow block. Otherwise, a callback/listener may leak in case of external cancellation.
See callbackFlow API documentation for the details.

blocks.text: The failure it is protecting against is concrete rather than theoretical. The listener stays registered; the source keeps a reference to it and to everything the listener captured, which in a UI application is frequently a screen that has already gone; and it keeps being invoked to deliver values to a consumer that no longer exists. awaitClose closes that hole by construction: it suspends until the channel is closed or cancelled, and its block is executed unconditionally before the function returns — the same guarantee a finally block gives, which is exactly the shape the cleanup Lesson taught.

Registering in the callbackFlow block and unregistering somewhere else — a lifecycle callback, a close() method, a disposal hook. The registration belongs to this collection, and awaitClose is the one place that runs when this collection ends, however it ends. Splitting the pair across two files is how a listener survives the thing that created it.

Because a callbackFlow is cold, each collection registers its own listener. Measured on this project's JVM target, one adapter collected by two coroutines registered twice while both were running, and when the scope was cancelled it unregistered twice. That is usually the behaviour you want — each consumer owns its own subscription and its own cleanup, and no consumer can end another's — but it is a genuine cost when registration is expensive, or when the underlying source only tolerates one listener. The remedy is not a different builder; it is sharing one collection among several consumers, which is the subject of the hot streams unit later in this curriculum.
With that, the choice among the three builders can be stated as reasoning rather than as a lookup table.

rows: A sequence of suspending calls made by one coroutine
flow
The simplest contract that works, and the one that keeps context preservation checkable. Nothing more is needed, so nothing more should be paid for.
Several coroutines producing values at the same time
channelFlow
Emission from more than one coroutine needs the thread-safe, context-preserving channel this builder supplies. Ordering is given up in exchange.
A callback or listener registered against an external source
callbackFlow
Values arrive outside any coroutine, and the registration needs a lifetime boundary that runs on cancellation — which is what awaitClose is.

blocks.text: The last two are not interchangeable, even though both are built on the same channel-backed producer scope. channelFlow answers a question about who is allowed to produce; callbackFlow answers a question about a subscription that has to be torn down. Reaching for channelFlow around a listener leaves you writing awaitClose anyway, without the builder's insistence that you did; reaching for callbackFlow around ordinary concurrent work names a callback that does not exist. And note what neither is: the channel is an implementation detail of the builder, and channels as a coordination primitive in their own right — capacities, fan-out, pipelines — are a separate subject this unit deliberately leaves alone.

One consequence of that implementation detail is worth naming before leaving it. Both builders use a channel with the default buffer size, so a producer that runs ahead of its collector is buffered rather than immediately suspended, and trySend returns a result that can report failure when the buffer is full or the channel is already closed. Deciding what should happen when a producer outpaces its collector — buffer more, drop values, cancel work in flight — is the buffering material in the flow composition unit later in this curriculum.

This Lesson's interview version is short and unusually specific. Which builder adapts a listener API? callbackFlow. Why must the block end in awaitClose? Because the block returns as soon as the listener is registered, so awaitClose is what keeps the collection alive while callbacks may still arrive and gives unregistration one place that runs however the collection ends — and the builder throws IllegalStateException if it is missing. Who unregisters, and when? The awaitClose block, when the collecting coroutine is cancelled or the channel closes. Then the question that separates having used it from having read about it: does a cold adapter create one subscription or one per collection? One per collection.

units.title: Flow Composition, Timing and Failure
units.summary: The previous unit settled what a Flow is: a description of production that runs inside the collecting coroutine, starts when a terminal operator asks for it, and ends when that coroutine does. This unit is about the decisions taken on top of that pipeline, and every one of them is a question about semantics rather than about which API exists. Filter by value or by time. Combine the current state of several sources, or pair their emissions. Let inner work overlap, run it in order, or cancel it when newer input arrives. Decide what may be lost when the producer outpaces the collector. And place failure handling where it can actually observe the failure. The order is one argument: transform a stream, then join streams, then map values into streams of their own, then deal with a speed mismatch, then deal with the ways collection ends.

lessons.title: Transforming and Filtering: by Value and by Time
lessons.summary: Two different questions an operator can answer about a value: what is it, and when did it arrive. map, filter and transform decide from the value alone; distinctUntilChanged compares it with the one before it; debounce and sample decide from the clock.

blocks.text: The previous unit established what an operator is: an intermediate operator returns another Flow and has started nothing, and collection only begins when a terminal operation asks for it. This unit is about choosing between them, and the choice is easier than the operator lists suggest, because almost every operator answers one of two questions about a value. What is this value? Or, when did it arrive?

Everything on the first side can be decided by looking at the value alone. Everything on the second side needs a clock, and needs to know what else arrived nearby. Keeping the two apart is most of the skill, because an operator picked from the wrong side of that line produces a pipeline that looks reasonable and behaves wrongly under exactly the conditions that matter.
Three operators carry the value side, and they differ only in how many outputs one input may produce.

map replaces each value with another; filter lets a value through unchanged or drops it; transform is the general form the other two are special cases of, and it is the one to reach for when one input should produce a placeholder and then a result, or nothing at all. All three take a suspending lambda, so calling a suspending function inside them is ordinary rather than exceptional — a mapping step that has to hit storage or the network does not need an escape hatch.

distinctUntilChanged is still on the value side, but it needs two values to decide, and precisely which two is the fact worth memorising: the new value is compared with the one immediately before it, using equals. It is not a deduplicator and it keeps no history.

Ask what the operator needs in order to decide. map, filter and transform need only the value. distinctUntilChanged needs the value and the one before it. debounce and sample need the clock. An operator can only be correct for a problem whose decision uses the same inputs.

The time side is where the two most confusable operators live, and the clearest way to separate them is to put them on one identical timeline. Take a search field where the user types kotlin one character at a time, pausing after kot and again at the end.

blocks.code:
val typing = flow {
    emit("k");      delay(80)
    emit("ko");     delay(80)
    emit("kot");    delay(520)   // the user pauses
    emit("kotl");   delay(100)
    emit("kotli");  delay(200)   // a hesitation, but not a pause
    emit("kotlin"); delay(520)   // and stops
}

blocks.text: debounce asks a question about quiet: emit a value only once nothing newer has arrived for the configured interval. Every new value restarts that interval, so a burst of keystrokes produces nothing at all until the burst ends. Measured on this project's JVM target, typing.debounce(300) produced kot and kotlin — one value per real pause. The two-hundred-millisecond hesitation before the last keystroke produced nothing, because it was shorter than the timeout.

sample asks a different question, about cadence: on a fixed tick, emit whatever the most recent value is, and emit nothing if there has been no new value since the last tick. It is indifferent to whether the user is still typing. Measured on this project's JVM target over the same timeline, typing.sample(300) produced kot, kotl and kotlin — three values, and the middle one is a string the user never paused at. It is simply what happened to be current when a tick arrived, which is also why the exact middle value is a property of where the emissions fall relative to the ticks rather than a guarantee of the operator.

That third value is the whole distinction. debounce is the operator for "act when the input has settled"; sample is the operator for "act at a steady rate regardless of what the input is doing". A telemetry feed reporting a position several hundred times a second is a natural fit for sample, because there is no such thing as the user finishing. A search field is a natural fit for debounce, because there is.
The two search-field operators solve different problems and are commonly wanted together, in this order:

blocks.code:
queries
    .debounce(300)            // first: collapse the timing noise of typing
    .distinctUntilChanged()   // then: drop a query equal to the one already run

blocks.text: The reason the order reads well is that each one removes something the other cannot see. debounce removes intermediate values that only existed because typing is incremental; it cannot tell that the settled query is the same one that was searched a moment ago. distinctUntilChanged removes that repeat; it has no notion of time, so it would happily pass every keystroke through. Measured on this project's JVM target with a user who typed kot, paused, added and deleted a character, and paused again, debounce alone emitted kot twice and the pair emitted it once.

Describing debounce as "slowing events down" or "throttling". It does not slow anything and it does not emit on a schedule — during a fast enough stream of values it emits nothing at all, indefinitely. Reaching for it when the requirement is a steady rate produces a pipeline that goes silent under exactly the load it was added to handle. Rate is sample's contract, not debounce's.

Two details separate a careful answer from a recognising one. First, the opt-in status. Checked against this project's resolved kotlinx-coroutines-core 1.11.0 artifact, debounce and sample are annotated @FlowPreview, not @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi. The distinction matters if you quote it: FlowPreview states that the declaration has no backward compatibility guarantees and its semantics can change between releases, and it is the stronger of the two opt-ins. Both are warning-level, so using them costs an @OptIn and nothing else, and both are the standard answers to the problems they solve. The annotation is a stability contract, not a warning about correctness.

Second, what each operator does at the end of the stream, which is where their designs differ most and where a plausible-looking pipeline quietly loses its last value. debounce always emits the latest value when the upstream completes, because a completed upstream is the ultimate quiet period. sample does not: its documentation states that the latest element is not emitted if it does not fit into the sampling window, so a value that arrives between the final tick and completion is dropped. For a finite stream ending in the value the collector actually cares about, that is a real difference.

The remaining operators on the value side are worth knowing and are not worth a section each, because their behaviour is predictable from their names and none of them carries a decision. take(n) ends collection after n values and completes the flow, which makes it a way to bound an otherwise endless stream. drop(n) skips the first n. onStart and onEach run an action before the first value and on each value, and both are intermediate — so onEach alone starts nothing. scan emits the running accumulation, which is the operator to reach for when the downstream wants each intermediate total rather than only the final one.

The question is usually debounce against distinctUntilChanged and the good answer names the decision inputs rather than the definitions: one decides from the clock, the other from the previous value, so they cannot substitute for one another. Add that distinctUntilChanged compares only with the immediately preceding value, so a repeated value that returns later still passes; and that debounce emits nothing while values keep arriving faster than the timeout, which is the property that makes it right for a settling input and wrong for a rate limit.

lessons.title: `combine` and `zip`: Current Values or Paired Emissions
lessons.summary: Two sources, two entirely different questions. combine asks what the current state of both is; zip asks which emission of one corresponds to which emission of the other. Choosing wrongly produces a screen that stops updating, or a pipeline throttled by its slowest input.

blocks.text: When two flows feed one result, there is a question to answer before any operator is chosen: are these sources describing the same thing at the same moment, or are they producing values that correspond to each other one for one?

A signed-in user and a settings snapshot are the first kind. They change independently, neither one is a response to the other, and what the screen wants is always the current combination — the latest user with the latest settings. A request stream and a response stream are the second kind. There, the third response belongs with the third request, and pairing them by recency would be wrong.
combine answers the first question. Its rule has two halves, and the first half is the one that produces production incidents.

items: Nothing is emitted until every source has emitted at least once. combine has no value to substitute for a source that has not produced one, and it does not invent one.
After that, an emission from any source produces a result built from that new value and the most recently seen value of every other source.

blocks.text: Read the first line again, because it is the diagnosis for one of the more baffling failures in this area: a screen that renders nothing at all, with no error, no crash, and every individual source working correctly when inspected on its own. If one of the combined sources has not yet produced its first value, the combined flow is silent. A source that queries an empty table and emits nothing, or a source waiting on a permission that was never granted, holds the entire screen. Measured on this project's JVM target, combining a working source with one that completes without ever emitting produced an empty result — not a partial one.

combine means "the current combination of these inputs". Its startup rule follows from that: there is no current combination until each input has a current value, so combine emits nothing until every source has emitted once.

zip answers the other question. It takes one unused value from each source and pairs them, so a value that has no partner yet waits, and a source that emits twice as fast as the other spends half its time waiting.

A3 never appears, and that is zip's documented completion contract rather than an accident: the resulting flow completes as soon as one of the flows completes, and cancel is called on the remaining flow. The pair ends when either side can no longer supply a partner. Measured on this project's JVM target with a four-value source zipped against a two-value one, the faster upstream produced three values and two pairs were emitted — one value was produced, found no partner, and was discarded when the zip completed.

Both halves of that are why zip is usually the wrong operator for screen state. Independent UI state sources emit at rates that have nothing to do with each other, so pairing them means the settings flow can only update the screen as often as the user flow does, and whichever source completes first silently ends the screen's updates. Neither behaviour is a defect in zip. They are the correct consequences of a contract the problem did not need.

The contract zip does need is correspondence. Pairing each element of a request stream with the response it produced, walking two ordered sequences together, or matching a stream of items against a stream of computed keys are all problems where recency would give the wrong answer and pairing gives the right one. Reach for zip when the sentence "this value goes with that value" is true about the data, not merely about the timing.

There is a third shape, and knowing it stops the other two being forced into problems that fit neither. merge takes several flows of the same type and interleaves their values into one flow without combining anything.

merge is the answer when the sources are alternative origins of the same kind of value rather than components of one result — several event sources feeding one handler, for example. It is a stable API in the configured version, unlike the flattening operators the next Lesson covers.

rows: What is the current state of all of these?
combine
One value per source emission, carrying the latest of every source, once all of them have emitted
Which value of this corresponds to which value of that?
zip
Pairs of unused values; completes when either source can no longer supply one
Where did this value come from? — irrelevant
merge
Every value from every source, interleaved in arrival order, unchanged

blocks.text: Reaching for zip because two flows must both be ready before the screen can render. That is combine's startup rule, which already waits for every source's first value — and then keeps updating from either side, which zip will not do. Wanting both sources present is not the same as wanting their emissions paired.

There is one precision about combine worth carrying into an interview, because a plausible over-reading of it produces wrong predictions. combine's contract is that it produces values from the most recently emitted value of each source. It is not a promise of exactly one output per upstream emission.

The implementation reads pending updates in batches and bails out of a batch as soon as it sees a second value from the same source, which means that when updates from different sources are already waiting, they can be folded into a single combined result. Measured on this project's JVM target, the same two-source timeline emitted three values when its emissions were two hundred milliseconds apart, and sometimes only two when they were compressed to a hundred — the intermediate combination was skipped rather than delayed. The documentation's own worked example, whose sources are ten and fifteen milliseconds apart, printed one fewer value here than the text beside it lists.

The right conclusion is not that the operator is unreliable. It is that combine is specified in terms of state rather than in terms of events, and that this is exactly the property that makes it correct for screen state and unsuitable for anything that must observe every change. If losing an intermediate combination would be a bug, the problem needed a different shape — a single source of ordered events, or the pairing zip provides.

This is also the point at which the current-value idea becomes interesting on its own. A source that always has a value, that a new collector can read immediately, and that therefore never causes combine's startup silence, is a different kind of stream from anything this unit has used. That is the subject of the hot streams and state unit later in this curriculum; everything here works with ordinary cold flows, and the reasoning transfers unchanged.

Name the two contracts before the two APIs: latest-of-each against matched pairs. Then be exact about the three behaviours that get asked. combine emits nothing until every source has emitted once. zip completes as soon as either source completes, cancelling the other. And zip throttles a fast source to the pace of a slow one, which is why it is usually wrong for independent UI state and right for genuine correspondence.

lessons.title: Flattening: Should New Input Cancel Old Work?
lessons.summary: When each value opens its own stream of results, the flattening operator decides what happens to the streams already running: finish them in order, run them together, or cancel the previous one. Ordering, overlap and cancellation of in-flight work are the three axes, and the third one has consequences the other two do not.

blocks.text: Some values are not transformed into other values; they are transformed into more work. A query becomes a stream of search results, a selected identifier becomes a stream of updates for that record, an upload request becomes a stream of progress reports. The mapping function returns a Flow, and so mapping produces a flow of flows.

blocks.code:
val queries: Flow<String> = searchField()

val nested: Flow<Flow<Result>> = queries.map { query ->
    repository.search(query)   // returns Flow<Result>
}

blocks.text: Nothing is wrong with that type; it is simply not what a collector wants. Flattening turns Flow<Flow<Result>> back into Flow<Result>, and the only interesting question is what happens to an inner flow that is still producing when the next upstream value arrives. Three answers exist, and they differ on exactly three axes: whether output order follows upstream order, whether inner flows may run at the same time, and whether starting the next one cancels the previous one.

rows: flatMapConcat
Yes — upstream order, exactly
No — one at a time
No — it runs to completion first
flatMapMerge
No — emissions interleave
Yes — up to a concurrency limit
No — every inner flow finishes
flatMapLatest
Only the surviving one
No
Yes — immediately

blocks.text: The decision is a question about the domain rather than about performance. Must every value's work complete? Then the answer is one of the first two. May the results of two values arrive interleaved? That separates the first from the second. And is work started for a superseded value still worth finishing? That is the third.

Flattening is not a way to make a chain faster. It is a statement about the lifetime relationship between the inner flows: sequential and ordered, concurrent and unordered, or superseding. Pick the one whose statement is true about the problem.
One timeline makes the three concrete. Two queries arrive fifty milliseconds apart; the first opens a slow inner flow and the second a fast one.

flatMapConcat collects one inner flow at a time and does not begin the next until the previous one has completed, so its output is upstream order exactly, and the fast second query waits behind the slow first one. That is frequently the correct contract rather than a cost: a sequence of edits applied to a document, or a set of requests that must reach a server in the order the user made them, needs precisely this and would be wrong with anything else. Sequential is not a synonym for inferior.

flatMapMerge collects several inner flows at once, so B's first result arrived before A's even though A started first. Two details are worth stating precisely. Its documentation notes that the transform function itself is still called sequentially — it is the resulting flows that are collected concurrently. And the number of inner flows collected at once is bounded by a concurrency parameter which defaults to DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY; read from this project's resolved kotlinx-coroutines-core 1.11.0 artifact, that value is 16, and on the JVM it is overridable through a system property. The bound is the point: an unbounded fan-out over a long upstream is a way to open more work than the process can carry.

Reach for flatMapMerge when the inner operations are genuinely independent and interleaved completion is acceptable — fanning out a list of identifiers into per-item requests, for instance. Note that concurrency here is the coroutine kind the second unit established, not a promise of parallel execution on separate cores; whether those inner flows ever run at the same instant is the dispatcher's business.

Both of the library's own documents for these two operators carry an unusual note: their usage is discouraged in regular application-specific flows, on the grounds that a suspending operation inside map is usually sufficient and linear transformations are easier to reason about. That is worth taking seriously as a design signal. If each value needs one asynchronous result rather than a stream of them, map with a suspending body is the simpler answer, and no flattening is required at all.

flatMapLatest cancels the inner flow started for the previous value and switches to the new one, which is why only B's results survived above. Search-as-you-type is its canonical use, and the reason is that a result set for a query the user has already replaced has no value to anyone.

blocks.code:
queries
    .debounce(300)
    .distinctUntilChanged()
    .flatMapLatest { query -> repository.search(query) }

blocks.text: Treating flatMapMerge as "the fast one" and flatMapConcat as "the slow one". They answer different questions. Merge is correct when interleaved results are acceptable; concat is correct when they are not. Choosing merge for ordered work produces results that arrive in an order the code below is not written to handle, and the failure is intermittent because it depends on which inner flow happens to finish first.

Everything flatMapLatest does to a superseded inner flow is ordinary coroutine cancellation, with no new mechanism and no additional guarantee. That has one consequence that decides whether the operator is safe for a given problem, and it is the consequence most often skipped.

Cancellation stops work from continuing. It does not undo work already performed. Measured on this project's JVM target, two queries flattened with flatMapLatest started two inner flows and completed one — but both inner flows had already executed their first statement before either was cancelled. If that first statement had sent a request, charged a card, or written a row, the cancellation would have arrived afterwards and changed nothing about it.

So the question to ask before choosing a latest-shaped operator is not whether newer input supersedes older input. It is whether the work started for the older input is safe to abandon halfway through.

items: Safe to abandon: computing suggestions, loading results for a query nobody is looking at any more, rendering a preview, transforming transient input. Nothing outside the process observed the partial work, so discarding it costs only the effort already spent.

Not safe without further design: submitting a payment, performing a durable write, incrementing a counter, or any request whose effect persists on a server. A cancelled attempt may have completed its externally visible half, and the caller will never learn that it did.

blocks.text: The honest framing is that latest semantics are appropriate when stale work is genuinely disposable, and that making an operation disposable — idempotency, cancellation tokens, transactional boundaries — is a design problem the operator does not solve. This is the same cooperative-cancellation model the cancellation Lesson established, applied to a flow: the inner flow stops at a suspension point it can observe, and whatever it did before that point stands.

One version-sensitive fact belongs in a complete answer. Checked against this project's resolved kotlinx-coroutines-core 1.11.0 artifact, flatMapConcat, flatMapMerge, flatMapLatest and their relatives transformLatest and mapLatest are all annotated @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi, at warning level. merge, by contrast, carries no opt-in annotation at all. The annotation is a statement about API stability — the semantics may change in some way in a future release — and not a statement about safety or fitness. These operators are the standard answers to the problems they solve, and using them means adding an @OptIn, not avoiding them.

Compare the three on the three axes rather than describing them one at a time: order, overlap, and what happens to work in flight. Then take the follow-up that separates a strong answer — what does flatMapLatest do to a request that has already been sent? It cancels the coroutine collecting it; it does not recall the request. That is why it fits search and does not, on its own, fit a submission.

lessons.title: When the Collector Cannot Keep Up
lessons.summary: A producer faster than its collector is a delivery-semantics problem before it is a performance problem. The default is that the producer waits. buffer, conflate and collectLatest each change that default in a different way, and each one decides what is allowed to be lost.

blocks.text: A producer that emits faster than its collector can process invites an immediate reach for buffer, and that is the wrong order. Establish what happens without any operator first, because the default is a deliberate design decision rather than an oversight, and it is frequently the behaviour the problem wants.
One example runs through the whole Lesson. The producer emits five values with a short pause between them; the collector takes three times as long on each one.

With no operator at all, the collector receives all five values, in order, and the whole thing takes as long as the slower of the two. Measured on this project's JVM target: values 1 through 5, in 2,676 milliseconds — the collector's five times three hundred milliseconds, not the producer's five times one hundred. The producer did not run ahead. It was suspended inside emit until the collector was ready for the next value.

That is backpressure, and the documentation states it as the default: the collector applies backpressure to the upstream flow, and the upstream suspends when the buffer is full. For a simple cold pipeline the producer's pace is therefore governed by the collector's. Nothing is lost, nothing is queued, and if the producer is reading a database or a network stream, it stops reading.

One qualification matters, and the previous unit already supplied it. It is not true that a Flow has no buffer. flowOn introduces one when it moves the upstream to a different dispatcher, channelFlow has one by construction, and the operators below add one on purpose. What is true is that an unbuffered pipeline coordinates the two paces, and that any statement about backpressure has to say which pipeline it is about.

The default is not "slow". The default is "nothing is lost and the producer runs at the collector's pace". Every operator in this Lesson buys speed or decoupling by giving something up, so the first question is what this pipeline is allowed to lose.
buffer gives the two ends room to run independently. It puts a channel between them, so the producer emits into the buffer and carries on rather than waiting for the collector to finish.

blocks.code:
producer.buffer().collect { value -> process(value); delay(300) }
// Measured on this project's JVM target: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in 1,870 ms

blocks.text: Every value still arrives, in order, and the total time falls because the producer's five hundred milliseconds now overlap the collector's fifteen hundred instead of adding to them. What has been bought with memory is decoupling; what has been given up is the guarantee that the producer is throttled. If the mismatch is permanent rather than a temporary burst, a buffer does not fix it — it fills, and once full its default overflow behaviour is to suspend the emitter again. An unbounded buffer removes the suspension and converts a rate mismatch into unbounded memory growth, which is a worse failure than a slow pipeline because it appears later and elsewhere.
conflate makes the opposite trade. Instead of retaining a backlog, it keeps only the most recent unconsumed value and discards the ones the collector never reached.

blocks.code:
producer.conflate().collect { value -> process(value); delay(300) }
// Measured on this project's JVM target: 1, 3, 5 in 1,101 ms

blocks.text: Values 2 and 4 were produced and never seen. The value being processed was not disturbed: the collector finished with 1 while 2 and 3 arrived, and when it was free it took 3, the latest, and 2 was gone. That is conflate's exact contract, and the documentation is explicit that it does not cancel processing that has already started. It is a shorthand for buffer with a drop-oldest overflow strategy and the smallest buffer that strategy needs, which is a precise way of saying: never suspend the emitter, and let a newer value replace a pending older one.
collectLatest changes something else entirely. It does not drop queued values; it cancels the processing of the current one.

Every value reached the collector block and every block but the last was cancelled part-way through by the arrival of the next value. Nothing was dropped upstream; what was abandoned is the downstream work. And because that abandonment is ordinary coroutine cancellation, the block must be cooperative for it to take effect at all — a collector block doing non-suspending work will finish it, exactly as the cancellation unit described.

rows: none
Every value, processed to completion
The producer runs at the collector's pace
buffer()
Every value, processed to completion
Memory for the backlog, and latency behind it
conflate()
1, 3, 5 — processed to completion
Values the collector never reached
collectLatest
All five started, only 5 finished
The partial work of every superseded value

blocks.text: Adding buffer() to a pipeline whose producer is permanently faster than its collector, and reading the improved timings as a fix. A buffer absorbs a burst; it cannot absorb a rate. The queue grows until it is full and the producer suspends again, only now with a backlog of stale values in front of the collector — so latency has been made worse in exchange for the throughput.

The comparison worth carrying out of this Lesson is conflate against collectLatest, because their timings are nearly identical and their semantics are opposites. One sentence separates them: should the work already in progress be allowed to finish?

If yes — the current value's processing is worth completing, but values queued behind it may be skipped — that is conflate. If no — a value becomes stale the moment a newer one exists, and continuing to process it is wasted or actively wrong — that is collectLatest. Whether unread values may be discarded is the second question, not the first, and answering it first is what makes the two operators look interchangeable.

The consequence is a safety one. collectLatest can cancel a collector block between any two suspension points, so its block must be written knowing that it may not reach its end. Rendering a preview, recomputing a layout or formatting a value for display are all fine: nothing outside the process observed the half-finished work. Performing a durable write is not, because the half that already happened stays happened — cancellation stops the next step and reverses nothing. If every value must be processed to completion, the operator is buffer or nothing at all, and if the rate genuinely cannot be sustained, the answer is upstream of Flow entirely.

Two smaller precisions round out a complete answer. Applying flowOn with a dispatcher change introduces a coroutine boundary between upstream and downstream, and the documentation notes that a channel with a default buffer size is used internally between them — so a chain that already contains flowOn is not unbuffered, and an explicit buffer call adjacent to it configures that same channel rather than adding a second one. And conflate applied to a stream that already conflates by construction does nothing; the state-holder types the hot streams unit introduces behave that way, which is why the operator has no effect on them.

Establish the default first — the collector backpressures the producer, and nothing is lost — because an answer that starts at buffer has skipped the design decision. Then give conflate and collectLatest as the two ways of losing something on purpose: conflate discards unread values and protects work in progress; collectLatest cancels work in progress and discards nothing upstream. Close on the consequence: a collector block under collectLatest may be cancelled part-way, so it must be safe to abandon.

lessons.title: `catch`, `retry` and `onCompletion`
lessons.summary: Flow failure handling is decided by position in the chain. catch sees what is declared above it and nothing below it; retry re-collects the upstream rather than re-running a line; and onCompletion observes success, failure and cancellation alike, which is why it is the wrong place for a success side effect.

blocks.text: Failure handling in a flow is not a question of which operator catches exceptions. It is a question of where in the chain the failing code sits relative to the operator that is supposed to see it. Get the position right and the API is obvious; get it wrong and a correct-looking catch never fires.
The rule is one line: catch observes failures produced by the part of the chain declared above it. Everything below it is out of scope, deliberately.

blocks.code:
source                       // \
    .map { transform(it) }   //  |  catch sees failures from here
    .catch { cause -> ... }  // <-'  the boundary
    .map { render(it) }      //     and not from here
    .collect { display(it) } //     nor here

blocks.text: So the arrangement that surprises people is this one, and it behaves exactly as the rule predicts.

The property behind that is called exception transparency, and the documentation states it directly: catch is transparent to exceptions that occur in downstream flow. Conceptually the operator wraps the upstream portion in a try/catch, and the collector is not part of the upstream portion. The restriction is a feature rather than a limitation — without it, an operator declared early in a chain could silently swallow a failure from code declared later, and no part of the chain could be reasoned about locally.
Read a flow chain top to bottom and put the failure handler below the code it is responsible for. "Does catch fire here?" is answered by looking at line order, not by looking at the exception type.
There are two fixes for a failure the collector produces, and choosing between them is a question about ownership rather than a matter of taste.

items: Handle it where it happens. If the failing operation belongs to the collector — writing to the screen, updating a widget, running an effect — wrap it in an ordinary try/catch inside the collect block. The stream is not involved in that failure and should not be made to carry it.

Move it upstream. If the failing operation is really a transformation of the value and only happens to be written inside collect, move it into an operator and put catch after it. Now it is part of the pipeline and the pipeline's failure handling applies.

blocks.text: What should not be done is relocating arbitrary collector work upstream merely so that catch can see it. That changes what the stream is responsible for in order to reach an operator, and it puts side effects in a chain that may later be retried.
catch's block can also emit, which turns a failure into data — the documentation shows exactly this, replacing a caught exception with a wrapper value.

blocks.code:
productFlow
    .catch { cause ->
        log(cause)
        emit(Products.Unavailable)   // the failure becomes a value
    }

blocks.text: Worth doing when the downstream genuinely has something to display for that case; worth being careful about, because it changes the contract. A collector that could previously distinguish "no products" from "could not load products" can no longer do so if both arrive as an empty list. Whether an expected failure is better modelled as a value in the stream than as an exception is a real design question, and the architecture curriculum owns it; the mechanism here is only that the operator permits it.

retry is a different operation from catch and the name invites the wrong mental model. It does not re-run the line that threw. It re-collects the upstream from the beginning, which for a cold flow means running the producer again.

Two things in that measurement are the whole lesson. The producer side effect happened three times, so retry is only appropriate where repeating the upstream operation is safe. And the values from the failed attempts were already delivered downstream — retrying does not un-emit them, so a collector that accumulates rather than replaces will see duplicates.

retryWhen is the conditional form, and its predicate receives both the cause and a zero-based attempt index. Measured on this project's JVM target, a flow that failed every time and stopped retrying at attempt 2 saw the indexes 0, 1 and 2. Because the predicate is a suspending function, a delay between attempts belongs inside it.

retry() with no argument. Its default retry count is Long.MAX_VALUE, which is an unbounded retry loop against a failure that may be permanent — a bad credential or a malformed request will never succeed, and the flow will keep asking. Bound the attempts and decide which causes are worth repeating at all.

onCompletion is the operator most often described wrongly, and the wrong description is "a finally block for a flow". Its own documentation is more careful: unlike catch, it reports exceptions that occur both upstream and downstream, and it observes exceptions thrown to cancel the flow. Its cause parameter is null if and only if the flow completed successfully.
Measured on this project's JVM target, across four endings of the same shape of pipeline:

rows: The flow completed normally
null
The producer threw
IllegalStateException — the upstream failure
The collect block threw
IllegalStateException — a downstream failure, which catch would not have seen
The collecting coroutine was cancelled
JobCancellationException

blocks.text: Which is why this is a defect rather than an idiom:

Three of the four endings above are not a successful sync, and all four run that line. The event fires when the server rejected the request and when the user navigated away mid-sync, and it will be believed by whoever reads the dashboard. The fix is the distinction the API is built around, and the documentation shows it: check the cause.

Cancellation deserves its own line here, because the third row invites a bad idea. Neither catch nor retry treats cancellation as a recoverable failure — both are documented as not catching or retrying on exceptions thrown to cancel the flow — and that is the coroutine model the cancellation Lesson established, unchanged. Cancellation is control flow, not an error to be absorbed, and an operator that swallowed it would break the structured guarantee that a cancelled scope actually stops. onCompletion may observe it; nothing here may consume it.
Finally, the argument the previous unit left half-finished. Context preservation and exception transparency are the same idea applied to two different things a flow carries.

blocks.code:
context transparency:
    an upstream operator cannot change the context the downstream runs in

exception transparency:
    an upstream operator cannot consume a failure the downstream produced

blocks.text: In both cases the property being protected is local readability: a reader of a chain can reason about a given line from the lines above it, without having to check whether something further up quietly redefined the rules. Treat that as a mental bridge between the two rather than a formal equivalence — the contracts are stated separately and neither implies the other — but it is the reason both restrictions look inconvenient in a small example and turn out to be what makes a long chain analysable.

Three answers worth having ready. Where does catch apply? To everything declared above it, so a throw inside collect escapes to the caller — and the two fixes are try/catch in the collector or moving the work into an operator above catch. What does retry do? Re-collects the upstream, re-running a cold producer's side effects, so it is only safe where repetition is. And what does onCompletion observe? Success, failure and cancellation alike, so completion is not success and a success side effect must test the cause for null.

units.title: StateFlow, SharedFlow and Hot Streams
units.summary: The previous two units settled cold Flow: production described once, run per collector, inside the collecting coroutine. This unit asks what changes when production exists independently of any one collector. Three questions get answered separately and are constantly confused with each other: where production lives, which is what hot and cold mean; what a subscriber can recover that was emitted before it arrived, which is retention and is configured; and when a shared upstream actually runs, which is a policy attached to the scope that owns it. StateFlow answers the first two by always holding one current value; SharedFlow answers them with a replay cache and a buffer you configure; stateIn and shareIn convert a cold upstream into either. The unit ends by choosing among a plain value, a suspending function, a cold Flow, a StateFlow, a SharedFlow and a Channel from the delivery guarantee the problem actually requires.

lessons.title: Hot and Cold: When Production Happens
lessons.summary: Hot and cold answer exactly one question: does production begin separately for each collector, or does the stream instance exist independently of any one of them? What a late subscriber then receives is a second, separate question, and when production starts and stops is a third.

blocks.text: Everything the previous two units taught was cold. A cold Flow is a description of how to produce values, and the description runs once per collector: the documentation calls it a recipe, and each collector cooks its own meal. Two collectors of the same cold Flow are two independent executions that happen to share a definition.

A hot stream inverts that relationship. The stream instance exists independently of any individual collector: it is there before anyone subscribes, it outlives them all leaving, and subscribing joins that one instance rather than creating a private copy of it. The StateFlow and SharedFlow documentation both use the same phrase, and it is the definition worth memorising: a flow is hot because its active instance exists independently of the presence of collectors.

Read that as a statement about the stream, not about whether anything is being produced into it right now. The two come apart, and the fourth lesson of this unit is where they do: a shared stream can exist with its production not yet started, and under some sharing policies the arrival of the first subscriber is exactly what starts it. Measured on this project's JVM target with a lazily started shared stream: before any subscriber the object was there and its current value readable, while the upstream had not run once; the first subscriber to arrive started it. So "a subscriber never starts anything" is not part of the definition. What is, is that production is not per-collector.

An active collector of a hot flow has its own name in this documentation. It is called a subscriber, and the word is a useful reminder that what it joins already exists as a stream — even when, as above, its arrival is what sets production going.

Everything else people say about hot streams is a claim about something else. "Hot" does not mean fast, eager, buffered, replaying, or immortal. It says where production lives. It says nothing about what has been kept for you, and nothing about whether production is running right now.

Cold means production begins separately for each collector. Hot means the stream instance exists independently of any one collector. That is the whole distinction, and it decides nothing else on its own.

Three questions get confused with each other constantly, and this unit keeps them apart on purpose. Production lifetime is this lesson. Retention — what a subscriber can obtain that was emitted before it arrived — belongs to StateFlow and SharedFlow, which are the next two lessons. Start and stop policy — when a shared upstream is actually collected — belongs to the sharing lesson after those.

rows: Does each collector get its own execution of the producer?
Production lifetime — hot or cold
This lesson
What can a subscriber obtain that was emitted before it subscribed?
Retention — a current value, a replay cache, or nothing
The StateFlow and SharedFlow lessons
When does the upstream of a shared stream actually run?
Start and stop policy
The sharing lesson

blocks.text: The reason the axes have to stay apart is that the interesting question — what does a late subscriber receive? — cannot be answered from hotness alone. Take a producer that emits four values over time and a subscriber that arrives between the second and the third.

blocks.code:
producer:    A----B----C----D
                    ^
                 subscribe

blocks.text: If the stream is cold, the question does not arise: the new collector starts its own execution and gets A, B, C and D from the beginning, because that is what its own execution produces. Nothing was missed, because nothing was shared.

If the stream is hot, the answer is genuinely "it depends", and what it depends on is retention. A hot stream that retains nothing delivers C and D and the subscriber never learns that A and B happened. A hot stream that retains one value hands over B immediately and then continues with C and D. A hot stream that retains two hands over A and B first. All three of those are hot; they differ in what was kept, not in where production lives.

The same split governs the other half of the question — what happens to a value emitted while nobody is subscribed. A cold Flow cannot be in that situation at all, because with no collector there is no production. A hot stream can be, and again the outcome is a retention decision rather than a hotness one. Measured on this project's JVM target against the configured coroutines version: a shared stream that keeps nothing produced six values before any subscriber existed, and the first value the subscriber saw was the seventh. The same stream configured to keep the last two handed over the two most recent and then continued live.

"A hot flow throws away anything emitted while nobody is listening" and "a hot flow replays what you missed" are both offered as definitions of hotness, and they contradict each other because neither is one. They are two different retention configurations of the same production model. Answer the question in two steps instead: is production per-collector, and separately, what was retained?

A third claim in the same family is that a hot producer keeps running whatever happens. That one is about the start-and-stop axis, and the sharing lesson shows a shared stream whose upstream stops the moment its last subscriber leaves — hot throughout, and not running.

Nothing about hotness is decided by the API's name either. A `callbackFlow` wraps a genuinely hot external source — a sensor, a listener, a socket — and the Flow it produces is still cold, because each collector registers its own callback and starts its own subscription. A cold repository Flow handed to `shareIn` becomes hot, because production moves out of the collector and into one shared coroutine. What changes in each case is where production lives, which is exactly the axis this lesson owns.

There is a sharper version of the retention argument, and the Compose curriculum already made it. The snapshot lesson observes that observable state is a lossy compression of the events that produced it: three edits that leave a field reading "abc" are indistinguishable, later, from one edit that typed it in full. That is why an observer of state can arrive late and still be completely correct, while an observer of events cannot.

Read the retention axis through that lens and it stops being a configuration table. A stream that retains one current value is representing state, and lateness is harmless by construction because the current value is the whole truth. A stream that retains nothing is representing occurrences, and lateness is loss, because what happened is not recoverable from what is. The configuration is downstream of what the stream is modelling.

This is also the honest answer to why the choice matters at all. If a stream carries state, an arriving observer needs the current value and nothing else, and conflation costs nothing. If it carries occurrences, every one may matter, and the delivery guarantee has to be stated rather than assumed. The last lesson in this unit turns that into a decision procedure across every abstraction the subject offers.

Answer "what is the difference between hot and cold?" with production lifetime, then volunteer the second axis before being asked: what a late subscriber receives is retention, which is configured separately. Candidates who give the one-line definition and stop are common; candidates who separate the axes and can say why "hot means it replays" is wrong are not.

lessons.title: `StateFlow`: One Current Value
lessons.summary: A StateFlow always has a current value, and everything else about it follows from that: the mandatory initial value, the replay of exactly one value, the equality comparison that decides whether an assignment is even observable, and the fact that it never completes.

blocks.text: The usual introduction to `StateFlow` is that it is for UI state. That is where it is most often used, but it is not its contract and it does not predict any of its behaviour. The contract is one sentence: there is always a current value. Every other property is a consequence.

Because there is always a current value, construction requires an initial one — there is no way to make a `StateFlow` that has not got a value yet. Because there is always a current value, it can be read synchronously through the `value` property without collecting anything. And because there is always a current value, a new collector receives it immediately rather than waiting for the next change.

The private mutable property with a read-only public one is API encapsulation rather than architecture: `MutableStateFlow` carries the setter, `StateFlow` does not, so exposing the narrower type is what stops callers writing to state they do not own. Where that state should live, and what shape it should take, is an architecture question this unit deliberately leaves alone.

The documentation states the retention rule precisely, and the precision matters: a state flow always has an initial value, replays one most recent value to new subscribers, and does not buffer any more values. One value, not a history. A `StateFlow` is not a queue of the changes that happened to it.

It also never completes. A call to `collect` on a state flow never returns normally, and there is no `close`. The documentation is explicit that a `StateFlow` can never represent a failure and that errors and completion signals must be materialised if they are needed — which in practice means a failed load is a value in your state type, not something done to the flow.

There is always a current value. Initial value mandatory, readable without collecting, replayed to every new subscriber, never completes, and never an error — all of it follows from that one sentence.

The behaviour that surprises people is what happens when you assign a value that is equal to the one already there. The documentation gives it a heading of its own — strong equality-based conflation — and states that values are conflated using `Any.equals`, suppressing emission when the new value is equal to the previously emitted one. Setting `value` to something equal to the previous value does nothing at all.

blocks.code:
val state = MutableStateFlow(User("Ada"))

state.value = User("Ada")   // data class: equal to the current value, nothing is emitted
state.value = User("Grace") // different: collectors are updated

blocks.text: Measured on this project's JVM target: a `MutableStateFlow` holding a `data class`, with a collector attached and three spaced assignments of an equal value, delivered exactly one value — the initial one, and nothing after it. The same experiment with a class that inherits identity equality delivered four: the initial value, plus one for each of the three assignments, because two distinct instances carrying the same field are not equal to each other. Same code, same assignments, different `equals`.

rows: `data class` with the field in the primary constructor
Compares equal to the current value
Nothing — the assignment is suppressed
Ordinary class with no `equals` override
Compares unequal, being a different instance
A new value every time
Class whose `equals` ignores a field that changed
Compares equal although the object differs
Nothing — the change is invisible

blocks.text: That third row is where real bugs live, and it is worth saying plainly: the equality semantics of the state type are part of the observable behaviour of the `StateFlow`. If two states that should look different to the user compare equal, the UI will not be told about the second one.

Mutable state inside the value makes the same failure worse, because there is no assignment for equality to suppress. Measured on this project's JVM target: an object held in a `MutableStateFlow` was mutated in place from 1 to 99, and then an equal instance was assigned. The collector received the value once, at subscription, and never again — while reading `value.count` afterwards returned 99. The state had changed twice and no collector was told either time.

Holding mutable objects in a `StateFlow` and expecting collectors to notice. Mutating in place emits nothing because nothing was assigned, and reassigning an equal instance emits nothing because conflation compares with `equals`. The documentation goes further and says behaviour with classes that violate the `Any.equals` contract is unspecified, so this is not a corner to be clever in — hold values whose equality means what you think it means.

The other half of what a collector sees is a speed question rather than an equality one, and the buffering lesson already established the model. Because updates are conflated, a slow collector skips fast updates but always collects the most recently emitted value. Measured on this project's JVM target, with the value assigned 1 through 10 at 20-millisecond intervals and a collector taking 200 milliseconds per value: the collector observed 0, 7 and 10. Seven intermediate states were never delivered, and the final state was.
