That is the property that makes `StateFlow` right for state and wrong for anything countable. Three "refresh finished" notices that arrive faster than the collector runs are not three notices; they may be one, and if two of them carried equal values they were already one before the collector's speed came into it.

Assigning to `value` is thread-safe, but a read-modify-write built out of it is not atomic — the read and the write are two operations, and another coroutine can assign in between. This is the shared-state problem from the cancellation and coordination unit, arriving in a place where it is easy to miss.

Measured on this project's JVM target: eight coroutines each performing 2,000 increments through `value = value + 1` produced 5,998 out of an expected 16,000. The same load through `update` produced exactly 16,000. `update` is a compare-and-set loop, which is why it works and also why its documentation warns that the function may be evaluated more than once if the value is being concurrently updated — so the lambda must compute a new value and do nothing else.

One further subtlety in the same family: `compareAndSet` compares with `equals`, and its documentation notes that when both the expected and the new value are equal to the current one it returns `true` without actually storing the new reference. An identity-sensitive caller cannot rely on the object it passed being the one that is now held.

Two smaller facts round out the model. Several operators are no-ops on a `StateFlow` — the documentation lists `flowOn`, `conflate`, `buffer` with conflated or rendezvous capacity, `distinctUntilChanged` and `cancellable` — because the type already provides what they would add. And a `StateFlow` is a specialised `SharedFlow`: the same document describes it as a high-performance implementation of shared flow for the narrow case of sharing state, which is the connection the next lesson picks up.

Finally, the honest boundary. `StateFlow` knows nothing about a UI, a lifecycle, or a ViewModel; it is a Kotlin Multiplatform type with no Android in it. How a Compose screen collects one safely, and how application state should be modelled and owned, are questions later material answers. This lesson's job is what a collector of one observes.

Be able to say why assigning an equal value produces no emission, and name `Any.equals` as the reason rather than saying "it deduplicates". Be able to say that a slow collector skips intermediate states but always ends on the latest. Be able to say why a state flow cannot fail, and where a failure goes instead.

lessons.title: `SharedFlow`: Replay, Buffering and Subscribers
lessons.summary: A SharedFlow broadcasts each value to every current subscriber, and its three configuration parameters decide the rest: what a late subscriber can recover, whether a slow subscriber makes the emitter wait, and what happens to a value emitted when nobody is subscribed at all.

blocks.text: `SharedFlow` is the general hot flow, and `StateFlow` is the special case of it that holds exactly one current value. The documentation defines it as a hot flow that shares emitted values among all its collectors in a broadcast fashion, so that all collectors get all emitted values. Broadcast is the word that matters, and what it fixes is **fan-out**: a value is offered to every subscriber rather than consumed by one of them at the others' expense. Whether a particular subscriber then actually receives every value is a second question, and the configuration below is what answers it.

Like `StateFlow` it never completes, and like `StateFlow` its active collectors are called subscribers. Unlike `StateFlow` it has no current value, no mandatory initial value, and no fixed retention — retention is something you configure.

Three parameters configure it, and they answer different questions. `replay` is how many of the most recent values a subscriber receives when it arrives. `extraBufferCapacity` is additional room beyond replay, so that an emitter is not held up by a subscriber that is behind. `onBufferOverflow` decides what happens when that room runs out: suspend the emitter, drop the oldest buffered value, or drop the value being emitted.

Replay and extra buffer are not the same knob, but the line between them is not the one usually drawn. `replay` does double duty: it is what a late subscriber recovers, **and** it counts as room for a subscriber that is present but behind. `extraBufferCapacity` reserves room that serves only the second purpose — it is never replayed. So the space a slow subscriber may lag by before the emitter has to wait is `replay + extraBufferCapacity`, while what a late subscriber can recover is `replay` alone.

headers: Room for a present slow subscriber
rows: `replay = 0, extraBufferCapacity = 0`
None — the emitter waits for every value
Nothing
`replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 0`
One value
One value
`replay = 0, extraBufferCapacity = 1`
One value
Nothing
`replay = 2, extraBufferCapacity = 3`
Five values
Two values

blocks.text: Both columns are measured on this project's JVM target. The left one counts how many values a present 400-millisecond subscriber could fall behind by before `tryEmit` began returning `false`, and it came out as `replay + extraBufferCapacity` in every configuration tried. The right one emitted six values with nobody subscribed and then subscribed: `replay = 0, extraBufferCapacity = 3` delivered nothing at all, which is the half of the rule that catches people out — extra capacity buys headroom for a subscriber that is there, and retains nothing for one that is not.

A value is fanned out to every current subscriber rather than consumed by one of them. `replay` decides what a subscriber who was not there can still recover; `extraBufferCapacity` and `onBufferOverflow` decide what happens when a present subscriber cannot keep up — and under a dropping strategy, that includes letting it miss values.
Start with what a subscriber that arrives late receives, because it is the question the configuration is usually chosen for and the one most often assumed rather than checked.

blocks.code:
emit(A)          subscribe        emit(B)
   |                 |               |
   v                 v               v
replay = 0:  A is gone            B delivered
replay = 1:  A delivered on subscribe, then B

blocks.text: With `replay = 0` the subscriber is not merely late to A; A is unrecoverable, because the replay cache is the only thing a later subscriber can see and there is none. This is the same fact seen from both ends: a value reaches whoever is subscribed at the moment it is emitted, plus whoever arrives while it is still in replay.

Now the emitter's side. A `MutableSharedFlow()` constructed with no arguments has neither replay nor extra buffer, and its `emit` suspends until all subscribers receive the emitted value. Measured on this project's JVM target with one subscriber taking 300 milliseconds per value: three emissions returned at roughly 109, 414 and 718 milliseconds from the start. The first handed straight over to a waiting subscriber; each later one waited for the subscriber to come back for the next value.

Configuring `onBufferOverflow` is how that waiting is avoided, and the cost is paid by whichever subscriber was behind. Measured on this project's JVM target with one subscriber taking 300 milliseconds per value and six values emitted 20 milliseconds apart: the default suspending strategy delivered all six, while the same flow with one slot of extra buffer and a drop-oldest strategy delivered 1 and 6. The subscriber was present throughout both runs. That is the qualification the broadcast rule needs — fan-out says the value is offered to everyone, not that everyone receives it.

The same unbuffered flow with nobody subscribed behaves completely differently, and this is the part that contradicts the folklore. The documentation says `emit` returns immediately if there are no subscribers, and the value is simply dropped when no replay cache was configured. Measured on this project's JVM target: a thousand emissions to an unbuffered `MutableSharedFlow` with no subscribers completed in about 1 millisecond and left an empty replay cache. Nothing suspended, nothing was queued, and every one of those values is gone.

"`SharedFlow` is for events" is a heuristic, not a delivery guarantee, and an unbuffered shared flow with `replay = 0` will silently discard an event emitted while nothing is collecting. That is a legitimate configuration — it is exactly right for "tell whoever is watching right now" — but it does not satisfy "this event must not be lost". Choose it because you have answered that question, not because the value is called an event.

The absence of subscribers changes buffering too, in a way worth stating because it looks like an exception. The documentation is explicit that buffer overflow can only happen when at least one subscriber is not ready for a new value; with no subscribers only the most recent `replay` values are stored, and the overflow strategy has no effect at all. Measured on this project's JVM target: ten emissions to a `replay = 2` flow with no subscribers left a replay cache of the last two.

`tryEmit` is the non-suspending variant, and its result is easy to over-read. It returns `false` only when the strategy is to suspend and there is a subscriber that cannot take the value; with no subscribers it returns `true`. Measured on this project's JVM target: `tryEmit` on an unbuffered flow with no subscribers returned `true` and the replay cache stayed empty — the value was accepted and immediately lost. With one slow subscriber attached, the same call returned `false`.

Reading `tryEmit(value) == true` as "someone received it". It means the flow accepted the value under its current configuration. On an unbuffered flow, `true` is precisely the case where there was nobody to give it to.
Put the two behaviours together and the design question stops being "state or event" and becomes a set of answerable questions about delivery.

rows: Must an observer arriving at any moment know the current truth?
`StateFlow` — no `SharedFlow` configuration gives a value that is always already there
Retention is optional
Should only observers present at emission receive the value?
`replay = 0`
Choose a replay size deliberately
Must a slow subscriber hold the emitter up?
Leave the default suspending strategy and size the buffer
Configure a dropping overflow strategy
Must the occurrence eventually be handled by somebody, even if nobody is subscribed when it happens?
No shared flow configuration guarantees this
`replay = 0` is honest and cheap, and a small replay window covers a short gap

blocks.text: The first row deserves as much care as the last, because `replay = 1` looks like it should do that job and does not. A freshly constructed `MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1)` has an empty replay cache until something is emitted into it, so a subscriber arriving before the first emission receives nothing and waits. Measured on this project's JVM target: it received nothing at all, and nothing again after a later `resetReplayCache()`, while a `MutableStateFlow` built alongside it handed over its initial value immediately. The mandatory initial value is what closes that gap, and the `StateFlow` documentation spells out the rest — a shared flow behaves like a state flow only when it is created with `replay = 1` and a drop-oldest strategy, seeded with `tryEmit(initialValue)`, and read through `distinctUntilChanged`. Three ingredients, of which `replay = 1` is one.

That last row is the one worth being able to defend in an interview. Replay retains values for a subscriber that arrives later, so a small replay window does cover a short gap — but it is retention, not delivery: nothing tracks whether anyone consumed the value, and nothing waits for someone to. If the requirement is that an occurrence must eventually be handled by somebody, no `SharedFlow` configuration expresses it, and the final lesson of this unit says what does.

The documentation's own event-bus example is a good illustration of choosing suspension deliberately: an unbuffered shared flow whose `emit` suspends until every subscriber has received the event, described as rendezvous delivery. That is a real guarantee about present subscribers, bought by letting the slowest of them backpressure the producer — which is the trade the buffering lesson framed for cold flows, appearing here with a hot stream's twist that no subscribers means no backpressure at all.

Two narrower APIs are worth knowing exist rather than studying. `subscriptionCount` is a `StateFlow<Int>` of the current number of subscribers, and it is the mechanism the sharing policies in the next lesson are built on. `resetReplayCache` clears retained values on a `MutableSharedFlow`. Neither carries a decision this unit needs.

State the broadcast rule, then distinguish replay from extra buffer capacity in one sentence each. Be able to say what an unbuffered `emit` does with subscribers and without them, and be able to say why `tryEmit` returning `true` is not evidence of delivery.

lessons.title: Sharing Cold Flows with `stateIn` and `shareIn`
lessons.summary: stateIn and shareIn do more than change a Flow's type. They move production of a cold upstream into a sharing coroutine owned by a scope you supply, and the SharingStarted policy — not the collectors — decides when that upstream actually runs.

blocks.text: A repository that exposes a cold Flow gives every collector its own execution. That is usually the right default, and occasionally it is expensive: two screens observing the same query run the query twice, and a flow that opens a connection opens two.

`shareIn` and `stateIn` change that. Each launches a single coroutine — the sharing coroutine — in a scope you pass in, and that one coroutine collects the upstream and fans out what it produces to the subscribers. What sharing removes is one collection **per collector**: however many subscribers are present, one upstream collection serves all of them. How many times that collection is started over the stream's lifetime is a separate question, and the policy below is what answers it — `WhileSubscribed` in particular stops and restarts it.

`stateIn` produces a hot `StateFlow`, so it needs an initial value and gives you the current-value contract from the state lesson. `shareIn` produces a hot `SharedFlow` with whatever replay you ask for, including none, and gives you the broadcast contract from the previous lesson. The difference between them is not the return type's name; it is whether the result is obliged to have a current value.

The change that actually matters is neither of those. It is that production has moved. The upstream is no longer run by whoever collects — it is run by a coroutine in the scope you supplied, which means the scope now decides how long that production can exist at all.

Sharing relocates a cold upstream's lifetime from the collector to a supplied scope. The scope bounds how long the shared production can live; the `SharingStarted` policy decides when, inside that bound, it actually runs.

Ownership is the first question, and the scope-ownership lesson answers it: a scope owns the coroutines launched in it, and cancelling the scope cancels them. Hand `stateIn` a screen-lifetime scope and the shared upstream cannot outlive that screen; hand it a process-lifetime scope and it can run for as long as the app does. Neither is wrong, but the choice is a lifetime decision made at the call site, not a detail of the operator.

The second question is what starts and stops the upstream inside that lifetime, and that is what `SharingStarted` answers. The three built-in policies are best learned as three different trades rather than three names.
Measured on this project's JVM target, using a cold source that counts how many times it is started and stopped, with one subscriber that arrives and later leaves:

rows: `Eagerly`
Upstream already started and producing
Keeps running; nothing stopped
Joins the run already in progress
`Lazily`
Not started
Keeps running; nothing stopped
Joins the run already in progress
`WhileSubscribed()`
Not started
Stopped immediately; retained value kept
Upstream is started again from the beginning
`WhileSubscribed(500)`
Not started
Still running for a further 500 ms, then stopped
Started again if the grace period expired

blocks.text: `Eagerly` starts sharing immediately and never stops. That costs work while nobody is observing, and it buys having the data ready when a subscriber does arrive. Note the consequence the `shareIn` documentation spells out: with `Eagerly`, values emitted beyond what `replay` retains are immediately discarded, so an eager stream with `replay = 0` produces into nothing until someone subscribes. Measured here: six values were produced before a subscriber joined, and the first value it saw was the seventh.

`Lazily` starts when the first subscriber appears and then never stops. The documentation notes what that buys: with `shareIn`'s default buffering, the first subscriber is guaranteed to get every emitted value, while later ones get only the replay. What it does not do is stop when subscribers leave — the symmetry its name suggests is not in the contract.
`WhileSubscribed` is the one with a decision in it. It starts on the first subscriber and stops after the last one leaves, with two independent delays, both defaulted.

blocks.code:
SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(
    stopTimeoutMillis = 0,                    // default: stop as soon as the last subscriber leaves
    replayExpirationMillis = Long.MAX_VALUE,  // default: keep the retained value forever
)

blocks.text: `stopTimeoutMillis` is a grace period after the last subscriber disappears, and nothing else. It is not a polling interval, not a refresh interval, and not a delay before a subscriber is served.

Reading `WhileSubscribed(5_000)` as "refresh every five seconds". It is "wait five seconds after the last subscriber goes away before stopping the upstream". Nothing in it delays a new subscriber or re-runs the upstream on a timer. What a subscriber has to show for joining at once is whatever was retained — the current value for `stateIn`, the replay cache for `shareIn`, and at `replay = 0` nothing at all, in which case it waits for the upstream exactly as it would have anyway.

The five-second figure is an application choice, not an API rule — the default is zero. It is common on Android because a configuration change destroys and recreates the collector within a few hundred milliseconds, and a grace period longer than that gap avoids tearing down and restarting an expensive query for a subscriber that is about to come straight back, while a real departure from the screen still stops the work. Pick the number from how long your gaps actually are and how expensive the restart actually is.

And `Eagerly` is not a mistake to be corrected on sight. This repository's own state holders use `stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, ...)`, and it is worth being precise about why, because the tempting reason is wrong. It is **not** that their scope lives as long as the process: the scope only sets the maximum lifetime, and `WhileSubscribed` on that same scope would still stop the upstream every time the subscriber count reached zero. The actual reason is what the upstream is — a derivation over shared history that several screens read — so keeping it running means the figures are already computed the first time a screen opens, and still current after a gap, instead of being re-derived on every entry. What that costs is the derivation running while nobody is looking, which is affordable here because the result is one small value. Ask what the upstream costs to keep running and what restarting it costs; the scope's lifetime is a different question.

`WhileSubscribed`'s two parameters are two clocks that start one after the other, and conflating them is the most common misreading of the policy. Stopping the upstream and clearing what was retained are separate decisions.

blocks.code:
subscriber count:
1 -------- 0 -------------------------------- 1
           |<--- stopTimeoutMillis --->|
upstream:
running ------- still running ------- stopped ------ restarted

upstream stopped
       |<--- replayExpirationMillis --->|
                                       retained value is reset

blocks.text: The default `replayExpirationMillis` is `Long.MAX_VALUE`, which the documentation glosses as keeping the replay cache forever and never resetting the buffer. So with a plain `WhileSubscribed()` the upstream stops immediately and the last value stays available indefinitely — measured here, the state still read its last upstream value long after the upstream had stopped. Give it a finite expiration and the reset happens on its own clock: measured with a 200-millisecond expiration, the value was still the last real one 150 milliseconds after the stop and had reverted to the `initialValue` 750 milliseconds after it. For `shareIn` the equivalent reset empties the replay cache.

That default is worth deciding about rather than inheriting, and it also disposes of a common assumption: stopping the upstream does not send a returning subscriber back to the initial value. Measured on this project's JVM target with a plain `WhileSubscribed()`, a subscriber returning after the upstream had stopped received the value retained from the previous run within a few milliseconds, and the restarted upstream's own first value only 250 milliseconds later. So a screen re-entered much later renders the figure from its previous visit until the restart produces a new one — right when that value is a cheap-to-confirm cache, wrong when a stale figure is misleading. That is `stateIn`, where there is always a value to retain: the same measurement against `shareIn(..., replay = 0)` gave the returning subscriber nothing for those 250 milliseconds, because retention is what fills the gap and at `replay = 0` there is none.

Upstream completion and failure both behave in ways that do not follow from the cold model. Normal completion of the upstream has no effect on subscribers: the sharing coroutine keeps running, the hot result does not complete, and the last value stays. Measured on this project's JVM target with an upstream that emitted once and finished, the collector was still active afterwards and the state still read that value. Failure is different — an exception in the upstream terminates the sharing coroutine without affecting subscribers, and is handled by the scope the sharing was launched in. If an upstream can fail recoverably, `catch` or `retry` belongs before the `shareIn` or `stateIn` call, where it can still see the failure.

Two smaller notes. There is a suspending `stateIn(scope)` overload with no initial value: it starts the upstream, suspends until the first value arrives, and throws `NoSuchElementException` if the upstream completes without emitting — useful when there is genuinely no sensible initial value, at the cost of a caller that has to wait. And the same operator-fusion rule from the state lesson applies to the result: applying `flowOn`, `conflate` or `distinctUntilChanged` to what `stateIn` returns has no effect.

Be able to say what owns the coroutine `shareIn` creates, and what that implies about lifetime. Be able to say what `WhileSubscribed(5_000)` delays and what it does not, that the figure is an application choice, and that replay expiration is a second, separate timer that defaults to never.

lessons.title: Choosing a Stream Abstraction by Delivery Guarantees
lessons.summary: A plain value, a suspending function, a cold Flow, a StateFlow, a SharedFlow and a Channel are not interchangeable styles. Each provides a different delivery guarantee, and the scenario decides which guarantee is required — not which type is fashionable.

blocks.text: This unit ends where the Flow half of this curriculum has been heading: given a problem, choose the abstraction and be able to name the property that decided it. The way to get there is not to memorise a table of types. It is to ask five questions in order, stopping at the first one that settles the choice.
The first is whether there is one value or a series of them over time. That question alone eliminates most of the candidates.

blocks.code:
fun currentConfig(): Config                 // one value, available now
suspend fun loadConfig(): Config            // one value, computed asynchronously
fun observeConfig(): Flow<Config>           // values over time

blocks.text: The second is whether each consumer should drive its own production. If two collectors should each perform the producer's work — each running the query, each opening its own subscription — a cold `Flow` is the answer, and no sharing is wanted. If they should observe one shared production, some hot or shared abstraction fits and the sharing lesson says how to get there from a cold source.

The third is whether there must always be a current value. Ask it as a question about observers: can a new observer arrive at any moment and still need to know the current truth immediately? If yes, current-value semantics are a requirement rather than a convenience, and `StateFlow` is the type that guarantees them.

The fourth is whether this is broadcast delivery — several active subscribers all receiving the same value. If it is, `SharedFlow` fits, and the follow-up questions are the ones the previous lesson listed: should late subscribers receive earlier values, how many, may values be dropped under load, should the emitter suspend for a slow subscriber, and what should happen when nobody is subscribed.
The fifth is whether each element is work for exactly one receiver. That is the question no Flow shape answers, and it is where the last candidate comes in.

One value or many; per-collector or shared production; is a current value obligatory; is delivery broadcast; is each element for exactly one receiver. The first question that a requirement answers decides the type.

A `Channel` has a delivery shape none of the Flow types offer. The documentation describes it as conceptually very similar to a `BlockingQueue`, with suspending `send` and `receive` instead of blocking ones, and it describes fan-out as several coroutines receiving from the same channel and distributing work between themselves. That is the property: a queued element is taken by one receiver, not broadcast to all of them.

This is why a `Channel` cannot be swapped for a `StateFlow` or a `SharedFlow` mechanically, and the difference is the **shape** of the delivery rather than how reliable it is. A shared flow offers the same value to all of its subscribers; a channel gives each element to one receiver, and the others never see it. A queue of outgoing commands worked through by a pool of workers is a channel problem, and expressing it as a shared flow would offer every command to every worker instead of dividing the queue between them.

What a channel does not provide deserves the same care, because it is the distinction this Lesson ends on. Receiving an element removes it, and nothing tracks what happens next. Measured on this project's JVM target with five queued elements and one worker: the worker took 1, 2 and 3 and finished 1 and 2 before being cancelled part-way through 3. A replacement receiver then drained 4 and 5 — and 3 was never redelivered and never finished by anyone. A channel decides which receiver gets an element, not that the work on it ever completes.

That is all this curriculum teaches about channels, and the boundary is deliberate. Pipelines, fan-in topologies, `produce`, `select` and the capacity taxonomy are a subject of their own, and none of them is needed to make this decision.

rows: A value that is simply available
A plain value or property
Nothing observes changes
One result, computed asynchronously
A suspending function
One value, and the caller waits for it
Repeated values, produced independently per consumer
Cold `Flow`
Production is per-collector
Repeated values, one production shared by several consumers
`shareIn` or `stateIn` over the cold source
Production moves to a supplied scope
A current value every observer needs, including late ones
`StateFlow`
There is always a current value
Values broadcast to whoever is subscribed, with chosen replay
`SharedFlow`
Each value is fanned out to current subscribers; what each one receives depends on the buffering configuration
Each element taken by exactly one receiver rather than by all of them
`Channel`
Queued delivery to a single receiver, not broadcast

blocks.text: The table is a summary of reasoning already done, not a substitute for it. It cannot tell you whether a value is state or an occurrence, whether a late observer needs history, or whether losing a value is acceptable — and those are the inputs. Every row is also about **delivery** and none of them is a guarantee of handling: no entry here promises that the work a value triggers ever finishes. Two rows can look equally plausible until the requirement is stated precisely enough to separate them, which is the actual work.

Worked briefly: current authentication state that any screen may start observing at any moment and must immediately know is a `StateFlow`, because arriving late must still be correct. A "sync finished" notice that only the screens currently open should react to is a `SharedFlow` with `replay = 0`, or a small replay window if a subscriber arriving a moment later should still hear it. A database query observed by two screens is a cold repository `Flow` shared with `stateIn`, because the query should run once and both screens need the current rows.

The slogan this unit set out to replace is "`StateFlow` for state, `SharedFlow` for events", and it is worth saying exactly what is wrong with it. The state half is close to right, because current-value semantics really are what state needs. The event half quietly promises a delivery guarantee that no `SharedFlow` provides.

Choosing `SharedFlow` for a one-off occurrence and assuming it will be delivered. A `replay = 0` shared flow with no subscriber accepts the value and drops it, as the previous lesson measured — though a replay window would have retained it for a subscriber arriving later, so retention across a gap is configurable. What no configuration provides is a guarantee that the occurrence is eventually **handled**: nothing records whether a subscriber consumed it, and nothing waits for one to appear. If that is the requirement, no setting meets it.

A `Channel` does not rescue it either, which is worth saying because single-receiver delivery sounds like the stronger guarantee: the measurement above lost an element to a receiver that was cancelled part-way through it. Take the requirement seriously and the honest options are outside this unit. Model the occurrence as durable state that is marked handled — the acknowledgement is what turns delivery into handling. Queue it somewhere that persists. Or accept the loss deliberately, having established that a missed notice is harmless. Each of those is an architectural answer, and the value of getting the stream semantics right first is that it tells you when you need one.

The Compose side of the same question — how a screen collects a stream safely, and how a one-off effect should be modelled and consumed in a UI — belongs to the effects and architecture material later in this path. Once the delivery guarantee is chosen, that material decides how a UI models and consumes it.

What this unit's five lessons contribute to the decision is worth recalling as one argument. Whether production is per-collector or shared is where the two families divide. What a late subscriber can recover is retention, configured independently. Where a shared upstream's lifetime lives, and what starts and stops it, is scope and policy. And from the earlier units: one value or a stream is the first question of all; whether every value or only the latest must be delivered is a delivery decision, not a performance tweak; and a scope owns the work it launches.

Given a scenario, name the deciding property before naming the type — "a late observer must know the current value, so this needs current-value semantics" rather than "use `StateFlow`". Be ready for the follow-up about one-off events, and answer that a shared flow with no subscribers drops the value, so a must-not-be-lost occurrence needs state, acknowledgement or a queue rather than a hot flow.

units.title: Architecture as Responsibilities and Boundaries
units.summary: Architecture is not the folder tree, the library list or the number of layers: it is the assignment of responsibility, ownership and dependency direction, and it only becomes visible when a requirement changes and something has to change with it. This unit builds the test every later architecture unit applies — what genuinely changes together, which way a dependency may point, when an abstraction is a real boundary rather than another file, and whether a layer earns what it costs — before any named component or layer stack exists to be argued about.

lessons.title: What Architecture Actually Decides
lessons.summary: Architecture is not the folder tree, the library list or the diagram in the README. It is the arrangement of responsibility, ownership, dependency direction, lifetime and change propagation — and the only way to see it is to name a requirement that changes and trace what has to change with it.

blocks.text: A product decision arrives on Monday. A borrowed item should no longer count as overdue the moment its due date passes, because the service now allows a three-day grace period. The rule itself is four lines of arithmetic. Before opening the editor, ask the question this whole subject is built on: which parts of the codebase should have to change for that requirement, and which should be able to ignore it completely?

That answer is not a matter of taste, and it was not decided on Monday. It was decided by arrangements made long before the requirement arrived, and those arrangements are what the word architecture actually refers to. Architecture is easiest to define by what it decides, and five decisions recur so often that almost every structural argument you will have is about one of them.

items: **Responsibility** — which component is answerable for a piece of behaviour: deciding, formatting, storing, coordinating. In front of code the question is *who owns this decision?*
**Ownership** — which component may change a value rather than merely read it. *Who is allowed to write this, and through what path?*
**Dependency direction** — which component is allowed to know that another exists. *Who may know about this, and who must be able to change without telling anyone?*
**Lifetime** — how long a responsibility and its data must exist, and what ends them. *How long does this need to live?*
**Change propagation** — which components a given requirement reaches and which it leaves alone. *What should have to change when this requirement changes?*

blocks.text: None of those five is visible in a directory listing. A codebase at rest is a set of files; the arrangement only becomes observable when something has to change, which is why the recurring device in this unit is a changing requirement rather than a diagram. It is also why two of the most common answers to "what is your architecture?" — a folder tree and a list of libraries — describe something real without describing the architecture. Both are examined in turn below, because getting them wrong is not a vocabulary slip: it leads engineers to believe they have made a decision when nothing has been decided.

Architecture is the set of decisions about responsibility, ownership, dependency direction, lifetime and change propagation. A folder tree or a dependency list can express those decisions, or hide the fact that nobody made them; neither creates them. To see the architecture of a codebase, name a plausible requirement change and trace what must change with it.

Two teams are handed the same feature — a list of borrowed items showing a due date, an overdue banner and a way to renew — and both ship the same five types with the same calls between them. They arrange the files differently.

blocks.code:
Team A                          Team B
loans/                          ui/
  LoanListScreen.kt               LoanListScreen.kt
  LoanRenderer.kt                 LoanRenderer.kt
  OverduePolicy.kt              domain/
  LoanStore.kt                    OverduePolicy.kt
  DueDateFormatter.kt           data/
                                  LoanStore.kt
                                util/
                                  DueDateFormatter.kt

blocks.text: Every dependency is identical. The screen asks the policy, the renderer calls the formatter, only the store writes, and nothing knows about the screen. The trees differ; the architecture does not, because the same components hold the same responsibilities and the same components know about each other. Moving a file between folders is a readability decision and a genuinely useful one — Team B's tree tells a newcomer where to look first — but it is not an architectural change, because no responsibility and no dependency moved. The same is true one level up: extracting `data/` into its own Gradle module changes how the code is built and what the compiler can enforce, and by itself still moves nothing. Build boundaries are the modularization curriculum's subject, and the last lesson in this unit says the one thing about them that belongs here.
Now the opposite case, which is far more common: names that claim a structure the code does not have.

This project has `ui`, `domain` and `data` packages and a three-layer diagram in its README. The screen names `LoanDatabase`, constructs `LoanStore` and compares the dates itself, so the UI depends on storage directly and the `domain` package is not on the path at all. Change the database and the screen changes. Change the overdue rule and you change a screen. The folder names describe an intention that nothing enforces; the import list describes the architecture, and only one of the two is true. Android's own recommendations state the same rule in stronger terms than a folder name can — components in the UI layer "don't interact directly with a data source" — but a rule in a document is not a boundary in a codebase either. Only the imports are.
The second category error swaps a library for an arrangement. Two versions of it turn up in interviews constantly.

rows: "We use Koin, so our architecture is dependency injection"
How objects are declared and resolved at run time, and where construction happens rather than being hard-coded
Which component owns which responsibility, who may depend on whom, and what each dependency costs. A module can wire a screen straight to a database as easily as to anything else
"We use Compose, so our architecture is MVVM"
How UI is described and updated from the current state, and that the UI is not a tree of widgets you mutate
Who owns that state, how long it lives, what may know about it, and where the rules that produce it run — the questions a pattern name is supposed to answer

blocks.text: The general form: a framework or library is a tool that can support architectural decisions, make some of them easy and make others awkward, but it does not make them. This is why the first property Clean Architecture claims for a system is that it is "independent of frameworks" — the architecture "does not depend on the existence of some library of feature laden software", which "allows you to use such frameworks as tools, rather than having to cram your system into their limited constraints". You do not have to adopt that architecture to take the point: whatever the library list says, somebody still decided who owns what.

Answering "what is your architecture?" with a stack — Compose, Koin, Room, Retrofit — describes the toolbox rather than the arrangement, and it is the most common weak answer to the question. A strong answer names what the main components are responsible for, says which way the dependencies point and why, and then gives one requirement that changed while you were there and what it touched.

If architecture is hard to see in a directory listing, what is it judged by? The most useful answer is the cost of change. Two codebases can have the same classes, the same call graph and class diagrams that a reviewer could not tell apart, and still differ completely in what a requirement costs — because a diagram shows which components exist and says nothing about where a decision is made.
Return the grace-period requirement to two such codebases.

rows: One policy answers the question; the renderer asks it, and storage keeps dates and nothing derived from them
One function and its tests
Screen, renderer, formatter, storage, and every test that does not concern the rule
The renderer compares dates while formatting, storage writes a precomputed `is_overdue` column, and a nightly job recomputes it
The renderer, the storage write path, a migration for the stored flag, the job, and every test that fixed a date near the boundary
Very little — and the three copies of the rule can now disagree with each other

blocks.text: That is the whole argument. Structure matters because of how it affects change, not because one shape is more elegant than another. It is worth noticing that the second codebase is not obviously bad: precomputing a flag is a reasonable performance decision, formatting and comparing a date in the same place is convenient, and the nightly job was somebody's bug fix. Each step had a local justification. Architecture is the part of those decisions nobody sees until a requirement arrives and asks three places to agree.

Resist turning this into a metric. Counting the files a requirement touches measures nothing on its own. Some changes are genuinely cross-cutting — adding a field the user must see, store and sync touches every component that handles it under any arrangement — and an arrangement that makes one requirement cheap usually makes a different one more expensive. What you are choosing is never "fewer changes" in general; it is *which* changes are cheap. That choice is only as good as your sense of which changes are actually coming, which is where the next lesson starts.

"Describe the architecture of your last app" is not a request for a folder tree or a library list. Name what the main components are responsible for, say which way the dependencies point and what each side would inherit if they pointed the other way, then take one requirement that actually changed while you were on the project and trace what it touched. That last part is what separates an answer about a diagram from an answer about a codebase.

lessons.title: Responsibility, Cohesion and What Changes Together
lessons.summary: A responsibility is a reason to change, not a description of what a class does. This lesson makes that usable: work out which behaviours in a component genuinely change for different reasons, which split creates a boundary, and which one only produces one concept spread over two files.

blocks.text: The previous lesson ended on a question it could not answer: which changes should be cheap? Answering it needs a way to say what a component is responsible for, and the most useful definition of a responsibility is not a description of what the code does. It is a statement about why the code would have to change.

That is the idea behind the principle you will hear named in interviews as SRP: "each software module should have one and only one reason to change". Stated that way it sounds like a rule about size, and it is not. The same author's more usable restatement gives the actual instruction — "Gather together the things that change for the same reasons. Separate those things that change for different reasons" — and adds the part that makes it concrete: "this principle is about people". A reason to change is somebody asking for something: a product decision about wording, a business rule owned by a different team, an infrastructure migration. It is not a technical category like "formatting" or "database work".

Two words describe the result and both are worth using precisely. **Cohesion** is how much the things inside a component belong to the same responsibility — how much of one thing it does. **Coupling** is how much one component must know about another, or must change when the other does. Neither is a number you compute, and treating them as metrics is how they stop being useful. They are questions you ask about a specific pair of plausible changes.

Which gives the operative question for the rest of this lesson, and a test you can apply to real code: **under which plausible requirement would these two behaviours have to change independently?** If you can name one, you have found a boundary. If you cannot name one, you have found two names for the same concept, and separating them will cost more than it returns.
Here is a small component from the borrowed-items feature. It is short, it has three public functions, and nothing about it looks careless.

Asking "how many things does this class do?" produces an argument, because the answer depends on how abstractly you describe it — it manages loans, or it does three things, or it does eight. Asking which requirement changes which part produces an answer.

headers: What should be able to ignore it
rows: Due dates are shown as "12 March" instead of "Due in 4 days", and translated
`dueLabel`, and anything else that turns a date into text
The overdue rule and the write path
An item counts as overdue only after a three-day grace period, and never on a weekend
`isOverdue`, and every other place that compares a due date with today
The wording of the label and the write path
Loans move from a local table to a store with a different write path
`renew`, and everything that names the database
The label and the overdue rule

blocks.text: Three requirements, three disjoint answers, and no reason any of them should wait for another. That is what "three responsibilities" means here, and notice how little the size of the class had to do with reaching it. What makes these three separable is that three different people can ask for three changes that do not overlap: a designer, whoever owns the lending rules, and whoever owns storage. Splitting them is then unremarkable — a formatter that turns a date into text, a policy that answers one question about a date, and a gateway that owns the write — and each piece can be read, changed and reasoned about without the other two.
The reverse mistake is easier to make, because it feels like progress. Here the same formatting responsibility has been split in two, for the reason usually given: classes should be small.

Nothing here is wrong and both classes are small. Now apply the test: name the requirement that changes one without the other. Every wording change, every new case, every plural rule and every locale touches both files in the same commit, because there is one reason to change and it reaches both. What the split produced is not two components; it is one concept spread over two files, plus a contract between them that has to be kept in sync and a hop to make while reading. "Classes should be small" is a heuristic about readability, and it is not the same claim as "these are two responsibilities".
The opposite failure is a container whose members share nothing except where they are stored.

blocks.code:
internal object Utils {
    fun formatDueDate(date: LocalDate, today: LocalDate): String =
        "Due in ${today.daysUntil(date)} days"

    fun isValidEmail(value: String): Boolean = value.matches(EmailPattern)

    fun toDatabaseTimestamp(date: LocalDate): Long =
        date.atStartOfDayIn(TimeZone.UTC).toEpochMilliseconds()

    fun shortTitle(title: String): String = title.take(40)
}

blocks.text: Four behaviours, four unrelated reasons to change, one name that half the codebase imports. Cohesion here is as low as it can be — nothing in `Utils` belongs with anything else in `Utils` — and the coupling it creates is real even though it feels harmless: every consumer now depends on a file that changes for reasons none of them cares about, and the storage format has arrived in a name the screen imports. The deeper cost is that a `Utils` file is where nobody has to decide who owns anything, which is exactly the decision this unit is about.

There is a sharper form of the same question, and the Compose curriculum already asked it at a smaller scale. `lesson_state_hoisting` decided where a value belongs by asking who reads it, who writes it and how long it must live, and the writer is the interesting half: the component allowed to change a value holds a responsibility that components merely reading it do not. That scales up unchanged. When two components can both write the same value, they share a responsibility whether or not anyone decided they should, and every requirement about that value reaches both of them.

"This class does three things, so it should be three classes" skips the only step that matters. Size is not the test and neither is the number of public functions. Name the requirement that would change one part and leave the others alone. If you cannot, the split adds a file, a contract and a navigation hop while leaving the concept exactly as coupled as it was.

"A class should have one responsibility" is unfalsifiable as usually stated, and it is worth being able to say why. Pick any class and you can describe it as one responsibility ("it handles loans") or as six, depending only on how abstractly you talk about it. The statement acquires meaning exactly when the possible reasons to change are named, which is why the original formulation is about people rather than about code shape: two stakeholders who can ask for changes independently are two reasons to change, and code serving both of them has two masters.

That makes a boundary a **prediction**, and it is more honest to treat it as one. When you separate the overdue policy from the formatter you are betting that those two requirements will arrive separately. Evidence beats imagination here: in the example the label wording and the lending rules have each changed twice this year, while the write path has not changed in two. A boundary drawn where change has actually happened is a far better bet than one drawn where change is merely imaginable — and everything is imaginable, which is how codebases acquire abstractions that nothing ever varied behind.

You will still be wrong sometimes, in both directions, and the two errors do not cost the same. A missing boundary announces itself when a change hurts, and repairing it is usually a mechanical extraction of code you now understand well. A boundary that was never needed is paid for on every read, by everyone, for as long as the code lives, and it is rarely removed because removing it looks like a regression. That asymmetry is the practical case for drawing fewer boundaries than you can imagine needing, and drawing them where the evidence already is.

The name for this idea is the single-responsibility principle, the S of SOLID, and recognising the acronym is worth something in an interview. This curriculum treats SOLID as vocabulary rather than as a structure to teach, because the principles that carry real reasoning for application architecture are better met where an engineer actually encounters them: designing an abstraction around what its consumer needs is the subject of the next two lessons, and inverting a dependency is taken up by the later unit on domain logic and dependency direction. Walking all five principles in order would be a tour of an acronym, not a way to decide anything.

Asked why you split a class, "separation of concerns" and "it was doing too much" are the weak answers. The strong one names two requirements: "the label wording changed three times last quarter and the lending rules are owned by another team, so those two had to stop sharing a file." Being able to name a case where you deliberately did *not* split — two functions that always change together — is worth just as much, because it shows the test is a test rather than a preference for more files.

lessons.title: Which Way May This Dependency Point?
lessons.summary: A dependency exists when one component names another, and which way it points is a decision with a price: the depending side inherits the other's reasons to change. Separating that from call direction and data flow is what makes the decision visible.

blocks.text: A dependency exists when one component names another. If `LoanRenderer` mentions `LoanStore` anywhere — a parameter type, a constructor call, a return type, an import — then `LoanRenderer` depends on `LoanStore`: it cannot be compiled, read or reasoned about without it. Nothing about that implies the reverse. `LoanStore` may know that renderers exist, or may know nothing about them at all, and choosing which is an architectural decision — usually made by whoever typed the import first.
Three different things are routinely collapsed into the phrase "which way does it point", and keeping them apart is most of this lesson.

rows: Source dependency
Which component names the other, and therefore cannot be compiled, understood or moved without it
The imports and the signatures
Call direction
Which component invokes the other while the program runs
The call stack
Data flow
Which way values actually travel
The arguments and return values, which frequently travel back along a call

blocks.text: They often coincide, which is why they are easy to merge into one idea, and the cases where they come apart are exactly the interesting ones. Only the first is the architectural decision: the source dependency is what decides which component can change without the other noticing.

The reason direction matters at all is the consequence: **a component that depends on another inherits some of that component's reasons to change.** Not all of them — a private implementation detail can change freely — but every part of the other component that this one names. So direction matters most exactly where the two sides differ in how often they change. A dependency from something that changes yearly to something that changes weekly imports that weekly change and pays for it forever.

You may already have heard the rule "dependencies point inward". It is a real rule, it belongs to a specific architecture with a specific justification, and the later unit on domain logic and dependency direction takes it seriously. On its own it is not usable, because "inward" presumes a set of concentric layers that the codebase in front of you may not have. The general form of the question fits any two components, and it is this lesson's title: which of these two should be allowed to know about the other, and what would the other direction cost?
The borrowed-items screen gets its data from a sync service. The shape the service sends is declared once and used everywhere, because doing anything else looked like pointless ceremony.

The saving is real. One type, no mapping code, and a field the service adds is available on the screen the moment it is deserialised. Then the service ships its next version: `due` becomes `dueAt` and carries a time zone, and `renewals` becomes a nested object because a renewal now has its own date. Both changes are legitimate and neither has anything to do with presentation. The renderer changes anyway. So does everything else that read a payload, and so do the tests that built one.

Direction is the whole diagnosis. The renderer names a type owned by the sync service, so it inherited the sync service's reasons to change; the rendering requirement did not change, the thing it was allowed to depend on did. The repair is in the same vocabulary: the renderer names a type the presentation side owns, and something on the sync side translates between the two. That translation is not free — it is an extra type, a mapping function and a place where a new field has to be added twice — and whether a given feature should pay for it is this unit's last lesson. What matters here is that the dependency had a direction, that the direction was chosen, and that it was chosen by default, which is how most architectural decisions get made.
A second case is quieter and more common. Two sides use dates, so a helper appears where both can reach it.

Ask which responsibility it serves and the answer is two: the functions change for different reasons and share only a parameter type. "Both sides use dates" is a shared vocabulary word, not a shared concept. Moving the file to `common` or `util` does not answer the ownership question, it makes the question unaskable — the storage key now lives in a package the presentation depends on, so a change to how dates are stored lands on a file everything imports.

The useful version is: does one stable concept exist that both callers genuinely need? Sometimes the answer is yes. A rule about which days count as business days is one concept, and both a renderer and a lending policy may legitimately depend on it; then you name the concept and let both depend on it deliberately. When the answer is no, the honest outcome is two small functions owned by two sides, which looks like duplication and is not. Duplicate code with one reason to change is a problem worth fixing; identical code with two different reasons to change is two things that happen to look alike today.
The third case is the one that shows call direction and dependency direction coming apart. The loader reports progress as batches arrive.

Trace the three directions separately. The **source dependency** points one way only: the screen names the loader, and the loader names nothing about screens. **Control** crosses in both directions — the screen calls `load`, and the loader then calls back into code the screen supplied. **Data** travels from the loader to the screen, against the source dependency. Replace the screen with something else entirely and the loader does not notice, because it never knew what was on the other end of `onBatch`.

This is the mechanism behind a claim worth being able to state precisely: the flow of control and the source-code dependency can point in different directions. Clean Architecture makes exactly that observation — "Note the flow of control … Note also the source code dependencies. Each one of them points inwards" — and then answers the harder question, which is who should *define* the abstraction so the arrow points where you intended even when the calls go the other way. That is dependency inversion, and this curriculum answers it in the unit on domain logic and dependency direction. All this lesson needs is the distinction: a callback moves control and data without moving the dependency.

"The screen calls the loader, so it depends on it; the loader calls back into the screen, so they depend on each other." The second half is where the reasoning goes wrong. A callback parameter is a function type: the loader names no screen, imports nothing from one and compiles without one. Cycles in the call graph are ordinary and mostly harmless. A cycle in the source dependencies is the thing that makes two components change together.

A dependency cycle is the most visible direction failure, and it is worth being precise about why it is bad, because the usual reason given is wrong. The compiler only complains when a cycle crosses a build module; inside one module a cycle is legal, and large codebases are full of them. The real cost is that two components with a cycle between them are one component for every purpose that matters: neither can be read, changed, moved or reused without the other, and every requirement that reaches one reaches both. The cycle is the symptom. The shared reason to change is the disease, and it usually arrives long before the cycle does.

Direction is therefore a bet on relative stability: depend in the direction of things that change less often than you do. "Stable" here means "changes rarely", not "important" or "low-level". A lending rule that has not changed in three years is more stable than the JSON a partner service ships every quarter, even though the JSON feels closer to the machine — which is why "the UI depends on the data layer" is a description of a common arrangement rather than a justification of it.

Being able to state what the reverse direction costs is the whole skill. For any pair, the answer has the same shape: the depending side inherits the other's reasons to change, and the price of not depending is the translation you now have to write and maintain at the boundary. In the payload example, refusing the dependency costs a presentation-owned type and a mapping function; accepting it costs a renderer that changes whenever a wire format does. Both are real costs. Which one is worth paying depends on how differently the two sides actually change, and that is the judgement the next two lessons sharpen.

One boundary note, deliberately short. A build module makes a direction enforceable rather than conventional: if the sync module does not depend on the UI module, nobody can add the import, whereas inside one module the same rule is a convention protected by code review. Where to draw build boundaries, and what they cost, is the build and modularization curriculum's subject. The claim this unit makes is only that the logical direction is the decision, and a module is one way to enforce it.

For any two components, be ready to answer in one breath: which one names the other, what does the depending side inherit, and what would reversing it cost? "The UI shouldn't know about the database" is a slogan until you can finish it — because the UI would then change whenever the schema does, for reasons that have nothing to do with what is on screen, and the price of avoiding that is a type and a mapping somebody has to maintain.

lessons.title: When an Interface Is a Boundary, and When It Is Only Indirection
lessons.summary: Adding an interface decouples nothing by itself. What makes an abstraction a boundary is that the contract belongs to its consumer and the two sides have genuinely different reasons to change — and when neither is true, the cost is concrete and permanent.

blocks.text: A team notices that `LoanListScreen` constructs `LoanStore` directly, agrees that the dependency points the wrong way, and fixes it: `LoanStore` becomes an interface, `FileLoanStore` implements it, and the screen takes the interface. Nothing else changes. Has anything been decoupled?

An interface is a language feature. A boundary is a property of an arrangement, and the test for it has nothing to do with the keyword: two components are decoupled when one can change without the other having to be edited. Whether that is true depends on three things the keyword does not decide — which side owns the contract, whether the two sides genuinely change for different reasons, and whether the contract describes what the consumer needs rather than what the implementation happens to do.

The third of those is where most single-implementation interfaces fail, and it has a crisp statement from Martin Fowler: "Interfaces should be designed around your clients' needs, often these don't match the implementation." The same page is equally direct about the cost of the common case — "Using interfaces when you aren't going to have multiple implementations is extra effort to keep everything in sync."

So the test to apply, before writing the keyword: name a change the implementation could absorb without the consumer being edited, and a change to the consumer's needs that would not dictate the implementation's shape. If both answers are "none", what you have is indirection — a second name for the same thing, moving in step with it — and the next section makes the price of that concrete.
Here is the interface that team extracted.

Read the contract and you can reconstruct the implementation from it: rows, one method per operation the file store happens to support, and a transaction pair that exists because the file store needs one. That is the signature of an interface extracted *from* an implementation rather than designed *for* a consumer, and the consequence shows up in the commit history. Adding a column adds a method to both files. Making writes suspend changes both. And every consumer now knows that storage has transactions, which is a storage detail that has just become part of the screen's vocabulary.

So ask the question directly: what did the interface buy? Architecturally, close to nothing — the screen still changes whenever the file store's shape changes, which is what coupling means. What it definitely bought is a list of costs, and they are worth naming concretely, because "abstractions add complexity" is the vaguest sentence in the subject.

items: Another name in the codebase, which every reader has to learn and keep distinct from the implementation's name.
Another file, and a navigation hop on the way to the code that actually does the work — paid on every read, by everyone, forever.
A contract that now has to be designed and kept in sync, so most changes touch two files instead of one.
A false signal to the next engineer, who will reasonably assume that a second implementation exists or is planned, and will design around a flexibility that is not there.

blocks.text: Now change the requirement so that a boundary has something to isolate. The product decides that loans are read from the device when it holds the learner's history and from an exported archive when it does not — two sources with different failure behaviour and different refresh rules — and that the screen must not know which one answered. Suddenly there is a decision to make, and the contract stops mirroring a file.

Three things changed, and the `interface` keyword was not one of them. The contract is written in the consumer's vocabulary — loans, a due window, an outcome — instead of the storage's rows and transactions. It is owned by the side that needs it, so it changes when the screen's requirements change and not when a file format does. And there is now a real difference in volatility: the archive's format, the on-device schema and the refresh rules can all move without the screen being edited. A second implementation is a *consequence* of that difference, not the cause of it, which is why counting implementations is a poor test.

The argument you will hear most often deserves a careful answer rather than a dismissal: "we need the interface so we can test it". It is true that a substitute is easier to supply through an abstraction, and easier substitution is a genuine benefit. It is also a consequence of a boundary rather than a reason to create one. If the contract is the file store's method list, the substitute you write is a fake file store, and the test proves that the consumer can drive a file store — which is what it could do before. The architectural question has not moved: is there a contract worth substituting? When the answer is yes, testing gets easier for free — which is the ordering Clean Architecture uses when it lists testability as a property that follows from the arrangement, business rules being testable "without the UI, Database, Web Server, or any other external element" precisely because nothing about them names one. What to fake, what to exercise for real and how to design the tests themselves belong to the testing curriculum, which is why this lesson deliberately shows no test.

"Adding an interface decouples the code." It does not. Two components are decoupled when one can change without the other being edited. An interface with one implementation, a contract extracted from that implementation, and both files changing in the same commit has moved the code into two files and left the coupling exactly where it was — while adding a name, a hop and a contract to keep in sync.

When there is one implementation, one change rate and no consumer-owned contract, the strongest option is often the one nobody proposes in review: do not add the abstraction yet. That is not an appeal to a slogan, and the trade is worth working out rather than asserting.

headers: Add it when the second responsibility appears
rows: When the cost is paid
Immediately, and then on every read for as long as the code lives
Once, as a mechanical extraction, at the moment it buys something
What the contract is designed from
One implementation, which is exactly the case where the guess mirrors it
Two real needs, which is the first moment you know what the contract should say
The risk
The abstraction is never varied behind, and is never removed because removing it looks like a regression
"Later" arrives with several consumers already coupled to the concrete type, making the extraction wider than it would have been

blocks.text: That second risk is real, and it is what decides the cases where adding the abstraction early is right. When the implementation genuinely does not exist yet — another team is writing it, or there will visibly be one per platform — the contract has to be agreed before either side can proceed. When the abstraction is published beyond the codebase, Fowler's own exception applies: a library's users "don't get that fast feedback", so a contract they depend on is worth designing up front. Neither exception is "we might need it later", which is an argument that can be made about anything.

This repository contains a useful example of the honest middle. `LessonStudyRepository` is an interface with exactly one implementation, `LocalLessonStudyRepository`, and counted alone that pair looks like the anti-pattern above. What makes it a boundary is the contract: it is written in the study feature's vocabulary — mark a Lesson studied, unmark it, ask whether one is studied, read the studied Lessons in a stated order — and it names no database type at all, so the entire storage mechanism can change without a consumer being edited. The point is not that this application is a model to copy; it is that the number of implementations was never the test, and the shape of the contract always was.

One question this lesson deliberately leaves open: *where* should the abstraction live, and which side should declare it, so the dependency arrow actually ends up pointing the way you intended? "The consumer owns the contract" appears here as a property to look for when judging an abstraction. Turning it into a technique — dependency inversion, what it costs in a layered application, and which module the interface belongs in — is the subject of the unit on domain logic and dependency direction. Keeping the two questions apart is deliberate: this one is *is this abstraction a boundary at all*, and that one is *how do I place it so the direction comes out right*.

"When would you not add an interface?" is a question that separates people who have a rule from people who have a test. Answer with the condition rather than the count: when the contract would just be the implementation's method list, when both would change in the same commit, and when no consumer needs to state its requirements independently of how they are met. Then say what would change your mind — a second source, a genuinely different change rate, an implementation somebody else is writing, or a contract several consumers must agree on.

lessons.title: Layers as One Answer, and What They Cost
lessons.summary: A layer is a group of responsibilities sharing one dependency rule — one possible answer to the boundary question rather than the definition of architecture. Every layer is a boundary and every boundary costs, so the only question worth asking about a proposed layer is what independent change it isolates and whether that is worth the mapping, forwarding and navigation it adds.

blocks.text: Only now is layering worth introducing, because a layer is an answer and the four previous lessons were the question. A **layer** is a group of components that share a level of responsibility and one dependency rule: everything in the presentation layer may know about the data layer, and nothing in the data layer may know about presentation. That is the whole definition, and its appeal is real — one rule covers many components, it can be stated in a sentence, and it can be checked without reading every file.

Two things follow, and the second is the one that usually gets left out. Layering is **one possible answer** to the boundary question, not the definition of architecture: an application can be well arranged with two layers, with boundaries that are not stacked at all, or with a strict stack that nobody respects. And **every layer is a boundary**, so every layer costs what a boundary costs. Each one therefore has to earn its existence separately.

Which disposes of the claim this lesson exists to correct. "More layers means better architecture" inverts the reasoning: it treats the boundary as the benefit, when the benefit is the independent change the boundary isolates. A layer that isolates no independent change has added a boundary's cost and none of a boundary's return — and the cost is not hypothetical, as the next section shows.

It is worth reading the official guidance carefully here, because it is more conditional than its reputation. Android's guide recommends designing each application with at least two layers, UI and data, and describes the domain layer as optional, recommended "in big apps" where business logic is reused across several consumers or one consumer has grown too complex. The recommendations page opens by saying to "treat the recommendations in the document as recommendations and not strict requirements" and to adapt them. The conditions are part of the advice; dropping them is how "add a domain layer when it earns its place" becomes "every app has three layers".
Start with the cost, stated as things rather than as the word "complexity". Introducing a layer between two existing ones typically adds:

items: a second representation of the same concept, and the mapping code that translates between them;
forwarding methods that exist only to pass a call through;
another name for something the codebase already had, and a vocabulary a new engineer must learn before reading one screen;
more files to open to follow one feature end to end, and more places a single change lands;
a contract that has to be agreed, documented and kept honest.

blocks.text: Here is that cost with nothing bought for it. A data layer has been introduced between the borrowed-items screen and its source, with a presentation model of its own.

Trace one requirement through it. The card should show how many renewals remain, so the service starts sending a renewal limit. `Loan` gains a field, `LoanSummary` gains the same field, `toSummary` gains a line, and the card reads it — four edits across three files, and the question to ask is what independent change the boundary absorbed. None. `LoanSummary` is `Loan` with a different name, and `LoanGateway` forwards. Every change to either side passes straight through, because the two sides have one reason to change between them. The layer is not isolating a difference; it is transcribing one.

Now let the two sides diverge for real reasons, which is what changes the verdict. Storage acquires sync bookkeeping — a row version, a soft-delete flag, a server id, and a due date kept as epoch milliseconds because that is what the sync protocol compares — while the card's needs move the other way, towards a due state that already accounts for the grace period and a renewals-remaining number derived from two fields.

blocks.code:
internal data class StoredLoan(
    val id: String,
    val serverId: String?,
    val title: String,
    val dueAtMillis: Long,
    val renewals: Int,
    val renewalLimit: Int,
    val rowVersion: Long,
    val deleted: Boolean,
)

internal data class LoanSummary(
    val id: String,
    val title: String,
    val due: DueState,          // Upcoming, DueToday or Overdue(days)
    val renewalsRemaining: Int,
)

blocks.text: The same two types and the same mapping function, and now the mapping is where a real difference is absorbed. A sync field added to `StoredLoan` does not reach the card at all. The grace period changes how `DueState` is computed and no storage code is edited. Soft deletion never becomes something a screen has to remember to filter. The boundary earns its cost because something genuinely different lives on each side of it — and note that nothing about the *number* of layers changed between the two versions. The same layer was worthless in one and valuable in the other, which is exactly why the count was never the thing to ask about.

headers: When the two shapes are the same
rows: What the boundary isolates
Nothing — every field is transcribed unchanged
Storage bookkeeping from display state, in both directions
What it costs
A type, a mapper, a forwarding class, a navigation hop
The same type, mapper and hop
What a new field costs
Two declarations and a mapping line, for no isolation
One declaration, on the side that owns it
Verdict
Indirection with a layer's price tag
A boundary that pays for itself

blocks.text: Testability deserves one careful paragraph here, because it is the argument most often used to justify a layer and it works in only one direction. A well-chosen boundary usually does make code easier to exercise on its own, and the reason is precise: fewer unrelated details cross the boundary, so less has to be constructed to run one side of it. In the second version the due-state rules can be exercised without a file, a schema or a sync protocol, because none of those appears in the types that cross. That is a consequence of the boundary being in the right place. It does not run backwards — adding a layer does not make code testable, and "so we can unit test it" is not by itself a reason for one. If the two sides still change together, you have added a boundary to test across rather than a smaller thing to test.

"We have four layers, so the architecture is good." A layer count says nothing on its own, and a layer that only forwards is worse than not having it: it costs exactly what a boundary costs, isolates nothing, and teaches everyone reading the codebase that boundaries here are a formality to pass through rather than a decision to respect. The question is never how many layers there are; it is what each one isolates and what it charges for that.

The confusion worth clearing last is between a layer and a module, because they answer different questions. A layer is a **logical** statement about responsibility and a dependency rule. A Gradle module is a **physical** build unit: a compilation boundary with its own dependency list, whose rules the compiler enforces and whose granularity affects build times. Aligning them buys enforcement — the rule stops being a convention that code review has to protect. They do not have to be aligned, and neither one implies the other.

This repository is a direct example. `LessonStudyRepository` sits beside the study feature that consumes it, `LocalLessonStudyRepository` sits under `data/local`, no Room type is visible above that package, and both compile in the same `:shared` module. The boundary is real, has a direction, and the module count is one. Android's own guidance points the same way when it says small apps may place data-layer types in "a `data` package or module", and the modularization guide is blunt about the other direction: "It doesn't always make sense to modularize your project", and every module "brings a certain amount of overhead in the form of increased build complexity and boilerplate code". So: not every layer needs a module, not every feature needs one, and more modules is not better architecture any more than more layers is. When and how to draw build boundaries is the build and modularization curriculum's subject, and this unit stops here.

One more claim to keep honest, because it is quoted far more often than it is read. The familiar concentric diagram is not a prescription of four layers; the article it comes from says so in as many words — "The circles are schematic. You may find that you need more than just these four. There's no rule that says you must always have just these four." What that article is actually about is the direction of source-code dependencies, which is a different claim from a layer count and one this curriculum takes up properly in the unit on domain logic and dependency direction.

The transfer, storage and display split used above is the clearest available example of mapping cost, and it is used here only as an example. Deciding which representations a real feature should have, where the translation belongs, and how failure crosses those boundaries is a design problem of its own, and the unit on data ownership owns it.

That closes the unit's argument. A requirement changes, and what should have to change with it is decided by arrangements made earlier; behaviours belong together when they change for the same reasons; a dependency direction decides which reasons to change a component inherits; an abstraction is a boundary only when the contract belongs to its consumer and the two sides genuinely differ; and a layer is a boundary applied wholesale, priced accordingly. What this unit has deliberately not done is name any of the components an Android application is actually built from. That starts next: the screen-level owner the Compose curriculum stopped at, the ownership of data behind it, and the question of whether another layer of domain logic earns its place — each of them judged by the test this unit just built.

"Why would you add this layer?" has a five-part answer, and "separation of concerns" is none of them: name the responsibility being isolated, name the independent change that motivates the boundary, say which way the dependency points, list what the boundary costs in types, mapping and navigation, and say why that trade is worth it for this requirement. The same five parts, with the last one negative, are how you justify *not* adding a layer — which is the answer interviewers hear least often and remember most.
